title: Property Left Behind
bodyText: Vermont has two separate tracks for a tenant's belongings. (1) Abandonment: a unit is abandoned only if a reasonable person would believe it is no longer a full-time residence, rent is not current, and you have made reasonable efforts to learn the tenant's intentions. You may throw out trash, but other property must be stored in a safe, dry, secured place, and you must mail written notice to the tenant's last known address that you will dispose of it after 60 days. If the tenant gives a reasonable written description and pays reasonable storage costs within 60 days, make it available immediately; otherwise it becomes yours. (2) No-notice disposal: if the tenant gave you actual notice of vacating, or moved out at the end of the rental agreement, you may dispose of property left behind without notice or liability. After an eviction, you may dispose of remaining property 15 days after the writ of possession is served or you are restored to possession, whichever is later (one day after restoration if the court stayed the writ). Never remove belongings or lock a tenant out outside these routes: denying access to the tenant's property except through judicial process is an illegal eviction.

title: Rent After a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: In Vermont, a tenant who abandons the unit stays liable for rent until the rental agreement expires. But if you rent the unit to someone else before then, the old agreement ends on the date the new tenancy begins, so you cannot collect rent from both tenants for the same period. A unit counts as abandoned only if a reasonable person would believe it is no longer occupied as a full-time residence, rent is not current, and you have made reasonable efforts to find out the tenant's intentions; document those efforts. Vermont's statutes do not state an express duty to re-rent (mitigate) after abandonment, and no case law was reviewed for this row. Courts in many states apply a mitigation duty as a matter of contract law, so the cautious course is to advertise and show the unit promptly at a reasonable rent and keep records, which also ends the departed tenant's liability once a new tenancy starts. A lease clause cannot waive the tenant's statutory protections.

title: Rent Payment Methods
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not list the rent payment methods you must accept, do not bar you from requiring a particular method such as an online portal, and contain no ban on card surcharges or payment-method fees that reaches rent. What the statutes do say is that rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed, so state the accepted methods, the due date and where to pay in the lease. Remember that in Vermont 'rent' includes all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement other than a security deposit, so any convenience or processing fee you charge is part of the rent bargain and should be disclosed in the lease. If rent is ever paid into court during an eviction, the court accepts only money order, certified check, cash or other guaranteed funds. Cautious course: offer at least one no-fee method, and if you charge a card fee, keep it to your actual cost and disclose it before signing.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Vermont's zoning law requires every town to allow one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) as a permitted use within or attached to a single-family home, except under flood hazard and fluvial erosion bylaws, and to review the home and ADU under the same controls as a home without one. From July 1, 2026, the statute no longer limits this to an owner-occupied lot, so a town cannot use the owner-occupancy condition to exclude a rented ADU. An ADU is a distinct unit, clearly subordinate to the house, with its own sleeping, cooking and sanitation facilities, on a property with enough wastewater capacity, and no larger than 30 percent of the house's habitable floor area or 900 square feet, whichever is greater. Towns may be less restrictive and may regulate short-term rentals separately from ordinary rentals. Once you rent the ADU, the building is a 'public building' under the state fire-safety law, and the ADU tenancy is covered by Vermont's landlord-tenant statute like any other.

title: How Legal Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText: Most Vermont landlord-tenant deadlines run from 'actual notice', which the statute defines as receipt of a written notice that is hand-delivered or mailed to the last known address. Mailing by first-class or certified mail creates a rebuttable presumption of receipt three days after mailing. Vermont's statutes contain no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text message or email, that counts as actual notice. Electronic notice is especially risky for termination: Vermont's electronic transactions law does not apply to any notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence, and where another law specifies a delivery method, that method still applies. Cautious course: deliver every termination, rent-increase and other statutory notice on paper, by hand or by first-class or certified mail, keep proof of mailing, and use email or text only as an extra courtesy copy. Count deadlines from the presumed receipt date, not the mailing date.

title: Foreclosure of the Rental Property
bodyText: If your lender starts a judicial foreclosure on the rental property, Vermont puts a duty on you: once you receive the foreclosure complaint, you must tell each tenant who signs a new rental agreement that the premises are subject to a pending foreclosure and that, if you cannot redeem, the tenant may have to vacate on 30 days' notice or any longer notice federal law requires. Failing to tell the tenant does not invalidate the foreclosure, but it exposes you to claims from a tenant who signed without knowing. The lender, not you, must name your existing tenants as defendants in the foreclosure and serve them a summons with a printed warning in at least 14-point type, and in a power-of-sale foreclosure the lender must mail a copy of the notice of sale to any tenant lawfully occupying the property at least 60 days before the sale. Keep your tenant list current so the lender's notices reach the right people, and disclose a pending foreclosure before signing any new lease.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: In Vermont, a building where people rent accommodations, overnight or longer, is a 'public building' under the state fire-safety law, and that includes a single-family house you rent out. By statute, a residential building in which people sleep, whether units are owned, leased or rented (other than a single-family owner-occupied house), must have one or more carbon monoxide detectors installed according to the manufacturer's requirements and is subject to the fire-prevention rules of the Division of Fire Safety. The detailed requirements are in the Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code, which applies to rented buildings. Its current edition, in effect since November 4, 2025, adopts national fire codes with Vermont changes. Under the Vermont changes, every smoke alarm must be photoelectric-only or UL 217 labeled, and must be wired to the building's electrical circuit with battery backup unless the Division of Fire Safety approves another method. In a rented one- or two-family house, smoke alarms must be hardwired (existing sleeping rooms excepted) and must also be in every sleeping room; sleeping rooms in buildings built before 1994 may instead use 10-year tamper-resistant lithium battery photoelectric or UL 217 alarms. In an existing apartment building, smoke alarms are required in common areas, on every level and in every sleeping room; wired alarms need a backup power source, and interconnection is required only in new construction. Carbon monoxide alarms are required outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms, on every occupied level including basements (not attics or crawl spaces), and inside any bedroom with a fuel-burning appliance. Newly installed carbon monoxide alarms must be wired with battery backup, though 10-year tamper-resistant alarms are allowed in existing sleeping rooms of units built before 1994. The national code text these changes amend, including who must test and replace alarms, was not reviewed here, so confirm the rules for your building with the Division of Fire Safety before each tenancy. The statute's own smoke-alarm installation rules (photoelectric or UL 217 alarms near bedrooms and on each level) apply to single-family homes being built or sold, not to rented buildings. Cautious course: install compliant smoke and CO alarms, test them at each turnover, and have tenants report any alarm that is missing or not working.

title: Alarm Tampering Charges
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not authorize, set or cap a lease fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and they contain no criminal or civil penalty aimed at tampering with an alarm inside a dwelling (the tampering crime covers public fire alarm apparatus). What does apply: a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, its fixtures or mechanical systems, or let anyone else do so, and if the tenant does, you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees and may treat it as grounds for termination on 30 days' notice. Any fee in the lease counts as 'rent' under Vermont's definition, and you may not take a flat charge out of a security deposit unless it reflects actual damage. Cautious course: have the lease require the tenant to pay your actual, reasonable cost to restore or replace a tampered alarm rather than a fixed penalty, and document the condition of each alarm at move-in. Detailed alarm duties are in the state Fire and Building Safety Code.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not specifically regulate setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or sharing nonpublic rent or occupancy data through a common pricing service. That does not make coordinated pricing safe. Vermont's Consumer Protection Act, which is also the state's antitrust law, declares unfair methods of competition in commerce unlawful, applies expressly to real estate transactions, and is construed in line with the Federal Trade Commission Act. Anyone injured by a violation of state antitrust law, including tenants who did not deal directly with you, can sue for damages or the consideration paid, reasonable attorney's fees, and exemplary damages up to three times the consideration or damages. Federal antitrust law applies as well. If you use revenue-management or pricing software, set your own rents, do not feed it competitors' nonpublic data or agree with other landlords to follow its recommendations, and keep records of how you decided each rent.

title: Alternate Housing During Repairs
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to provide a hotel room, another unit or relocation money when a unit becomes unlivable or must be vacated for repairs, whether or not the tenant asks. What applies instead: if a habitability problem that materially affects health and safety is not repaired within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice. One specific relocation rule exists: when residential rental property (other than an individually owned single-family home) is converted to condominiums or another ownership form, the declarant must pay a tenant who does not buy the actual documented relocation cost, up to $1,000, within 10 days after the tenant vacates, if rent is paid and the tenant left by the halfway point of the notice period. Cautious course: when repairs need the unit empty, agree in writing on temporary housing or a rent abatement for that period.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText: Your lease may require your written consent before a tenant alters the unit, but Vermont fair housing law limits that for tenants with disabilities. You must permit reasonable modifications of the existing premises that are necessary to give a person with a disability full enjoyment of the premises, at that person's expense; Vermont does not shift the cost to larger or subsidized landlords, and you are not required to modify the building yourself. If reasonable, you may require the tenant to agree to restore the premises to their prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, but you may not require an additional security deposit for that purpose. You must also make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services, including for public and common areas. These rental rules do not apply to a unit in a building with three or fewer units where you or an immediate family member live in one of them, though your advertising must still be nondiscriminatory. Remember too that other statutes give tenants specific installation rights, such as plug-in solar devices and, for protected victims, lock changes and security measures.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give a landlord no special right to enter a unit to check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. Entry follows the general rule: with the tenant's consent (which may not be unreasonably withheld); for inspections, repairs, agreed services or showings between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice; and without consent or notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to any person or to property. Vermont's boarding-animal abandonment procedure applies to animals placed with a veterinarian, kennel or stable, not to pets left in a rental, and abandoning an animal is a crime under the cruelty statute, which humane officers and police enforce. Cautious course: ask tenants for an emergency contact who can care for their animals, and if you suspect an animal is in distress and the tenant cannot be reached, call the local humane officer, animal control or police rather than entering on your own.

title: Excluding Appliances
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not presume that appliances left in a unit are supplied by you, and they do not list appliances a lease may not exclude. You may say in the lease which appliances you supply and maintain, and that any other item, such as a tenant-owned washer or a refrigerator left by a former occupant, is not yours to maintain. That exclusion cannot reach your habitability duties, which no lease can waive. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, every unit must have space to store, prepare and serve food in a sanitary manner, including a kitchen sink; heating able to keep habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms at 65°F; hot water to every sink, tub and shower; at least two duplex outlets and a light fixture in each kitchen; and clothes dryers vented to the outside. A rental agreement that tries to shift these code responsibilities to the tenant is not effective for code purposes. Cautious course: list supplied appliances by name and say who maintains anything not listed.

title: Listing Supplied Appliances
bodyText: Vermont does not require you to supply any particular appliance such as a stove or refrigerator; the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires space to store, prepare and serve food and a kitchen sink, plus working heat and hot water. But once your lease promises to provide and maintain an appliance, that promise has teeth. Vermont's repair-and-deduct statute lets a tenant fix a minor defect that you fail to repair within 30 days of notice, where the repair is needed to comply with the landlord-tenant statute or 'a material provision of the rental agreement', and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, up to one-half of one month's rent, after giving you actual notice of the cost. The remedy is not available if the tenant or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the problem through negligence or a deliberate act. So list only appliances you are prepared to keep working, respond to repair requests promptly, and keep records of when you were notified and when the repair was made.

title: Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: Since July 1, 2025, Vermont bars you and your agent from charging any individual an application fee to apply to rent a residential dwelling unit. There is no exception for the cost of a background or credit check, no cap to work within and no refund procedure, because no fee of any amount may be charged to apply; absorb screening costs or build them into your operating budget. (The ban does not cover applications for commercial or nonresidential property.) For a background or credit check, you must accept any one of these: an original or copy of any unexpired government-issued identification, an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, or a Social Security number. You may not require a Social Security number to complete a residential rental application, and you may not refuse an application because the applicant lacks one. Remember that applicants are also protected from discrimination based on citizenship and immigration status. Review any online application portal or screening vendor you use to be sure it does not collect a fee from applicants or force a Social Security number field.

title: Applying Tenant Payments
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not set the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment to rent, fees or other charges. The order still matters. Vermont defines 'rent' broadly as all consideration paid to or for your benefit under the rental agreement, except security deposits, so lease fees are part of the rent bargain. If you give a 14-day notice for nonpayment, the tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which payment is made, and accepting a partial payment does not waive your remedies. Once an eviction for nonpayment is filed, the tenant can still stop it by paying into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period plus interest and costs before the writ is executed, once in any 12 months. Applying payments to disputed fees first invites a fight over whether the tenant truly owed rent. Cautious course: apply payments to the oldest periodic rent first, then to other charges, and show the allocation on each receipt or ledger.

title: Asbestos Work in Rentals
bodyText: Vermont law does not require you to disclose asbestos to tenants or to give tenants advance notice of asbestos work. Vermont regulates the work itself. 'Asbestos abatement' means the repair, enclosure, removal, encapsulation or any other activity to evaluate or control any material containing more than one percent asbestos by weight. No person may perform asbestos abatement without certification and a permit from the Commissioner of Health; certification standards and procedures are set by Health Department rule, and any contractor performing abatement must notify the Commissioner 10 working days before starting. The Health Department's asbestos rules add more. Before any renovation or demolition of a rental building (any building other than an owner-occupied home), the owner must have an asbestos assessment done by a certified asbestos inspector, and no one may renovate or demolish without first getting the owner's confirmation that it was done. If asbestos-containing materials will be disturbed, they must be removed under the rules' work standards before the renovation or demolition starts. The Health Department must be notified 10 working days before any demolition, even if no asbestos is found. The exemption that lets homeowners do their own abatement covers only their own private residence, not a rental. Some lower-risk materials (vinyl asbestos flooring and mastics, and exterior asbestos roofing, siding, cement piping and transite board) are exempt from the certification and permit requirements if the rules' handling standards for them are followed. The rules require asbestos danger signs at the approaches to the work site, and occupants may ask the asbestos consultant for copies of the clearance results after a project. Your general duties still apply: you must keep the premises safe and fit for habitation and in compliance with health regulations, and without the tenant's consent you may enter for repairs only on at least 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. (or without notice if you reasonably believe there is imminent danger). Cautious course: before any renovation or demolition, have a certified asbestos inspector assess the building, hire a certified asbestos contractor for any removal, and tell tenants what work will occur and how they will be protected.

title: Assistance Animals
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law makes it unlawful to discriminate in renting a dwelling because a person relies on aids such as specially trained animals, and to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, including no-pet rules and common areas, when needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home. Vermont's statutes do not separately define emotional support animals, set documentation standards, ban assistance-animal fees, limit species, or make misrepresenting an assistance animal a crime; those questions follow the reasonable-accommodation standard and federal Fair Housing Act guidance. Practical rules: treat an assistance animal as an accommodation, not a pet; do not charge pet rent, pet fees or a pet deposit for it; if the disability or need is not apparent, ask only for reliable information showing the disability-related need; the tenant remains responsible for actual damage the animal causes. Small owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer units are exempt from these rental rules, but not from the advertising rule. Violations can bring damages, punitive damages and penalties.

title: Association Rules and Tenants
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring a lease of a condominium or other common interest community unit to disclose the association's obligations, budget or governing documents to the tenant. The resale certificate and documents a selling owner must furnish go only to a purchaser, and a 'purchaser' does not include someone acquiring a leasehold of less than 20 years. Your tenant is still bound in practice: if a tenant violates the declaration, bylaws or rules, the association may act against you and also directly against the tenant, including levying reasonable fines after notice and a chance to be heard, and, if the violation is not cured within 10 days after notice to both of you, enforcing rights you as landlord could have used under the lease. Associations may also restrict leasing, through the declaration or through rules reasonably designed to meet institutional mortgage lenders' requirements. Cautious course: confirm that leasing is allowed, attach the current declaration, bylaws and rules to the lease, and require the tenant to follow them.

title: Attorney Fee Rules
bodyText: In a Vermont eviction case, the court may award you reasonable attorney's fees along with possession, rent due, damages and costs only 'when a written rental agreement so provides', so an oral lease or a written lease without a fee term gives the court no basis under that statute, and even with one the award is discretionary. Separately, if a tenant violates the statutory duties not to create code violations, disturb other tenants or damage the premises, you are entitled by statute to damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Tenants have many statutory fee rights against you: for habitability violations, security deposit withholding that is willful, illegal evictions and retaliation. You may recover fees against a tenant's illegal-eviction suit only if the court finds it was not brought in good faith and was frivolous or intended for harassment. Vermont's statutes contain no rule making a one-way lease fee clause reciprocal, no percentage cap and no required bold notice, but a lease cannot cut off the tenant's statutory fee remedies. Include a written fee clause if you want fees in eviction cases.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal
bodyText: Vermont's consumer protection law limits automatic renewal of contracts between a consumer and a lessor that have an initial term of one year or longer and renew for a term longer than one month. Such a contract may not renew automatically unless: (1) the renewal terms are stated clearly and conspicuously, in plain, unambiguous language in bold-face type; (2) the tenant takes an affirmative action to opt in to the renewal, beyond signing the lease; and (3) you send written or electronic notice 30 to 60 days before the earliest of the renewal date, the termination date or the cancel-by date, stating when the lease ends, that it will renew unless the tenant cancels, and the length and terms of the renewal period. You must also give an easy way to cancel, such as an email or postal address, and allow online cancellation if the tenant signed online. A violation is an unfair and deceptive act. Rolling into month-to-month after a one-year lease is a renewal of one month or less and falls outside this rule. Your own no-cause termination notices for written leases are separate.

title: Balconies, Decks and Porches
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require periodic inspection of balconies, decks, porches or other exterior elevated elements on rental buildings, and set no inspection schedule, engineer certification or report to tenants or the town. The general duties still cover them. Your warranty of habitability requires you to deliver and maintain premises that are safe, clean and fit for habitation and that comply with building, housing and health regulations, and 'premises' includes the building, grounds and facilities held out for tenants' use. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires you to keep staircases and other structural elements in good repair, and the state Fire and Building Safety Code, an agency rule not reviewed here, may set guardrail and egress standards. Towns may also adopt housing codes covering the condition and repair of stairs and porches; check local rules. No lease clause can waive the habitability warranty. Cautious course: inspect exterior elevated structures at least yearly and at turnover, fix rot and loose railings promptly, and keep records.

title: Pests and Bed Bugs
bodyText: Vermont's Rental Housing Health and Safety Code divides pest and bed bug responsibilities. You must keep all common spaces free from infestation and pay for extermination there. You must also exterminate inside a unit when the infestation was caused by your failure to maintain the building, or when two or more units in the building are infested. In a rooming house, you handle all units and common spaces. The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant exclusively occupies free from infestation and is responsible for extermination only when the infestation results from the tenant's own failure to maintain the unit, and not where two or more units are infested. Extermination means removing harborage and food sources and treating by methods such as spraying, heat treatment or trapping. A lease term that shifts these code duties is not effective for code purposes. Vermont's statutes set no bed bug inspection or treatment deadlines; you may enter to inspect or treat on 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., and an infestation affecting health can trigger habitability remedies.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Vermont's statutes and its Rental Housing Health and Safety Code do not require you to disclose current or past bed bug infestations in the unit or in adjacent units before renting, and set no inspection or treatment timeline. Related rules still apply. The code bars you from letting any dwelling unit that does not comply with the code, and an infestation is a presence of pests or bed bugs that creates a health hazard; you must exterminate in common spaces, in any unit where your failure to maintain caused the infestation, and in every case where two or more units are infested. Your warranty of habitability requires safe, clean premises fit for habitation. Separately, Vermont's consumer protection law forbids unfair or deceptive acts in real estate transactions, so do not misstate a unit's pest history if asked. Cautious course: treat and clear any known infestation before re-renting, keep pest-control records, and answer prospective tenants' questions truthfully. Vermont's code applies to every rented dwelling, with no small-landlord or owner-occupied exemption.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: From July 1, 2026, a Vermont rental agreement may not contain a provision that prohibits a tenant from possessing cannabis or cannabis products within the rental premises, or from using cannabis or cannabis products within the dwelling unit. You may still prohibit the use of lighted cannabis or cannabis products intended for inhalation anywhere within the rental premises. That clearly covers smoking cannabis. It most likely covers vaping too, but the wording can also be read to cover only cannabis that is lit, and no court has decided the point, so a lease that bans vaping cannabis should say it does so only as far as Vermont law allows. A lease may not ban keeping cannabis on the property or consuming edibles, tinctures or topicals inside the unit. The rule does not apply where federal law requires the rental agreement to prohibit cannabis possession or use, as in some federally assisted housing. Adults 21 and older may grow up to two mature and four immature plants per dwelling unit, only on property they lawfully possess or with the written consent of the person in lawful possession, screened from public view with access limited; whether a lease may ban home growing is not settled by the statute. Vermont's statutes give medical-cannabis patients no separate housing protection. Review existing leases and house rules for blanket cannabis bans.

title: Fire and Casualty Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no fire-or-casualty provision for residential leases: no automatic rent abatement, no statutory right for either side to end the lease, no rebuilding duty and no notice period. Your habitability duties fill the gap. You warrant that the premises will be safe, clean and fit for habitation for the whole tenancy, and that warranty cannot be waived. If a casualty leaves the unit noncompliant in a way that materially affects health and safety and you do not repair within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice, unless the tenant or someone there with the tenant's consent caused the damage negligently or deliberately, in which case the tenant is also liable to you for the damage. Because the statutes leave termination to contract, a lease clause saying either party may end the lease if the unit becomes uninhabitable, with rent abated from the casualty date, is the cleanest approach. The state fire-safety Commissioner may also order premises that fail fire-safety standards repaired, closed or, if dangerous, demolished.

title: Certificate of Occupancy
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to give a tenant a certificate of occupancy or attach one to the lease. The certificate still matters before you rent. In a town whose zoning bylaws so provide, it is unlawful to use or occupy, or permit the use or occupancy of, any structure created, converted, altered or enlarged after the bylaws took effect until the town's administrative officer issues a certificate of occupancy stating that the use conforms to the bylaws, and the residential building energy standards certificate is a condition of issuing it. Rental buildings are also 'public buildings' under the state fire-safety law, and the Commissioner of Public Safety's rules may require a final occupancy permit for new construction or changes of use. If you create a new unit, convert space or change a building's use, confirm the town and state permits before a tenant moves in. You may not let a unit that does not comply with the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code.

title: Children as Occupants
bodyText: Vermont does not require a lease to address occupancy by children, list children as occupants, or include any statement about them. But Vermont's fair housing law makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, to set different terms, conditions or privileges, to harass, to advertise any preference or limitation, or to misrepresent availability because a person intends to occupy a dwelling with one or more minor children. Occupancy limits are allowed where the unit is inadequate under applicable occupancy laws and ordinances to house everyone who intends to live there, so base any limit on those laws, not on whether occupants are children. You may refuse to rent to a person because that person is under the age of majority, meaning you may require an adult to sign. Housing for older persons that meets the statutory conditions (62-and-over, or 55-and-over with the required facilities, occupancy and policies) is exempt from the children rule. A building with three or fewer units where you or an immediate family member live is exempt from the rental rules, but not from the advertising rule. Violations can bring damages, punitive damages and fines up to $10,000.

title: Cold-Weather Absences
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit vacant during cold weather. If you want that notice, for example so you can check that pipes do not freeze, put it in the lease; the library's extended absence notice clause can serve this purpose. Keep it practical: ask for notice of long absences and for heat to be left at a safe level, rather than penalties. Your own duties matter more. You must provide heating facilities capable of safely providing a reasonable amount of heat, and if heat is part of the rental agreement you must supply a reasonable amount at all times. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires heat to be available whenever the outdoor temperature is below 55°F and able to keep habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms at 65°F; an owner who provides heat must maintain it at those levels. You may enter during an absence only with consent, on 48 hours' notice for a listed purpose, or without notice if you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or to property, such as freezing pipes.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not regulate collection fees on unpaid rent: they neither authorize a collection fee nor bar one, and no Vermont statute requires the lease to authorize it first. Related rules limit what you can recover. In Vermont, anything payable to you under the rental agreement other than a security deposit is 'rent', so a collection fee must be in the lease to be owed at all. You may keep a security deposit only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay to you or a utility, and removing abandoned articles, and you must itemize within 14 days. In an eviction, the court may award attorney's fees only if a written rental agreement so provides. Collection agencies are also subject to federal debt collection law and to any Vermont Attorney General consumer protection rules, which were not reviewed here, and unfair or deceptive collection practices violate the Consumer Protection Act. Cautious course: state any collection cost in the lease as your actual, reasonable cost, and tell the agency what the lease allows.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: Under Vermont's Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, all building entrances, and all common areas in buildings with two or more dwelling units and in rooming houses, must be adequately lighted for safe and reasonable use and safe access and egress, and all electrical systems must be kept in safe working condition. That is your duty as owner, and a rental agreement that purports to shift code responsibilities to a tenant is not effective for purposes of the code. Vermont's statutes and the code do not say whether common-area lights wired to a tenant's electric meter may be billed to that tenant. Because the code puts lighting on you, and an unpaid tenant account could leave hallways dark, the cautious course is to put common-area lighting and other shared loads on a house meter in your name. If a shared load is on a tenant's meter, disclose it before signing and give a written rent reduction that roughly matches the cost. Shutting off required utilities is barred except for temporary repairs or emergencies.

title: Common Areas
bodyText: In Vermont, the 'premises' you rent include the building and the grounds, areas and facilities held out for tenants' general use or promised to the tenant, so your habitability warranty and the tenant's duties reach common areas too. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code you must keep common areas clean and free of trash, recyclables and food scraps, keep common spaces free from infestation, light building entrances and common areas in buildings of two or more units, and ventilate common hallways and stairways; these duties cannot be shifted to tenants by lease for code purposes. Tenants must not disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment and must make their guests behave, and must not damage any part of the premises. Your lease rules for common areas, such as storage limits and furniture restrictions, are contract terms. Vermont has no statute giving tenants a right to waterbeds, and its clothesline and solar-device protections run against town bylaws and deed covenants, not against leases; the separate plug-in solar statute does give tenants a notice-based installation right.

title: Rent After a Closure Order
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not, in general terms, bar you from collecting rent once a building has been condemned, placarded or ordered closed. Several rules reach a similar result. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code forbids letting any dwelling unit that does not comply with the code, and the state fire-safety Commissioner may order noncompliant premises repaired and, if not repaired in time or if a violation is imminently hazardous, closed until corrected; such orders are served on owners and tenants with a recorded interest. After a complaint inspection, the Division of Fire Safety's report tells you that you may not rent the affected unit to a new tenant until the violation is corrected, and missed deadlines can bring penalties up to $1,000 per violation. If a habitability violation that materially affects health and safety is not fixed within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, recover damages and attorney's fees, or end the tenancy on reasonable notice. Serving a termination notice (other than for nonpayment) within 90 days after a government notice of noncompliance creates a presumption of retaliation. Cautious course: do not charge rent for any period a unit is under a closure order or cannot lawfully be occupied, and refund prepaid rent for that period.

title: Move-In Condition Records
bodyText: Vermont does not require a move-in or move-out condition checklist, a joint inspection, or any notice to the tenant about one. Doing one anyway is strongly advised. You may keep part of a security deposit for damage only if it is not normal wear and tear or the result of actions or events beyond the tenant's control, and Vermont defines normal wear and tear as deterioration from the intended reasonable use, without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests. You must return the deposit with a written statement itemizing any deductions within 14 days (60 days for a seasonal rental that is not a primary residence), by hand delivery or mail to the tenant's last known address. Missing the deadline forfeits your right to withhold anything, and a willful failure costs double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. A dated move-in report with photos, signed by the tenant if possible, is your best evidence of what changed. You may inspect during the tenancy on 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M.

title: Confession of Judgment Clauses
bodyText: Do not put a confession-of-judgment or similar clause in a Vermont residential lease. Vermont's Consumer Protection Act makes void, as to any party, any agreement of a consumer in a contract that a power of attorney is given to confess judgment, or an assignment of wages, or any agreement of similar effect, and a 'consumer' includes a person who leases or contracts for real estate for household use. Vermont's landlord-tenant statute also voids any rental agreement provision that circumvents the tenant's statutory obligations and remedies, and you may recover possession only through the court ejectment process: denying a tenant access to the unit or the tenant's belongings except through proper judicial process is an illegal eviction, for which the tenant can recover damages and attorney's fees. In an ejectment case, the complaint must attach the rental agreement and any termination notice, and either side may demand a jury. A debtor may still voluntarily confess a debt before a judge after a dispute arises, but a lease cannot authorize it in advance.

title: Habitability Rules Vermont Does Not Have
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Vermont statutory counterpart, while one common gap is filled. (1) No air-conditioning or cooling duty: Vermont's heat rules require heating facilities able to keep habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms at 65°F when it is below 55°F outside, but nothing requires cooling. (2) Unlike some states, Vermont does let a tenant withhold rent on the tenant's own when a habitability violation materially affecting health and safety goes unrepaired for a reasonable time after actual notice; separately, you may ask the court to order rent paid into court during an eviction. (3) No general repair deadline: the standard is a reasonable time, except that repair-and-deduct opens if a minor defect is not fixed within 30 days of notice. (4) No duty to provide substitute housing during repairs, apart from relocation costs in condominium conversions. (5) No statutory right for you to end a tenancy because repairs cost too much; termination follows the notice rules. Vermont's statutes, 2025-2026 acts, constitution and Rental Housing Health and Safety Code were searched; case law and local ordinances were not, and town housing codes may add duties.

title: Other Rules Vermont Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states do not exist in Vermont's statutes. (1) No statute bars renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date; the lease and contract law apply. (2) No statute makes smoke or carbon monoxide alarm compliance inadmissible or limits what an insurer may do. (3) No statute gives you a special right to end a tenancy because the rental application was false; a material misstatement can support a 30-day breach notice only if the lease makes accuracy a material term. Applicants may lawfully decline to disclose expunged or sealed criminal records, because in an application for a civil right or privilege a person may be asked only about records that have not been expunged or sealed. (4) No Vermont rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs. (5) No general lease type-size, initialing or translation rule, though specific provisions have their own formats, such as bold-face type for automatic renewal terms. Vermont's statutes, 2025-2026 acts, constitution and Rental Housing Health and Safety Code were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Whole-Code Checks
bodyText: Vermont's statutes, 2025-2026 acts, constitution and Rental Housing Health and Safety Code were searched, not only the landlord-tenant chapter, for three things landlords ask about. (1) Unauthorized occupants: Vermont does have a faster route. If your written rental agreement prohibits subleasing, you or the tenant may bring an ejectment action against a person occupying the unit without right or permission and move for an expedited hearing on 10 days' notice; if the court rules for you, the sheriff may put you in possession not sooner than five days after serving the writ. Occupants without right are outside the landlord-tenant chapter. (2) No statute requires a written receipt for rent paid in cash, though giving one is wise. (3) No state statute makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of a possession judgment, but general business registration can be. If you rent as an individual under an assumed business name, or as a partnership, you must register with the Secretary of State within 10 days after starting, and an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here needs a certificate of authority. Until it registers, the business may not maintain an action or proceeding, or even raise a counterclaim or affirmative defense, in a Vermont court, and the State may collect $50 a day, up to $10,000 a year (11 V.S.A. §§ 1621, 1626 and 4119; 11A V.S.A. § 15.02). Owning property is not by itself transacting business for an entity, but renting it out may be; that is a case-law question (11 V.S.A. § 4113(c)(9); 11A V.S.A. § 15.01(c)(10)). Separately, every owner of rental property must file a landlord certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes by January 31 each year, listing renters, units and contact information; a knowing failure carries a $200 penalty for each failure. Some towns run their own registration or inspection programs, so check local rules.

title: Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: Vermont's mechanic's lien statute gives a person who contracts, in writing or not, to erect, repair, move or alter improvements to real property, or to furnish labor or materials, a lien on the improvements and the land they stand on. A subcontractor or supplier working through the owner's agent or contractor gets a lien by giving the owner written notice that it will claim one, limited to the unpaid contract price when notice is received. A lien lapses unless a notice of lien is filed with the town clerk within 180 days after payment for the last labor or materials became due. Lien rights may not be waived in advance of the work. Vermont's statutes do not say whether a tenant's contractor can lien the landlord's land, and they contain no rule letting a lease clause, recorded or not, keep your interest free of such liens; no case law was reviewed. Cautious course: require written consent before any tenant alteration, require the tenant to use paid, insured contractors and to obtain lien releases as payments are made, and respond promptly to any written lien notice you receive.

title: Consumer Protection Act and Leases
bodyText: Vermont's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing. It declares unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce unlawful and expressly applies to real estate transactions, and 'goods or services' include real estate, while a 'consumer' includes a person who leases or contracts for property for household use. A tenant who contracts in reliance on false or fraudulent representations or prohibited practices, or who is damaged by them, may sue for equitable relief and recover damages or the consideration paid, reasonable attorney's fees and exemplary damages up to three times the consideration; any language trying to exclude that recovery or the attorney's fees is unenforceable, and the defendant may demand a jury. Courts construe the Act in line with the Federal Trade Commission Act, and Attorney General rules carry weight. Specific Vermont rules that run through the Act include the automatic-renewal rule and the ban on confession-of-judgment clauses. Vermont's statutes have no residential-lease rule about blank spaces at signing or giving the tenant a copy, but delivering a complete signed copy is the safe practice.

title: Condominium Conversions
bodyText: Converting a Vermont rental building to condominiums, a cooperative or another ownership form triggers mandatory tenant protections (single-family homes that are individually owned and rented are exempt; mobile home parks have their own rules). You must give each tenant written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, stating the building will be converted and generally describing tenant rights. Minimum notice to vacate or purchase: in a building of more than five units or part of a complex, two years for tenants who are elders (62+) or have a disability, one year for low-income households, six months for others; in five or fewer units, one year, six months and three months. Missing notice is a defense to eviction. During the notice period you may evict only for nonpayment or breach, rent increases are limited to reasonable profit and actual cost increases (not conversion costs), the tenant may leave on 30 days' written notice, and a written lease cannot be cut short. For 90 days the tenant has the exclusive right to buy the unit. Tenants who do not buy get documented relocation costs up to $1,000, paid within 10 days after they move out, if all rent was paid and they left voluntarily by the halfway point of the notice period. Waivers are void, and violations are consumer protection violations.

title: Crime at the Property
bodyText: Vermont gives you a shorter notice for crime. When termination is based on criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence, any of which threaten the health or safety of other residents, you may end the tenancy by actual notice stating a termination date at least 14 days after the notice, instead of the 30 days required for other breaches. There is no statutory right to cure. The notice must state the termination date specifically, and you must start the eviction case within 60 days after that date. Accepting rent after terminating for a non-rent reason does not waive the eviction. Vermont has no mandatory-eviction duty, no third-party or prosecutor-initiated eviction, no crime-free lease statute and no rule voiding a lease for illegal use. Separately, it is a crime to knowingly permit a dwelling or building you own or control to be used for illegally selling regulated drugs (up to two years and $15,000, but not if you take action to address the activity) or for prostitution. Do not treat a tenant's status as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking as grounds for eviction, which fair housing law forbids, and remember that lawful adult cannabis possession is not illegal drug activity.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure
bodyText: Vermont has no general right for a tenant to cure a lease violation before termination, except for rent. Notice periods by ground, all by actual notice stating a specific termination date: nonpayment of rent, at least 14 days; breach of a material lease term or the tenant's statutory duties (not creating code violations, not disturbing neighbors, not damaging the premises), at least 30 days; criminal activity, illegal drug activity or violence threatening other residents, at least 14 days. No-cause terminations: without a written agreement, monthly tenancies need 60 days (90 days after two years' residence) and weekly 21 days, or 30 days if you have contracted to sell the building; with a written agreement, at least 30 days before the term ends (60 days after two years), or 7 days for a written week-to-week agreement. Shared occupancy in your own home: 15 days (monthly) or 7 days (weekly). Rent is the only cure: a nonpayment termination does not take effect if the tenant pays or tenders rent due through the end of the current rental period, and after filing the tenant may pay everything due into court before the writ is executed, once in 12 months. You must sue within 60 days after the termination date.

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant. General rules still apply. Your warranty of habitability requires you to deliver and maintain premises that are safe, clean and fit for human habitation and that comply with building, housing and health regulations, and no lease can waive it. A building material that gives off fumes, corrodes wiring or causes moisture problems can breach that warranty, and if it materially affects health and safety and is not repaired within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent, sue or end the tenancy. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code also requires electrical systems to be kept in safe working condition and units to be free of excessive moisture that may cause mold. Vermont's consumer protection law bars deceptive acts in real estate transactions, so answer questions about known building defects truthfully. Cautious course: if you know of a problem material in a unit, fix it before renting or disclose it in writing.

title: Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that lets a lease fix in advance what you will charge against the security deposit for cleaning, carpet, painting, rekeying or repairs, and a flat preset charge is risky. You may keep deposit money only for four purposes: unpaid rent; damage to your property that is not normal wear and tear or the result of actions or events beyond the tenant's control; unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you or to a utility; and expenses to remove articles the tenant abandoned. Normal wear and tear means deterioration from the intended reasonable use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, so routine repainting or carpet aging after a normal tenancy is not chargeable. You must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days; missing the deadline forfeits your right to withhold anything, and a willful failure costs double plus attorney's fees. A lease clause that circumvents these rules is void. Cautious course: itemize actual costs, keep invoices and photos, and use any lease price list only as an estimate.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a former tenant never cashes or claims a security deposit refund you owe, the money does not become yours. Vermont's unclaimed property law expressly lists security deposits and refunds as property, and a holder includes a business of any kind, including a sole proprietorship. A debt of a business, or other property not specifically listed, is presumed abandoned three years after the obligation to pay arises. You then become a holder with duties: if the refund is $50 or more and you have a valid mailing address, send the former tenant notice by first-class mail 60 to 180 days before you report; file your report with the State Treasurer's unclaimed property administrator before May 1, covering the 12 months before January 1; and pay the money over when you report. Late reporting or payment brings interest and a civil penalty of $200 a day up to $5,000. A dormancy charge may be deducted only if a valid contract authorizes it and you regularly impose it. A lease clause forfeiting an unclaimed refund to you would conflict with these rules and with the deposit statute. Keep tenants' forwarding addresses.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not give a tenant a right to pay the security deposit in installments, and they set no cap on the deposit amount, so you may require the full deposit when the tenancy begins. You may agree to accept it in installments; if you do, put the schedule in writing and state that a missed installment is a lease breach. Whatever the schedule, every refundable advance, deposit or prepaid rent counts as a security deposit, however you label it, and must be returned with an itemized statement of deductions within 14 days after the tenancy ends (60 days for a seasonal rental that is not a primary residence). You may not require an additional security deposit for a disabled tenant's reasonable modifications. Some towns may adopt security deposit ordinances that add protections, such as interest, so check local rules. Remember that you may not charge an application fee of any amount.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Vermont does not cap security deposits or limit what you may collect at signing, so you may require first month's rent, last month's rent and a security deposit. But in Vermont any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, that is refundable to the tenant when the tenancy ends is a security deposit. So money you collect as 'last month's rent' is treated as a security deposit if any of it could be refunded, and the deposit rules apply to it: you may apply it only to unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid charges the tenant had to pay you or a utility, and removal of abandoned articles, and you must account for it with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenancy ends. If you hold last month's rent and the tenant leaves early or stays through the final month, show on the statement how it was applied. On a sale, transfer all deposits, including prepaid rent, to the buyer, who must notify tenants. Do not let total move-in money disguise an application fee, which Vermont bans.

title: Deposit Refund Timing and Notice
bodyText: Vermont does not let you make the security deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out or a forwarding address, but notice does affect when your clock starts. You must return the deposit with a written statement itemizing deductions within 14 days from the date you discover that the tenant vacated or abandoned the unit, or from the date the tenant vacated if the tenant gave you notice of that date. For a seasonal rental that is not a primary residence, the deadline is 60 days. You comply by hand-delivering or mailing the statement and any payment to the tenant's last known address, so a missing forwarding address does not excuse a late refund. If you miss the 14 days, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit, and a willful failure makes you liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. A lease clause requiring notice as a condition of any refund would circumvent the statute and be void. Ask for a forwarding address at move-out, and calendar the deadline as soon as you learn the unit is empty.

title: Who May Make Repairs
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease naming who must make repairs. You may require repair requests to come to you and use your own contractors for work you do, and the lease may bar tenant alterations without consent. What a lease cannot do is cut off the tenant's statutory remedies. If you fail within 30 days of notice to repair a minor defect needed to comply with the landlord-tenant statute or a material lease provision, the tenant may repair it and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, up to one-half of one month's rent, after giving you actual notice of the cost; the statute does not require the tenant to use a licensed or designated contractor. For serious habitability problems the tenant may withhold rent or sue instead. One specific rule: for a tenant's plug-in solar device, you may respond within 10 days with reasonable restrictions, including requiring a licensed electrician at the tenant's cost, and the tenant may not do electrical work for it without your permission. Answer repair requests quickly so the tenant never gains the self-help remedy.

title: Disability Accommodations
bodyText: Under Vermont's fair housing law it is unlawful to refuse to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling unit, including public and common areas; examples include a reserved accessible parking space, a different rent due date tied to benefit payments, or an exception to a no-pet rule. You must also permit reasonable modifications of the premises at the disabled person's expense, and, if reasonable, you may require restoration at the end, reasonable wear and tear excepted, but you may not demand an additional security deposit for it, so Vermont has no interest-bearing restoration deposit. Vermont does not require the lease itself to state the restoration condition. 'Disability' covers physical or mental impairments that limit a major life activity, a record of one, or being regarded as having one. Newer covered multifamily buildings must also meet state accessible-design rules. Buildings of three or fewer units where you or immediate family live are exempt from the rental rules, but not the advertising rule. Handle requests promptly and in writing.

title: Disaster Guests
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not let a tenant house people displaced by a flood, fire or declared emergency as guests notwithstanding the lease, and do not limit your remedies when a tenant does. Your lease's guest, occupancy and subletting terms control, but use them carefully. Breach of a material lease term supports termination only on at least 30 days' actual notice, and the faster expedited ejectment against an occupant without right is available only where your written rental agreement prohibits subleasing. Without a written agreement, a tenant who sublets must give you written notice of the sublessee's name and contact information. Any occupancy limit should rest on applicable occupancy laws and ordinances, and fair housing law bars treating households differently because of children or other protected characteristics. Vermont's emergency powers let the Governor arrange temporary housing for disaster victims and, during a declared emergency, temporarily suspend some health, safety or zoning rules to provide it. Cautious course: after a disaster, agree in writing with the tenant on who may stay, for how long, and any change in utilities or rent.

title: Natural Disasters
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that ends a tenancy, or suspends rent, because of a declared natural disaster or emergency, and no casualty statute either. Your habitability duties govern. You must maintain premises that are safe, clean and fit for habitation throughout the tenancy, and that warranty cannot be waived. If flood, storm or other damage leaves the unit noncompliant in a way that materially affects health and safety and you do not repair within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice. You may interrupt utilities only temporarily for emergency repairs, and you may enter without notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property. The state fire-safety Commissioner may order damaged premises repaired or closed. Before signing a lease, you must disclose in a separate document whether any part of the premises is in a FEMA special flood hazard area. Cautious course: include a lease clause on termination and rent abatement if the unit becomes uninhabitable.

title: Disturbances
bodyText: Vermont puts a statutory duty on every tenant, implied in every rental agreement: the tenant must conduct himself or herself, and require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves, in a manner that will not disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises. If a tenant violates that duty, you are entitled to recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the violation is grounds for terminating the tenancy on at least 30 days' actual notice stating the termination date. If the conduct is criminal activity, illegal drug activity or violence threatening other residents' health or safety, the notice may be 14 days. The lease's no-disturbance clause adds detail, such as noise rules, but cannot shorten these notice periods. Fair housing law forbids treating a tenant differently because the tenant is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, so do not terminate a victim because of incidents committed against them. Document complaints with dates, witnesses and warnings, and accepting rent after a non-rent termination notice does not waive the eviction.

title: Double Letting and Late Possession
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on renting the same room or unit to two different tenants for the same period, no special rent-abatement remedy for it, and no statute on a landlord's failure to deliver possession at the start of a lease; the lease and contract law govern a late or failed move-in. General rules still bite. Once a tenant has rented the unit, denying that tenant access to and possession of it, or to the tenant's belongings, except through proper judicial process is an illegal eviction, and the tenant may sue for injunctive relief, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. If a prior occupant holds over, only the court ejectment process can remove them. Misrepresenting availability can also violate the Consumer Protection Act, which applies to real estate. Avoid signing overlapping leases; if a prior occupant may not leave on time, say in the new lease what happens, such as rent abatement until possession is delivered and the new tenant's right to cancel after a stated date, which the library's possession-delay clause covers.

title: Drug-Free Lease Addenda
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing about drug-free or crime-free lease addenda: none requires one, sets its wording or bars it. A drug-free term is an ordinary lease term, and a violation can support termination for breach of a material term on at least 30 days' notice, or on at least 14 days' notice when the conduct is illegal drug activity or criminal activity that threatens other residents' health or safety. Limits to keep in mind: from July 1, 2026, a rental agreement may not prohibit a tenant from possessing cannabis on the rental premises or using it inside the unit, though you may ban smoking or vaping it, so a drug-free addendum must carve out lawful adult cannabis unless federal law requires the ban. It is a crime to knowingly permit a dwelling you own or control to be used for illegally selling regulated drugs, but not if you take action to address the activity, so act promptly on credible reports. Fair housing law protects tenants with disabilities, including people in recovery from substance use disorders who are not currently using illegally, and victims of abuse.

title: Victim Information Confidentiality
bodyText: If you hold documentation or information about a tenant's status as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, such as the papers a tenant gives you to end a lease early or to have the locks changed, Vermont requires you to keep it confidential. You may not allow or provide access to anyone else unless: the tenant authorizes it; a court order, government regulation or governmental audit requires it; or it is required as evidence in a court proceeding, and then only if it stays under seal and its use is limited to a claim under the victim termination or lock-change statutes. The same duty applies to owners and housing subsidy providers. Separately, Vermont's fair housing law makes it unlawful to disclose information about a tenant's or occupant's status as a victim for the purpose of harassing or intimidating them, retaliating against them for exercising their rights, pressuring them to leave, or recovering possession of the dwelling. Store victim documents separately from the general tenant file, limit staff access, and never mention victim status in a termination notice or eviction filing unless a court requires it.

title: Deposits After a Victim Ends the Lease
bodyText: Vermont has no special rule on when you return a security deposit after a protected tenant (a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or a parent or caretaker of one) ends a rental agreement early, and no rule that the deposit clock waits until remaining occupants leave. The protected tenant terminates without penalty or liability, so you may not charge an early-termination fee or lost future rent against the deposit. The ordinary deposit rules apply: you may deduct only unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid charges the tenant owed you or a utility, and removal of abandoned articles, and you must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days after you discover the tenant vacated, or after the vacate date if the tenant gave you notice of it. Where the victim shares the lease with others who stay, the statutes do not say how the deposit is divided, so handle it by written agreement with all tenants, and never send deposit papers or forwarding information in a way that reveals the victim's new address to the perpetrator.

title: Victim Eviction Protections
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law makes a person's status as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking a protected characteristic. It is unlawful to refuse to rent, otherwise make unavailable or deny a dwelling, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions, privileges or protections of a rental, because a person is a victim; so do not terminate or refuse to renew a tenancy because of violence committed against the tenant, police calls about it, or resulting disturbance. It is also unlawful to disclose information about a tenant's victim status to harass or intimidate the tenant, retaliate, pressure the tenant to leave, or recover possession. Vermont has no statute letting you split (bifurcate) a lease to evict only the perpetrator, and no statute capping a victim's liability for damage the perpetrator caused; a perpetrator who is a tenant can be removed through a court protection order or through ordinary termination for that tenant's own breach. A protected tenant may also end the lease early or require a lock change. Violations can bring damages, punitive damages, attorney's fees and fines up to $10,000. The owner-occupied three-or-fewer-unit exemption applies to the rental rules.

title: Victim Early Termination
bodyText: A Vermont 'protected tenant' may end a rental agreement early, notwithstanding anything in the lease, without penalty or liability. A protected tenant is a tenant who is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or a parent, foster parent, legal guardian or caretaker with at least partial physical custody of such a victim. The right applies when the tenant reasonably believes it is necessary to vacate based on fear of imminent harm to a protected tenant from abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or because a protected tenant was sexually assaulted on the premises within the preceding six months. At least 30 days before the termination date, the tenant must give you written notice plus supporting documentation. The notice can be revoked, and the lease stays in effect, if the tenant revokes it in writing, or simply has not moved out by the termination date, before you sign a lease with someone else. 'Abuse' covers acts between family or household members; sexual assault and stalking can be by anyone. The statute does not say whether co-tenants' obligations also end, and it gives no separate route for a tenant harassed by the landlord. Keep all documentation confidential.

title: Victim Lock Changes
bodyText: In Vermont, a protected tenant (a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or a parent or caretaker of one) may ask you to change the unit's locks, and you must do so within 48 hours of the request when it is based on fear of imminent harm from abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or on a sexual assault on the premises within the previous six months. If the perpetrator is also a tenant of the unit, the request must include a copy of a court order requiring the perpetrator to leave. When you change the locks, give a new key to each tenant except a perpetrator under such an order. If you do not change them as requested, the tenant may change them without your permission, but must match or exceed the original quality, notify you within 24 hours and give you a key. Unless you agree otherwise, the tenant pays for the new locks. A protected tenant may also ask to install extra security such as a camera or alarm system, at least seven days ahead, at the tenant's own cost and risk; you may not unreasonably refuse. No lease term overrides these rights.

title: Victim Law Definitions
bodyText: Vermont's landlord-tenant victim protections borrow their definitions from other titles, and those sources have changed recently. 'Abuse' has the meaning in the family-abuse statute: physical harm or attempted harm, placing someone in fear of imminent serious physical harm, child abuse, stalking or sexual assault between family or household members, and also coercive controlling behavior between them, meaning a pattern that unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and liberty. 'Sexual assault' and 'stalking' take their meanings from the civil stalking and sexual assault order statute, which defines stalking as a purposeful course of conduct that would make a reasonable person fear for safety or suffer substantial emotional distress; a June 2026 amendment says the acts in a course of conduct need not occur on separate calendar days. The fair housing law uses the same definitions for its 'victim of abuse, sexual assault, or stalking' protected class. When a tenant invokes these protections, judge the request under the current definitions, not older versions in forms or policies, and update your internal procedures to match.

title: Victim Documentation
bodyText: When a protected tenant ends a rental agreement early under Vermont's victim statute, the tenant must give you, at least 30 days before the termination date, a written notice of termination and documentation from one or more of these sources supporting the tenant's reasonable belief that it is necessary to vacate: (A) a court, law enforcement or other government agency; (B) an abuse, sexual assault or stalking assistance program; (C) a legal, clerical, medical or other professional from whom the tenant, or the tenant's minor or dependent, received counseling or other assistance about abuse, sexual assault or stalking; or (D) a self-certification of the tenant's status as a victim, signed under penalty of perjury, on a standard form adopted by a federal or state agency (such as HUD or the Vermont Department for Children and Families) or by a nonprofit that serves protected tenants. You may not demand more than this. For a lock change, the statute requires no documentation, except a court order requiring the perpetrator to leave when the perpetrator is a co-tenant. Keep all documents confidential, and you are immune from liability for good-faith reliance on them.

title: Early Termination Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not regulate early-termination or lease-break fees: none authorizes, caps or bans a buy-out, and none requires a separate addendum. Related rules shape what you can recover. Without a written agreement saying otherwise, a tenant may end a tenancy by actual notice at least one rental payment period before the termination date. If a tenant under a fixed-term lease simply leaves, the tenant stays liable for rent until the lease expires, but once you rent the unit to someone else, the old lease ends on the date the new tenancy begins, so you cannot collect double rent. A unit counts as abandoned only if it no longer appears to be a full-time residence, rent is not current, and you have made reasonable efforts to learn the tenant's intentions, so a lease clause treating any absence without notice as abandonment goes further than the statute. A protected victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking may end the lease on 30 days' notice without penalty or liability. A security deposit may cover unpaid rent and damage, not a penalty. Cautious course: tie any fee to your actual re-rental costs.

title: Electric Submetering
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not authorize or regulate landlord submetering of electricity to residential tenants, and prescribe no submetering disclosure, form or notice at lease signing. The only express submetering permission is for recreational campgrounds, which may provide submetered electric service to campground users on a nonprofit basis under Public Utility Commission rules on rates, meter accuracy and billing. Electric distribution is otherwise organized around utility service territories under the Commission's jurisdiction, and a company that sells electricity directly to the public falls under the Commission's jurisdiction. The Commission's current rules have no residential submetering or resale rule; its only submetering rule is for campgrounds. Whether a landlord who resells electricity to tenants becomes a regulated utility is not settled by the statutes or the rules, and no court decisions were searched. The Commission's disconnection rule assumes tenants can get their own service: when a landlord's account in a rented building is to be disconnected, the utility must offer tenants service in their own names and, in a building on a single master meter, arrange individual meters for the units where possible. Two landlord-tenant rules apply regardless: anything a tenant pays you under the rental agreement is 'rent', and you may deduct from a security deposit unpaid utility charges only where the tenant was required to pay them directly to you or to a utility. You also may not willfully interrupt a tenant's utility service except temporarily for emergency repairs. Cautious course: have tenants contract directly with the utility for separately metered units, or include electricity in rent, and get regulatory advice before billing tenants from submeters.

title: Electronic Leases and Signatures
bodyText: Vermont's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you sign leases and deliver required writings electronically, but only with a tenant who has agreed to conduct transactions electronically, judged from the context, surrounding circumstances and the parties' conduct. A record, signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic, and an electronic record or signature satisfies a law requiring a writing or signature. A tenant who agreed to deal electronically may refuse to do so for other transactions, and that right cannot be waived. When a law requires you to deliver information in writing, an electronic record works only if the tenant can retain it, and a record you prevent the tenant from printing or storing is not enforceable against the tenant. If another law specifies a delivery method, such as hand delivery or mail for 'actual notice', that method still applies.
