Importantly, the Act does not apply at all to notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence, so serve termination notices on paper. Keep signed copies in a format both sides can download.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Vermont has no statute giving every tenant a non-waivable right to call police or emergency services, and none voiding lease terms or nuisance rules that penalize such calls in general. Related protections still limit what you can do. Fair housing law makes being a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking a protected characteristic, so you may not terminate, refuse to renew or change the terms of a tenancy because a victim called for help or because police responded to violence against the victim, and you may not use information about victim status to recover possession. Vermont's retaliation statute bars you from changing lease terms or bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant complained to a government agency about a health or safety code violation or complained to you about a landlord-tenant violation, and a non-rent termination within 90 days after a government notice of noncompliance is presumed retaliatory. Cautious course: do not count calls for police, fire or medical help against a tenant, and base any termination on the tenant's own conduct, not on the fact that help was summoned.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency phone number, post a 24-hour contact, disclose the owner's or manager's identity in the lease, or make tenants name an emergency contact. Related rules apply. When ownership changes, the new landlord must give tenants actual notice of the new landlord's name and address with a statement that the security deposit has been transferred. You may require a tenant under a written rental agreement to give you written notice of the name and contact information of any sublessee, and a tenant without a written agreement must do so. You must file an annual landlord certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes that includes your phone number, email and mailing address as available. In an emergency you may enter without consent or notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property, and tenants' repair remedies run from the date you receive notice, so a reliable contact channel protects you. Cautious course: give tenants a written 24-hour contact for emergencies and ask each tenant for an emergency contact person.

title: Eminent Domain and Leases
bodyText: Vermont has no general statute saying what happens to a residential lease or the rent when the property is taken by eminent domain, and no statute letting the court in a condemnation case cancel the lease or end the rent. The lease and general law govern, so a lease should say whether it ends on a taking and that any condemnation award belongs to you except amounts awarded to the tenant for the tenant's own moving costs or property. One state program helps displaced occupants directly: when the State undertakes a highway project, the Agency of Transportation must pay eligible persons, including individuals and families displaced from real property acquired for the project, reasonable and necessary moving expenses, or fixed amounts under a statewide schedule, and federal relocation rules may add more where federal funds are involved. If a taking leaves the unit uninhabitable before the tenancy ends, your habitability duties still apply, and any termination must follow Vermont's notice rules unless the lease ends by its own terms. Cautious course: add a condemnation clause that ends the lease on the date possession is taken, with rent prorated to that date.

title: Screening Your Staff
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to run background checks on apartment employees, maintenance staff or managers, and none forbidding it. If you do screen, Vermont's employment law limits how: an employer may not ask about criminal history on its initial job application form, except for positions where a federal or state law disqualifies people with certain convictions (and then only about those offenses); you may ask during an interview or once the applicant is otherwise qualified, and you must give the applicant a chance to explain the record and any rehabilitation. Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $100 each. Applicants need not disclose expunged or sealed records. Your staff act for you with tenants: they may enter a unit only with consent, on 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. for listed purposes, or without notice in a reasonably believed imminent emergency; they must keep any victim-status information confidential; and they must not discriminate or harass. Train staff on these rules, and give tenants a way to verify that a worker at the door is yours.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a Vermont business corporation, the statute requires a court to let the corporation appear through a non-lawyer representative, such as an officer or manager, but only if that person (A) is authorized to represent the corporation, (B) shows adequate legal knowledge and skills to represent it without unduly burdening the other side or the court, and (C) shares a common interest with the corporation. The judge decides whether the person qualifies, so be ready to show authority (for example, a board resolution) and familiarity with eviction procedure. In small claims court, a statute says any person, corporation or other legal entity may, but need not, be represented by a lawyer, so an LLC or partnership may bring a small claims case (a money claim of $10,000 or less, such as unpaid rent or damages) without one. An eviction is not a small claims case, because small claims court can award only money. For an LLC, partnership or other non-corporate entity in an eviction case, Vermont's statutes don't say whether a member or manager may appear without a lawyer; the court rules (published only through a paid legal service) and court decisions were not searched, so assume an LLC landlord needs a Vermont lawyer for an eviction unless the court confirms otherwise. Individual owners may represent themselves. Ejectment cases have technical requirements: the complaint must attach the rental agreement and termination notice, and either side may demand a jury, so consider counsel for contested cases.

title: Environmental Events
bodyText: Vermont has no statute giving a landlord or tenant the right to end a lease after an environmental event such as wildfire smoke, flooding or contamination, and no rental radon testing or termination rule. Related rules apply. Your warranty of habitability requires safe, clean premises fit for habitation that meet health and housing regulations; if an event leaves the unit noncompliant in a way that materially affects health and safety and you do not repair within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent, sue, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires units to be kept free from standing water or excessive moisture that may cause visible mold, private water supplies to be free of harmful contaminants (with treatment where a health-based contaminant is elevated), and an alternate water supply during short-term water deficiencies. Before signing a lease you must disclose, on a separate form, whether any part of the premises is in a FEMA special flood hazard area. Because the statutes leave termination to contract, add a lease clause for uninhabitability after such an event.

title: EV Charging
bodyText: Vermont gives tenants no statutory right, against their landlord, to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental; whether to allow one is a lease and consent decision. A new law effective July 1, 2026 does protect charging in common interest communities such as condominiums: a declaration, bylaw, rule, deed covenant or similar instrument that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts a unit owner from installing EV supply equipment in the owner's unit, limited common element or exclusively designated parking space, or that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts noncommercial use of that equipment by the unit owner or the occupants of the owner's unit, is void and unenforceable, though the association may impose reasonable restrictions. The rule reaches only communities with 12 or more units that may be used for residential purposes, other than planned communities of 24 or fewer units with no development rights and limited-expense planned communities (unless their declaration adopts the whole common interest community law); in a community created on or before January 1, 2011 it governs only events after June 30, 2026 and does not invalidate existing declaration, bylaw, plat or plan provisions. Where it applies, the association generally cannot stop you from installing a charger for your tenant's use, and your tenant, as an occupant, may use it. Under Vermont's definition of rent, any charging fee you collect is part of the rent bargain and should be stated in the lease. If you allow a tenant-installed charger, put installation, electricity cost, insurance and removal terms in a signed addendum.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when a tenancy ends: no rule on removal, restoration, reimbursement or transfer to you. Settle it in a written addendum before installation. Without one, ordinary rules apply: you may deduct from the security deposit only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid rent and charges owed to you or a utility, and removal of articles the tenant abandoned, and you must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days. Personal property left after the tenant vacates at the end of the agreement or after giving notice may be disposed of without notice; property left on abandonment must be stored and handled under the 60-day notice procedure. Whether a hard-wired charger becomes part of the building is a fixtures question for case law, which was not reviewed. For condominium units, the new common interest community EV law makes the unit owner who installs equipment responsible for repair, electricity and restoration costs and requires removal before a sale unless the buyer agrees in writing to take over those duties; that rule binds owners, not tenants.

title: EV Charger Installation Terms
bodyText: Vermont sets no conditions for a tenant's installation of an electric vehicle charger in a rental, because tenants have no statutory right to install one; plan approval, a licensed installer, permits, insurance, separate metering and payment terms are matters for your written agreement. The new common interest community EV law, effective July 1, 2026, gives a useful model, and it governs if your unit is in a condominium or other common interest community with 12 or more residential units (other than a planned community of 24 or fewer units with no development rights or a limited-expense planned community, unless its declaration adopts the whole law; in one created on or before January 1, 2011, only for events after June 30, 2026 and without invalidating existing declaration, bylaw, plat or plan provisions): the association may require the unit owner to comply with health and safety laws and building codes, follow reasonable architectural standards that do not prohibit the equipment or substantially raise its cost, use a licensed electrician, reimburse any added insurance premium for equipment in a common or limited common element within 14 days of the invoice, and follow other reasonable restrictions; an application not denied in writing within 90 days is deemed approved unless delayed by a reasonable request for information. Remember that a tenant may not lawfully do electrical work without your permission under general lease terms, any charging fee is part of the rent, and you may not interrupt utilities the tenant relies on except temporarily for emergency repairs.

title: EV Charging in Shared Areas
bodyText: Vermont has no rule for EV charging in the shared parking areas of an ordinary rental building; you decide whether to offer chargers, who may use them and what you charge, and any fee is part of the rent bargain. In common interest communities such as condominiums with 12 or more units that may be used for residential purposes, a law effective July 1, 2026 applies (planned communities of 24 or fewer units with no development rights, and limited-expense planned communities, are excepted unless their declaration adopts the whole common interest community law); in a community created on or before January 1, 2011 it governs only events after June 30, 2026 and does not invalidate existing declaration, bylaw, plat or plan provisions. A unit owner may install EV supply equipment in the owner's unit, limited common element or exclusively designated parking space, and occupants of the unit may use it for noncommercial purposes, subject to reasonable restrictions. Installing equipment is not a division or reallocation of a common element and does not change any owner's allocated interests. If the equipment sits in a common or limited common element, the association may require the owner to reimburse it for any added insurance premium. If the executive board finds that charging requires electrical infrastructure improvements, the association may assess those costs against the units that have installed, or will install, chargers. The installing owner bears damage, maintenance, electricity and restoration costs. If you rent a condo unit, clear any charger with the association first and allocate these costs with your tenant in writing.

title: Delays After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Vermont has no statute creating a hardship stay keyed to the tenant's circumstances, but the court has a general power: when it rules for you, a writ of possession issues on the date judgment is entered unless the court, for good cause, orders a stay. Even without a stay, the sheriff may not put you into possession until at least 14 days after serving the writ. Other timing rules: if the tenant fails to pay rent into court as ordered, the writ issues immediately and possession may follow no earlier than seven days after service; in an expedited case against an unauthorized occupant, no earlier than five days after service. In a nonpayment case, the tenant can stop the eviction by paying into court all rent through the end of the current rental period plus interest and costs before the writ is executed, once in any 12 months. After possession, you may dispose of remaining belongings 15 days after the writ is served or you regain possession, whichever is later, or one day after regaining possession if the court stayed the writ. Federal law may add protections for servicemembers. Plan move-in dates for the next tenant around these periods.

title: Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that names or bans a lease clause imposing a fee or penalty because of a termination notice or an eviction case, but its rules limit such clauses. Any rental agreement provision that attempts to circumvent the tenant's statutory obligations and remedies is unenforceable and void, so a fee that effectively shortens notice periods, burdens the tenant's right to stop a nonpayment termination by paying the rent due, or penalizes a tenant for raising habitability defenses will not hold up. In the eviction case itself, the court awards possession, rent due, damages and costs, and may award you reasonable attorney's fees only if a written rental agreement provides for them. Charging a fee in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint, complaint to you, or tenant-union activity is prohibited, and fees cannot be used to discriminate. Anything payable under the lease is 'rent', so a flat 'eviction fee' could also be challenged as an unenforceable penalty, though no case law was reviewed. Cautious course: recover eviction costs only through the court's award of costs and any lease-based attorney's fees.

title: Eviction Process
bodyText: Vermont evictions run through a court ejectment action; self-help is illegal. Start with a written termination notice delivered by hand or mail (actual notice) that states a specific termination date and allows the required time: 14 days for nonpayment (void if the tenant pays rent due through the current rental period), 30 days for other breaches, 14 days for criminal or drug activity or violence threatening other residents, or the no-cause periods. You must file within 60 days after the termination date. The complaint must attach the rental agreement, if any, and the termination notice, and either side may demand a jury. You may move for an order that the tenant pay rent into court while the case is pending; if the tenant misses ordered payments, you get judgment for immediate possession, executed no earlier than seven days after service. On judgment you recover possession, rent due, damages and costs, plus reasonable attorney's fees if the written lease so provides; the writ issues the same day unless stayed for good cause and is executed at least 14 days after service. In nonpayment cases, the tenant can still stop the case by paying all rent, interest and costs into court before the writ is executed, once in 12 months.

title: Eviction Records
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not seal, expunge or remove eviction (ejectment) case records, set a time after which they leave public indexes, or give landlords a right to object to sealing. Vermont's record-sealing laws cover criminal, juvenile, diversion and similar records, not civil eviction cases. Public access to court records is governed by the Vermont Supreme Court's rules for public access to court records, under which the public has access to all case records except those the rules list as exceptions. The full current rules, including any limits on remote online access, are published only through a paid legal service and were not reviewed here, so check with the court before relying on an eviction search. Related limits on how you use records in screening: applicants may decline to disclose expunged or sealed criminal records, fair housing law bars using past eviction history as a pretext for discrimination, and fair housing law bars refusing to rent to someone because the person is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, so an earlier eviction caused by abuse committed against an applicant should not be held against them. Cautious course: if you screen for eviction history, apply a written policy uniformly, consider only judgments (not filings that were dismissed or settled), and give applicants a chance to explain.

title: Serving Eviction Papers
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not let a lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. The ejectment statute says only that process shall be served and notice given as in other civil actions, which means the Vermont Rules of Civil Procedure govern who may serve the summons and complaint and how; those court rules were not reviewed here. Termination notices are separate: they must be 'actual notice', meaning written notice the tenant receives by hand delivery or mail to the last known address, with a rebuttable presumption of receipt three days after first-class or certified mailing. Electronic delivery does not substitute for eviction or cure notices for a primary residence. A different rule applies only in foreclosure, where the lender may serve a tenant by first-class mail at the address in a recorded rental agreement or to the 'occupant'. Cautious course: serve termination notices by both hand delivery and first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, use a sheriff or other authorized server for the court papers, and keep proof of every step.

title: No Exculpatory-Clause Statute; Waivers Still Void
bodyText: Vermont's statutes contain no provision that specifically addresses lease clauses excusing a landlord from liability for its own negligence or requiring the tenant to indemnify or hold the landlord harmless. That does not make such clauses safe. Vermont's rental statute voids any lease provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies it establishes, and separately voids any waiver of the implied warranty of habitability. A clause therefore cannot excuse you from keeping the unit safe, clean and fit, or take away the tenant's repair-and-deduct, rent-withholding, damages or illegal-eviction remedies. Two statutes limit your liability directly, without any lease term: a landlord who acts in good faith under the protections for victims of abuse, sexual assault or stalking is immune except for gross negligence or willful misconduct, and an owner in compliance with the lead-paint law is shielded from certain lead-exposure habitability claims. A clause making the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household or guests cause matches the tenant's statutory duty not to damage the premises and is ordinary. Do not rely on broad exculpatory or indemnity wording; carry liability insurance instead.

title: Move-In Condition Acknowledgments
bodyText: A lease clause in which the tenant acknowledges that the unit is in good, satisfactory condition is useful evidence of its condition at move-in, but in Vermont it cannot take away the tenant's habitability rights. Every Vermont residential rental carries an implied warranty that you will deliver and maintain, for the whole tenancy, premises that are safe, clean, fit for human habitation and compliant with building, housing and health regulations, and any lease provision waiving that warranty is void. Unlike some states, Vermont's statute has no exception for a tenant who accepts known defects in exchange for reduced rent. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code also bars letting a unit that does not comply with the code. So do not use a condition acknowledgment to accept defects; fix code problems before move-in. Vermont has no statute requiring a move-in condition report, but record existing damage in writing (photos help) because you may keep deposit money only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, and a clear move-in record is your best evidence when you itemize deductions within 14 days.

title: No Expedited Criminal Eviction
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no special expedited eviction track for criminal activity. Speed comes from the ordinary rules. When you terminate because of criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence that threaten the health or safety of other residents, the termination notice needs only 14 days, instead of the 30 days required for other breaches, given by actual notice with the termination date stated. You must then bring an ejectment action in court within 60 days after that termination date; you may not remove the tenant yourself. After judgment, the writ of possession issues the same day and the sheriff may put you in possession no earlier than 14 days after serving it. You may ask the court to order rent paid into court while the case is pending, with a writ on 7 days if the tenant fails to pay. The one statutory expedited hearing is for a person occupying the unit without right where your written lease prohibits subleasing; it does not cover a tenant's own criminal conduct. Separately, a person who is not a legal tenant and is cited for selling drugs at a dwelling must be arraigned the next business day, and the court may order the person to stay away from the dwelling. In an emergency, call the police.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no special procedure, election or fee for an early or expedited return of a security deposit, and none is needed: the deadline is an outer limit. You must return the deposit, with a written statement itemizing any deductions, within 14 days from the date you discover the tenant vacated or abandoned the unit, or from the date the tenant vacated if the tenant told you that date in advance; for a seasonal rental that is not a primary residence the deadline is 60 days. Hand-deliver or mail it to the tenant's last known address. Missing the 14 days forfeits your right to keep any part of the deposit, and a willful failure costs double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. Deductions are limited to the statute's list: unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay, and the cost of removing abandoned articles. Do not charge a fee for returning the deposit or for processing the statement, and return the deposit as soon as you know what you may keep.

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a tenant to tell you before an extended absence and give you no extra entry rights while the tenant is away. A lease may require such notice, as the library's extended-absence clause does, and may let you recover actual damages from a willful failure to give it, such as freeze damage that notice would have let you prevent. Your entry rules do not change when the tenant is away: you may enter with consent, or between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, supply agreed services or show the unit; without consent or notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property. An absence is not abandonment. Vermont treats a unit as abandoned only when circumstances would lead a reasonable person to believe it is no longer occupied as a full-time residence, rent is not current, and you have made reasonable efforts to learn the tenant's intentions. A tenant who is away but paying rent has not abandoned the unit, so do not re-rent it or remove belongings.

title: Fair Housing in Vermont
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law covers more people than federal law. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, harass, misrepresent availability or advertise a preference because of race (including hair texture and protective hairstyles), sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, marital status, religious creed, color, national origin, citizenship, immigration status or disability, or because a person intends to live with minor children, receives public assistance (including housing assistance such as vouchers), or is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking. Harassment need not be severe or pervasive; a single incident can count. You must allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (you may require reasonable restoration but no extra deposit) and make reasonable accommodations. Exemptions are narrow: a unit too small under occupancy law; a building of three or fewer units where you or your immediate family live, though your ads must still comply; refusing to rent to a minor; qualifying 55+ or 62+ housing for age and children; and religious organizations. Legitimate screening such as references is allowed but not as a pretext. Violations bring Human Rights Commission complaints, lawsuits with punitive damages and attorney's fees, and a criminal fine of up to $10,000 per violation; retaliation is also barred.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental or set terms, such as waivers or insurance, for permitting one. Your lease may limit or prohibit business use, including child care, as the library's residential-use clause does; apply any limit evenly so it is not used against families with children, a protected class in Vermont. A state zoning statute treats a licensed or registered family child care home serving six or fewer children as a permitted single-family residential use, but that limits town bylaws, not landlords. If you choose to allow child care, put conditions in writing: state licensing or registration with the Department for Children and Families, local approvals where required, liability insurance, limits on common areas, and responsibility for extra wear. Two rules follow automatically: no one may smoke or use cannabis indoors or in the outdoor child care area while children are present and in care, and cultivating cannabis in a licensed or registered family child care home is not permitted. If the building was built before 1978, the lead law applies to child care facilities, and you must fully inform a tenant who intends to run one of the lead-law requirements.

title: Deposit Alternatives and No-Deposit Fees
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no provision on fees, insurance products or surety bonds offered in place of a security deposit, and no rule on reporting a no-deposit damage claim to a credit bureau or collector. The general rules decide how such a program is treated. Any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, that is refundable at the end of the tenancy is a security deposit, with the 14-day itemized-return rule. A nonrefundable payment to you is not a deposit; Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to or for the benefit of the landlord under the rental agreement, so a recurring deposit-alternative fee you collect is likely rent, and raising it would need 60 days' actual notice. Vermont also bars application fees of any amount, so do not charge a program enrollment fee at application. If you offer a third-party deposit-alternative product, make it optional, describe it truthfully in writing (Vermont's consumer protection act reaches rental housing), and make clear the tenant still owes rent and damages. Do not require it from some applicants and not others based on a protected characteristic, including receipt of public assistance such as a voucher.

title: Fee Disclosure and Total Price
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law: nothing requires a total-price disclosure, a single all-in rent figure in the lease, or a fee list on the lease's first page. The general rules still shape how you present fees. Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to or for the benefit of the landlord under the rental agreement, so every recurring fee you collect is treated as part of the rent; rent is payable at the time and place agreed, and any increase, including a new or higher fee, takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice. You may not charge an application fee of any amount. Vermont's consumer protection act covers rental housing and bars unfair or deceptive acts, so advertising a rent that omits mandatory charges, or collecting a charge the lease does not provide for, carries real risk. Best practice: list every fee and its amount in the lease, state the total monthly amount the tenant must pay, and use the same total in advertising. Automatic lease renewals have separate bold-type and opt-in rules.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no provision that expressly bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not provide. Other rules make the practice risky. Every fee you collect under the lease counts as rent, so charging for a service the lease promises, such as snow removal, trash pickup, a parking space or an amenity, makes that service a material provision of the rental agreement. If you fail to supply it, the tenant may give notice and, if you do not fix a minor defect within 30 days, repair it and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, up to half of one month's rent; where the failure materially affects health and safety, such as heat you agreed to supply, the tenant may also withhold rent, sue for damages and attorney's fees, or terminate. Vermont's consumer protection act covers rental housing and bars unfair or deceptive acts, and billing for a service that is not delivered is a classic example. Charge only for services you actually provide, describe each one in the lease, and stop or credit the charge promptly if a service ends.

title: Fees Count as Rent in Vermont
bodyText: Unlike states that exclude fees from rent, Vermont's rental statute defines rent as all consideration to be made to or for the benefit of the landlord under the rental agreement, excluding only security deposits. No special lease wording is needed: recurring charges you collect under the lease, such as parking, pet or amenity fees, fall within that definition. Consequences follow. Rent is payable at the time and place agreed without demand, and any increase, including a new or higher fee, takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice. A tenant facing a nonpayment termination keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering the rent due through the end of the rental period, and in an ejectment for nonpayment the case is discontinued if the tenant pays all rent due, interest and costs into court before the writ is executed, once in 12 months. Because fees count toward what must be paid, keep a clear ledger showing which amounts are base rent and which are fees. Vermont's statutes do not make a one-way attorney-fee clause reciprocal; the court may award you reasonable attorney's fees in ejectment only when a written rental agreement so provides. Subsidized tenancies follow their federal program rules.

title: Fire Code for Rentals
bodyText: In Vermont, any building in which people rent accommodations, whether overnight or for a longer term, is a "public building" under the state fire-safety statute, and using any part of a building that way makes the whole building one. You must observe the fire-prevention rules adopted by the Commissioner of Public Safety (the Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code), must not operate the premises in a way likely to cause harm from fire or carbon monoxide, and must provide properly installed carbon monoxide detectors in residential buildings people sleep in, whether units are owned or rented. Rental housing is also covered by the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, enforced through complaint-driven inspections, which bans unvented fuel-fired space heaters. The detailed requirements for your building type (smoke alarms, egress, separations, sprinklers) are in the rules, not the statutes, so check the current edition with the Division of Fire Safety and any local code before renovating or changing use. Penalties are significant: fines up to $10,000 per violation, administrative penalties up to $1,000, and a rule violation is prima facie evidence of negligence in an injury lawsuit. Short-term rental operators must also post the Division's health and safety guidance.

title: Grills and Fire Safety
bodyText: Vermont's statutes contain no rule on grills, open-flame cooking or fire pits at rental properties, on balconies, decks or porches. The controlling rules, if any, are in the Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code adopted by the Division of Fire Safety, which applies to every building in which people rent accommodations, and in local fire codes. The current Vermont code, in effect since November 4, 2025, adopts the 2021 edition of the national NFPA 1 Fire Code with Vermont changes. The Vermont changes say nothing specific about grills; for open fires and burning they drop the national code's permit and point instead to the town forest fire warden permit described below. The national code's own rules on open flames and cooking equipment, which may restrict grills on multifamily balconies or near buildings, were not reviewed here, so ask the Division of Fire Safety or your local fire department. The statutes do require you not to operate premises in a way likely to cause harm from fire or carbon monoxide, and a fire-code violation is prima facie evidence of negligence in an injury lawsuit. A separate statute requires a permit to kindle a fire from the town forest fire warden to burn natural wood, brush, weeds or grass in the open air; since July 1, 2026 no permit is needed where snow surrounds the site or for a 'Category 1' campfire (36 inches in diameter or less, in a stone arch, outdoor fireplace or existing fire ring, including on private property, or 200 feet or more from forestland), and the old exception for cities with a fire department is repealed. A lease may set a stricter grill rule than the law, as the library's grilling clause does; check the current fire code and any local ordinance before writing one, state the rule in the lease or written rules, and apply it to all tenants.

title: Sprinkler Requirements
bodyText: Vermont's statutes impose no general duty on landlords to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in existing rental buildings. Whether a sprinkler system is required for your building depends on the Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code adopted by the Division of Fire Safety, which governs construction, maintenance and operation of every building in which people rent accommodations, and on any local code. The current Vermont code, in effect since November 4, 2025, removes the national code's sprinkler requirement for one- and two-family dwellings. A new apartment building must have a supervised automatic sprinkler system unless it has six or fewer units and every unit has either (1) its own exit door opening straight to the street or yard at ground level, with the unit separated by at least 1-hour fire-rated construction, or (2) its own interior stair, separated from the rest of the building by 1-hour fire barriers with no openings; in both cases the rating must extend to the outside exit. Requirements for existing apartment buildings, additions and changes of use come from the national codes the Vermont code adopts (the 2021 editions of NFPA 101 and NFPA 1), whose text was not reviewed here, so check with the Division of Fire Safety before construction or a change of use. If a system exists, keep it maintained: the statutes set fees for proof of inspection of fire suppression systems and certification of the people who design, install and test them, and a fire-code violation can bring fines up to $10,000 and is prima facie evidence of negligence. Incentives exist: the state Downtown and Village Center program offers a tax credit of up to $50,000 for installing or improving a sprinkler system in a qualified building, and some city charters allow local property-tax credits for sprinklered buildings.

title: Firearms Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not address firearms rules in residential leases: nothing bars a private landlord from restricting firearms in a lease, nothing makes such a term unenforceable against a permit holder, and nothing protects firearms locked in tenants' vehicles in your parking area. Towns are generally barred from regulating firearm possession, but that limit applies to governments, not private landlords. If you adopt a firearms rule, state it clearly in the lease or written rules before the tenancy begins, apply it to everyone, and tie it to safety, such as no discharge on the premises, no display in common areas, and safe storage. Make reasonable accommodation requests for disability-related needs part of your process as with any rule. Vermont law separately makes it a crime to store a firearm where the person knows or should know a child or prohibited person is likely to get access to it, if that person then uses it in a crime, displays it threateningly, or causes death or serious injury; storage in a locked container or with a locking device is a defense. Federally assisted housing may have program rules of its own; check them before restricting tenants in subsidized units.

title: No Just Cause Requirement
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no just-cause or good-cause eviction requirement for ordinary residential rentals. You may end a tenancy without stating a reason if you give the notice the statute requires. With no written lease: 60 days for monthly rent if the tenant has lived there two years or less, 90 days if longer, and 21 days for weekly rent. With a written lease: notice at least 30 days before the end of the stated term (60 days if the tenancy has lasted more than two years), or 7 days for a written week-to-week agreement. Shared housing in your own residence needs 15 days (monthly) or 7 days (weekly). The notice must be actual notice and state the termination date, and you must file in court within 60 days after that date. The limits are indirect: retaliation against a tenant who complained to a code agency, complained to you about a chapter violation, or joined a tenants' union is barred, with a presumption of retaliation for any termination other than for nonpayment served within 90 days after a governmental notice of noncompliance; and fair housing law bars discriminatory terminations. Good cause is required only in narrow settings: condominium conversions, cooperative housing, and mobile home parks.

title: Tenants in Foreclosure
bodyText: A foreclosure does not let a lender or buyer simply remove your tenants. In a Vermont judicial foreclosure of property subject to a residential rental agreement, the lender must join each tenant as a defendant, and the summons must carry a statutory notice in at least 14-point type telling the tenant the property is being foreclosed and that the tenant's right to remain may end. In a foreclosure by power of sale, the lender must send any tenant lawfully occupying the property a copy of the notice of sale at least 60 days before the sale. After a foreclosure judgment or sale, the writ of possession must be served on the tenant, and the lender or buyer may be put in possession no sooner than 30 days after service, or a longer period if federal law requires; check the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which can give bona fide tenants more time. As owner, once you receive a foreclosure complaint you must tell each new tenant who signs a rental agreement that the property is in foreclosure and that the tenant may have to leave on 30 days' notice, or longer federal notice, if you cannot redeem. Keep handling deposits under the deposit statute; on transfer the deposit goes to the new landlord.

title: Foreclosure Notice to New Tenants
bodyText: Vermont requires a foreclosure disclosure to new tenants in one situation. Once you, as owner of a mortgaged rental property, receive the complaint in a judicial foreclosure, you must notify each tenant who then enters into a residential rental agreement that the premises are the subject of a pending foreclosure action and that, if you cannot redeem the property, the tenant may be required to vacate on 30 days' notice, or on any longer notice federal law requires. Give it in writing before the tenant signs, and keep a copy. Your failure to give the notice does not invalidate the foreclosure, but it can expose you to claims from the tenant, including under Vermont's consumer protection act, which covers rental housing. Vermont's statutes do not require you to tell existing tenants about a mortgage default or a foreclosure; the lender must name existing tenants as defendants, with a large-type notice in the summons, or, in a power-of-sale foreclosure, mail them the notice of sale at least 60 days before the sale. No statute requires a foreclosure statement in the lease itself, and no separate form is prescribed.

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not restrict foreign adversaries, foreign governments or nonresident aliens from owning or leasing residential real estate, and contain no lease-duration carve-out of the kind some states have adopted. A foreign-national landlord faces no state-law bar to owning rental property, and a residential lease to a foreign-national tenant is not void or restricted under Vermont statute. The relevant Vermont rule runs the other way: fair housing law makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms or advertise a preference because of a person's citizenship or immigration status, and allows verification of immigration status only where federal law requires it. Vermont also bars requiring a Social Security number on a rental application; you must accept unexpired government-issued identification, an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number or an SSN for a background or credit check. The only Vermont alien-ownership restriction located concerns railroads, not housing. Federal rules, such as sanctions programs, foreign-investment review and tax withholding on payments to foreign persons, may still apply to a foreign owner or a transaction and should be reviewed with a professional.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Vermont gives tenants two statutory chances to undo a termination for nonpayment, and both apply to every residential tenancy, whether weekly, monthly or a written fixed term. First, after you serve a 14-day nonpayment notice, the rental agreement does not terminate if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made or tendered. Accepting a partial payment does not waive your remedies and is not an accord and satisfaction, but a partial payment does not stop the termination. Second, once you have filed an ejectment action for nonpayment, the case must be discontinued if, before the writ of possession is executed, the tenant pays into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, plus interest and the costs of suit. A tenant may use this court-payment cure only once in any 12-month period, counted from the day of payment. Keep an accurate ledger and accept a full tender within these rules; refusing a complete tender may defeat the eviction. A termination for other breaches, or for no cause, has no comparable statutory pay-to-stay right.

title: Building and Fire Code Editions
bodyText: Vermont's statutes generally do not freeze an outside building or fire code at a named edition for rental housing; they leave editions to agency rules. The Commissioner of Public Safety adopts the Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code by rule, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires noncompliant existing structures to be altered or repaired to comply with the currently adopted Fire and Building Safety Code, so the edition in force when work is done is the one that matters. The current Vermont Fire and Building Safety Code took effect November 4, 2025 and adopts the 2021 editions of the NFPA 101 Life Safety Code, the NFPA 1 Fire Code, the International Building Code and the International Existing Building Code, with Vermont amendments; it replaced the code based on the 2015 editions. A building with a construction permit that started construction within 180 days of that date under the 2015 code need not change its plans, but it must also meet the 2025 code's requirements for existing buildings. Energy codes work the same way: the residential and commercial building energy standards are updated by rule after new national (IECC or ASHRAE) editions issue, and anyone starting construction after an amended standard takes effect must meet the most recent version, while projects begun before an amended standard takes effect may follow either version. The single-family alarm statute, which does not reach a rented building because a building in which people rent accommodations is a 'public building', requires smoke alarms that are photoelectric-type or UL 217 compliant, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms listed by Underwriters Laboratory or another nationally recognized testing laboratory. Before renovating, adding units or changing use, confirm the fire and building code editions in force with the Division of Fire Safety and the energy-standard editions with the Department of Public Service, and check any local code.

title: Furnished Units
bodyText: Vermont has no statute specifically about furnished rentals: no list of required furnishings, no inventory requirement, and no separate rule for a furniture deposit. The general rules cover furniture you supply. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the premises or its fixtures, mechanical systems or furnishings, or permit anyone else to; if the tenant does, you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the breach is a ground for a 30-day termination. Vermont does not cap security deposits, and any refundable advance, however named, including a "furniture deposit," is a security deposit subject to the 14-day itemized-return rule. You may deduct for damage to your property beyond normal wear and tear, which Vermont defines as deterioration from reasonable use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse of the premises, equipment or chattels by the tenant, household, invitees or guests. List the furnishings and their condition in the lease or a signed inventory with photos at move-in, so you can show what was damaged. Furnished short-term rentals to transient guests are regulated separately.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Vermont has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law for ordinary rentals, so it has no required notice telling a tenant whether a unit is covered by one, and nothing of that kind belongs in a Vermont lease. What a Vermont termination notice must do is set by the termination statute: it must be actual notice (written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the last known address, presumed received three days after first-class or certified mailing), it must give at least the statutory notice period for the ground used, and the termination date must be specifically stated. Vermont's statutes do not require a termination notice to include a statement of the tenant's right to contest in court or a legal-aid referral, and prescribe no state form for it, though including the ground and the date clearly is good practice. Limits that work like cause rules still apply: retaliation is barred, with a presumption when a termination other than for nonpayment follows within 90 days of a governmental notice of noncompliance, and fair housing law bars discriminatory terminations. Condominium conversions, cooperatives and mobile home parks have their own cause rules.

title: Governing Law
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no provision on governing-law or venue clauses in residential leases. A lease of a Vermont dwelling should name Vermont law, as the library's governing-law clause does. Vermont's rental statute applies to the tenancy whatever the lease says: its obligations are implied in every rental agreement, and any provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies it establishes is void. Do not use a clause choosing another state's law or courts to avoid Vermont rules. In a standard-form lease between a business landlord and an individual tenant, a term requiring claims to be resolved in an inconvenient venue outside Vermont is presumed unconscionable, though a term naming a Vermont state or federal court is allowed, and a court may treat enforcing an unconscionable term as an unfair practice with statutory damages. Eviction (ejectment) cases are brought in the Superior Court, and actions concerning real estate must be filed in the court unit where the property lies. Local law also matters: some Vermont towns have ordinances on security deposits and other rental matters, so the clause's reference to applicable local law is useful.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not address whether you may pass a town's rental registration, licensing or inspection fee on to your tenants, and Vermont has no statewide registry for long-term rentals (short-term rental operators register for meals and rooms tax purposes). Some towns and cities have their own rental registration or inspection ordinances, so check local rules for the fee and for any limit on passing it through. If you want the tenant to bear such a cost, Vermont's general rent rules control. Anything the tenant pays you under the rental agreement is rent, so build the cost into the rent or state the charge in the lease from the start; adding a new charge or raising one during the tenancy is a rent increase that takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice. You may not charge an application fee of any amount, so do not collect a registration or screening cost from applicants. Disclose the charge clearly; misleading charges can violate Vermont's consumer protection act, which covers rental housing.

title: Passing Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not bar you from passing governmental fines on to tenants, and do not limit pass-through to fines the tenant caused. The general rules point the way. Fines and penalties for your own obligations are yours: the Division of Fire Safety can impose administrative penalties of up to $1,000 per violation on the person responsible for a rental housing code violation, and fire-code violations carry fines up to $10,000, and you may not shift code responsibilities to the tenant by lease. Tenants, though, must not create or contribute to code noncompliance or damage the premises, and when a tenant violates those duties you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A lease may therefore make the tenant reimburse a fine charged to you because of the tenant's own conduct, such as an ordinance fine for the tenant's trash or parking violation, described specifically in the lease. Because anything paid to you under the lease is rent, treat a reimbursement as a lease charge, bill it promptly with the notice or citation attached, and do not use it to cover fines for conditions you were responsible for.

title: No Guarantor Statute
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on residential lease guaranties: nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires renewal terms to be stated, or requires a maximum amount or end date. A guaranty is an ordinary contract that must be in a writing signed by the guarantor, so write it clearly, stating whether it covers renewals, extensions, month-to-month continuation and holdover periods, any dollar cap, and how the guarantor may end future liability. Vermont's co-signer notice statute applies to lenders' loan instruments, not leases, but giving the guarantor a plain statement of the liability assumed is good practice. Vermont does not cap security deposits. Any refundable advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, is a security deposit subject to the 14-day itemized-return rule; if you take money from a guarantor to secure the lease, handle it under the same rules and return it with an itemized statement. You may not charge an application fee of any amount, including to a guarantor applying with the tenant. Screen and treat guarantors without regard to protected characteristics, including receipt of public assistance. To recover from a guarantor, sue on the guaranty; the ejectment judgment runs against the tenant.

title: Guests
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on tenant guests, guest stay limits or guest fees, so guest rules are lease terms, but several statutes turn on guests. The tenant must require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to behave so as not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and must not deliberately or negligently permit anyone to damage the premises; a violation lets you recover damages, costs and attorney's fees and is a ground for a 30-day termination. Damage caused by guests is not normal wear and tear, and a tenant cannot use the habitability or repair-and-deduct remedies for conditions caused by a person on the premises with the tenant's consent. A guest who becomes a long-term occupant may really be a sublessee: under a written lease you may condition or prohibit subleasing and require the tenant to tell you each sublessee's name and contact information, and where the written lease prohibits subleasing you or the tenant can use an expedited court hearing against a person occupying the unit without right. Apply guest limits evenly; fair housing law bars rules that target protected classes, including families with children.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give tenants' guests, visitors and service suppliers no statutory right of access to multi-unit buildings, do not bar guest fees, and do not limit your control over who enters common areas. Guest rules are lease terms. Some limits still apply. Fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or in services or facilities, because of a protected characteristic, so guest rules must not single out, for example, visitors of a particular race or religion, or families with children, and you must make reasonable accommodations, such as for a caregiver or attendant a person with a disability relies on. Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, so a guest fee you collect is part of the rent; state it in the lease from the start, and add or raise one only on 60 days' actual notice. A tenant is responsible for the conduct of persons on the premises with the tenant's consent. If you limit common-area access by non-residents, write the rule down, post it, and apply it consistently.

title: What Makes a Unit Unfit
bodyText: Vermont's warranty of habitability requires you to deliver and maintain, for the whole tenancy, premises that are safe, clean and fit for human habitation and that comply with applicable building, housing and health regulations, a term that reaches any law, ordinance or regulation on health, safety, sanitation or fitness. The strongest tenant remedies turn on materiality: if, after actual notice from the tenant, a government agency or a qualified independent inspector, you fail to repair within a reasonable time and the noncompliance materially affects health and safety, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and attorney's fees, or terminate on reasonable notice. A minor defect that breaches the statute or a material lease provision is handled differently: if you do not repair within 30 days of notice, the tenant may fix it and deduct the reasonable cost, up to half a month's rent. Neither remedy applies to conditions the tenant or the tenant's guests caused. Concrete standards come from the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, such as heat able to keep 65°F in habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms, provided whenever it is below 55°F outside, and adequate hot and cold water.

title: Changing Habitability Duties by Agreement
bodyText: Vermont does not let the parties change the habitability duty by agreement. Any lease provision by which the tenant waives the protections of the implied warranty of habitability is void, any provision that attempts to circumvent the rental statute's obligations and remedies is void, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code says a rental agreement that shifts code responsibilities between owner and occupant is not effective for code purposes. Unlike some states, Vermont has no exception for a tenant who accepts specified defects in exchange for reduced rent, so do not use an "accepted conditions" clause. What the lease can decide is who pays for and arranges services the statute leaves to the agreement. Heat is the main example: you must always provide heating facilities capable of safely providing a reasonable amount of heat, but the duty to actually supply heat at all times applies when you provide heat as part of the rental agreement, so a lease may make the tenant responsible for buying fuel or paying the heating utility. Remember that a service you promise in the lease becomes a material provision the tenant can enforce through repair-and-deduct if you fail to provide it.

title: Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Vermont's statutes create no presumption about the value of a unit with habitability defects, such as a rule that agreed rent equals the value of a defect-free unit; how much rent a tenant may withhold or recover is left to the courts. Several other presumptions matter in habitability disputes. If you serve a termination notice on any ground other than nonpayment within 90 days after a town or state agency notifies you that the premises do not comply with health or safety regulations, the termination is presumed retaliatory, and you must rebut that presumption. Notice sent by first-class or certified mail is presumed received three days after mailing, which helps both you and the tenant prove the notice that triggers repair deadlines. In pre-1978 housing, paint is presumed to be lead-based for purposes of the lead law's work-practice rules unless the component is exempt. A violation of the fire-safety rules is prima facie evidence of negligence in an injury lawsuit. Keep dated records of repair requests, inspection reports and your responses.

title: No Lease Habitability Statement Required
bodyText: Vermont does not require the lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The warranty is implied by law: in every residential rental agreement, written or oral, you are deemed to covenant and warrant to deliver and maintain, for the whole tenancy, premises that are safe, clean and fit for human habitation and that comply with applicable building, housing and health regulations, and all of the rental statute's obligations are implied in every rental agreement whether or not the lease mentions them. A statement in the lease that the unit is habitable, or that you will comply with the warranty, is optional and harmless. What you must avoid is wording that waives the warranty or that attempts to circumvent the statute's obligations and remedies, such as a clause having the tenant accept the unit "as is" with defects or give up repair or withholding rights; those provisions are void. Vermont's statutes impose no general list of required lease contents for ordinary rentals, though some disclosures, such as the flood-zone notice and lead materials, must be given in separate documents.

title: Habitability Waivers Are Void
bodyText: In Vermont a tenant cannot waive the warranty of habitability, in the lease or in any separate agreement. The statute's waiver rule has two sentences and no exception: no rental agreement may contain a provision by which the tenant waives the protections of the implied warranty, and any such waiver is contrary to public policy, unenforceable and void. Vermont has no provision letting a tenant accept specified defects for a stated rent reduction, and no procedure for agreeing to a lower heat level; the heat standard in the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code (65°F in habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms when it is below 55°F outside) applies whenever heat is required. The broader anti-circumvention rule voids any lease term that attempts to get around the rental statute's obligations or remedies, and the Code refuses effect to lease terms shifting code duties between owner and occupant. A rent concession for a known defect does not cure it: the tenant keeps the right to notice, repair-and-deduct, rent withholding, damages and termination. If a unit has a condition you will not fix, do not rent it until it meets code; letting a noncompliant unit is itself a code violation.

title: Environmental Restrictions and Tenants
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a landlord to give tenants a general contamination disclosure or to write recorded environmental use restrictions into a residential lease. A cleanup restriction on your property can still matter. Under the brownfield program, when a cleanup is finished the Agency of Natural Resources issues a certificate of completion describing any land use restrictions and other conditions required by the corrective action plan, and the certificate must be filed in the town land records. Those restrictions, such as limits on groundwater use, soil disturbance or residential use of part of a site, are conditions on the property, so make sure your tenants' use does not violate them: describe any that affect tenants (for example, no gardening in a capped area or no use of a well) in the lease or rules and keep the certificate on file. The Agency's cleanup rule does not add a tenant notice either. It lets the Agency record restrictions through a notice in the land records, an environmental easement or the certificate of completion, and a recorded notice warns that anyone who fails to follow the restrictions may be liable for further investigation, cleanup and penalties. The rule also requires notice to the Agency, and its approval, before any digging or other earth disturbance within an area of known contamination at an active or closed hazardous site, so check before tenants or contractors dig. Separate disclosure duties apply to lead-based paint and flood zones, and fire officials may order dangerous conditions involving hazardous materials corrected by order served on the owner or occupant.

title: No Health District Rental Rules
bodyText: Vermont has no health districts that issue rental regulations, and no statute requires you to give tenants copies of health or housing regulations on request or to refer them to a health agency. Statewide rental standards are in the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code adopted by the Division of Fire Safety, which took over primary responsibility for rental housing safety from town health officers in 2022. Inspections are complaint-driven: after an inspection the Division issues a written report with findings, correction deadlines and notice that you may not rent the affected unit to a new tenant until the violation is corrected, sends it to you, the complaining person and affected tenants, makes it a public record, and may impose administrative penalties of up to $1,000 per violation if you miss the deadlines. Town health officers still investigate public health hazards and may assist the Division in inspecting rental housing. Tenants must give you access to make ordered repairs under the normal 48-hour notice rule. Knowing the Code's standards (heat, water, sanitation, pests, ventilation, electrical, structure) is the best way to avoid a complaint.

title: Heat Standards
bodyText: As part of the warranty of habitability, every Vermont rental must have heating facilities capable of safely providing a reasonable amount of heat, and adequate hot and cold water. Who supplies the heat is up to the lease: if you provide heat as part of the rental agreement, you must supply a reasonable amount at all times; if the lease makes the tenant responsible for fuel or the heating utility, you still must provide and maintain working equipment. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code sets the measurable standard: heating systems must be provided when it is below 55°F outside, be properly functioning and in good repair, be able to keep at least 65°F in all habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms (measured three feet above the floor and three feet from an exterior wall), and be vented outside; unvented fuel-fired space heaters are prohibited. An owner who provides heat must maintain it whenever it is below 55°F outside. You may not willfully cause heat or any other utility service to be interrupted except temporarily for emergency repairs. Vermont has no procedure for agreeing to a lower heat level, and the heat and water rule in the statute does not apply to units rented for summer occupancy or as hunting camps.

title: Condominium Rental Restrictions
bodyText: If your rental is a unit in a Vermont condominium or other common interest community, the association's documents can limit how you rent it, and the Common Interest Ownership Act sets the framework. Leasing restrictions generally must be in the declaration, which must state any restrictions on alienation, including leasing restrictions beyond what the board may adopt by rule; the board may adopt rules restricting leasing of residential units only to the extent reasonably designed to meet institutional mortgage lenders' underwriting requirements, and every rule must be reasonable. If your tenant violates the declaration, bylaws or rules, the association may, in addition to acting against you, charge late fees directly to the tenant, levy reasonable fines against the tenant after notice and an opportunity to be heard, and enforce rights you as landlord could exercise under the lease, but those lease rights only if the violation is not cured within 10 days after notice to you and the tenant. Unless the lease provides otherwise, the association may not enforce your lease in the absence of a violation of its documents. Vermont's statutes do not cap association lease-approval fees, regulate association-held tenant deposits, or let the association collect rent from your tenant when you are delinquent.

title: Association Rules and Tenants
bodyText: When you rent out a unit in a Vermont condominium or other common interest community, the declaration, bylaws and rules bind you as owner, and the Common Interest Ownership Act also lets the association act against your tenant. If the tenant violates the association's documents, the association may, in addition to acting against you, charge late fees directly to the tenant, levy reasonable fines against the tenant after notice to you and the tenant and an opportunity to be heard, and enforce rights you could exercise as landlord under the lease, but those lease rights only if the violation is not cured within 10 days after notice to both of you. Your lease should therefore require the tenant to follow the association's rules, as the library's association-compliance clause does, and you should give the tenant a copy of the current declaration provisions and rules before signing. Vermont's statutes do not let an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you are behind on assessments. No Vermont statute governs tenant satellite dishes or antennas; the federal over-the-air reception rule (not reviewed here) may protect a tenant's dish in areas under the tenant's exclusive use.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Vermont has no statute written for holding deposits, earnest money or other money taken to reserve a unit before a lease is signed, so handle such payments carefully. You may not charge an application fee of any amount to apply for a residential unit, so a nonrefundable "holding fee" collected with or as a condition of an application risks being treated as a prohibited application fee. Once a tenancy exists, any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, that is refundable to the tenant at the end of the tenancy is a security deposit, subject to the 14-day itemized-return rule; Vermont does not cap deposits. The safest practice is to take money only after you have approved the applicant and both sides have agreed in writing that the payment holds the unit, will be credited to the first month's rent or the security deposit when the lease begins, and will be refunded in full if you do not offer the lease or within a stated time if the applicant withdraws, unless the writing says otherwise. If a licensed real estate broker or property manager takes the money, the broker must deposit it in a trust or escrow account within five banking days.

title: Tenants Who Stay Past the Term
bodyText: When a Vermont tenancy ends and the tenant stays without your express consent, you may bring an ejectment action for possession, damages and costs in Superior Court; you may not remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself. The case must be commenced within 60 days after the termination date stated in your notice, or the notice will not support a judgment. Before suing, make sure the tenancy actually ended: for a written lease, a no-cause termination requires notice at least 30 days before the end of the stated term (60 days if the tenancy has lasted more than two years), and Vermont's statutes do not say what happens if neither side gives notice. Accepting rent after a termination for reasons other than nonpayment does not waive your eviction case. Vermont's rental statute sets no holdover damages formula and no double-rent penalty for residential tenants; the court awards possession, rents due, damages and costs, and reasonable attorney's fees only if a written rental agreement provides for them. An older forcible-entry statute allows treble damages against someone who wrongfully stays after written demand, but it expressly does not apply to a tenant holding over after a written lease, so do not rely on it for tenants.

title: Holdover Charge Limits
bodyText: Vermont has no statute setting or capping a holdover rate for a residential tenant who stays after the tenancy ends, so a lease may set an agreed daily holdover charge. Keep it defensible: tie the amount to a reasonable estimate of your actual loss, such as the daily rent plus the cost of a delayed incoming tenancy, rather than a punishment; do not collect both the holdover charge and rent for the same day; and say that accepting it does not create a new tenancy or give express consent to the tenant staying. Vermont defines rent broadly as all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, so a holdover charge you collect may be treated as rent, and how a court would treat an oversized charge is a question of general contract law, which was not searched. The holdover charge does not change the eviction process: you still need a court ejectment action, commenced within 60 days after the termination date, and you recover attorney's fees only if the written lease provides for them. The older statute allowing treble damages for wrongful detainer does not apply to a tenant holding over after a written lease.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that makes running a home-based business a protected use of a rented home, so your lease may limit or prohibit business use, as the library's residential-use clause does, or allow it on conditions. Vermont's home-occupation protection is a zoning rule: town bylaws may not infringe on a resident's right to use a minor portion of a dwelling unit for an occupation that is customary in residential areas and does not have an undue adverse effect on the neighborhood. That limits towns, not landlords. If you allow a business, set written conditions: no employees or customer traffic beyond what you approve, no signs, no hazardous materials, compliance with any state licensing (for example, food operations licensed by the Department of Health, with an exemption for small cottage food operations), adequate insurance, and responsibility for extra wear. Keep business rules even-handed; fair housing law bars applying them differently because of a protected characteristic. A tenant's business use that creates code violations or disturbs other tenants also breaches the tenant's statutory duties, whether or not the lease addresses business use.

title: No Exemption Waivers
bodyText: Vermont has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the exemptions that protect a debtor's property from attachment and execution, and no statute addressing such a lease waiver at all. The exemptions are set by statute: among others, a homestead (dwelling and land the person owns and uses as a homestead) up to $125,000; up to $2,500 in motor vehicles; up to $5,000 in tools of the trade; up to $2,500 in household furnishings, goods, appliances, clothing and similar items; a cooking stove, heating appliances, a refrigerator, freezer and water heater; ten cords of firewood or 500 gallons of oil; up to $700 in bank deposits; health aids; and public and other benefits reasonably necessary for support. The goods-and-chattels statute says the listed articles are exempt unless the debtor turns them out to the officer at the time of levy, which is a choice made then, not in advance by lease. Do not include exemption waivers in a Vermont lease; a clause that tried to reach a tenant's property outside the court process could also conflict with the rule that you may deny a tenant access to the tenant's property only through judicial process.

title: Immigration Status and Tenants
bodyText: Vermont protects tenants and applicants based on immigration status. Its fair housing law makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, harass, advertise a preference or misrepresent availability because of a person's citizenship or immigration status; verifying immigration status or treating people differently on that basis is allowed only if federal law requires it, as some subsidized housing programs do. For screening, you must accept an unexpired government-issued ID, an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number or a Social Security number for a background or credit check, and you may not require an SSN or refuse an application for lack of one. Vermont has no statute making it unlawful to rent to someone unlawfully present. Do not ask about immigration status unless a federal program requires it, and never use it as leverage: threatening to report a tenant's status in a dispute can support a fair housing harassment or retaliation claim, and threatening to report someone's immigration status to coerce sexual conduct or images is a crime. From January 1, 2028, large data holders covered by Vermont's new data privacy act must treat citizenship and immigration status as sensitive data.

title: No Infirmity Termination Right
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give tenants no right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, admission to a nursing home or assisted living, or death, and contain no tenant-death rule. The only statutory early-exit right for a fixed-term tenant is for victims of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, who may terminate on 30 days' written notice with documentation. Other rules soften the result. A tenant without a written lease, or whose written lease does not say otherwise, may end the tenancy by actual notice at least one rental period before the termination date. If a tenant under a fixed-term lease leaves and you re-rent the unit before the lease ends, the lease terminates on the date the new tenancy begins, so rent stops accruing then. A tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies or practices, such as releasing the lease or shortening notice when the tenant must move to a care facility, and fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations that are necessary to give equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing; consider such requests seriously and in writing. Many landlords include an early-termination option for these situations.

title: Mediation and Dispute Resolution
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing about lease clauses requiring landlord and tenant to try to resolve disputes informally before going to court, and create no court eviction-mediation program in statute. A cooperative step such as written notice and a meeting before suit is a contract term, but write it so it cannot defeat your statutory deadlines: an ejectment must be filed within 60 days after the termination date in your notice, and any provision that attempts to circumvent the rental statute's obligations or remedies is void, so exclude possession actions, nonpayment, emergencies and the tenant's habitability remedies from any pre-suit requirement. Binding arbitration is different.
