Under Vermont's Arbitration Act, an agreement to arbitrate future disputes is enforceable only if accompanied by or containing a written acknowledgment of arbitration, signed by each party, in substantially the statutory words, displayed prominently when it is in the same document; and no arbitration agreement may prevent a person from going to court to enforce constitutional or civil rights, such as fair housing claims. Given those limits and the court-based eviction process, most residential leases should not require arbitration; voluntary mediation through community programs remains available.

title: No Code Order Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to tell a prospective tenant about past or outstanding code inspection reports, violation notices or condemnation orders on the property. Other rules make hiding them risky. When the Division of Fire Safety (or a town health officer assisting it) inspects rental housing and finds violations, the written report gives you deadlines to correct them and notice that you are prohibited from renting the affected unit to a new tenant until the violation is corrected, and the report is a public record that is also sent to affected tenants. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code separately bars letting any unit that does not comply with the code. Missing correction deadlines can bring administrative penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. Misrepresenting a unit's condition or the status of an order can violate Vermont's consumer protection act, which covers rental housing, and any unit you rent carries the warranty of habitability from the first day. In pre-1978 housing you must give approved tenants the lead materials and your most recent lead-safety compliance statement before the lease. Correct orders before re-renting, and answer tenant questions about them truthfully.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Vermont does not require you to tell a tenant about move-in or move-out inspection rights, and has no move-in condition report requirement, so there is no penalty for failing to give such a notice. Vermont's deposit penalties attach to other duties. If you do not return the deposit, with a written statement itemizing any deductions, within 14 days after you discover the tenant vacated or abandoned the unit (or after the tenant's announced move-out date), or within 60 days for a seasonal rental that is not a primary residence, you forfeit the right to keep any part of it. If the failure is willful, you owe double the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Deductions are allowed only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other required charges, and the cost of removing abandoned articles. Although no inspection is required, a documented move-in and move-out walk-through with photos, offered to the tenant, is the best way to support deductions; if you inspect while the tenant still lives there, give the 48-hour notice and enter between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M.

title: Co-Tenant Liability
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that sets how co-tenants share responsibility under a residential lease, so the lease's joint-and-several liability clause governs: each tenant who signs can be held responsible for the full rent and all obligations. Vermont law creates exceptions and procedures to know. A protected tenant (a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or a parent or caretaker with custody of one) may terminate the rental agreement without penalty or liability, notwithstanding any contrary lease provision, on at least 30 days' written notice with supporting documentation, which may be a signed self-certification on an approved form; the notice can be revoked before you sign a new lease with someone else. A protected tenant may ask you to change the locks within 48 hours; if the perpetrator is a co-tenant, the request must include a court order requiring the perpetrator to leave, and you give new keys to every tenant except that person. You may not disclose a tenant's victim status to harass, retaliate or recover possession. In an ejectment, name every adult tenant on the lease so the judgment reaches all of them, and attach the rental agreement and termination notice to the complaint.

title: No Jury Waiver in Residential Leases
bodyText: A Vermont residential lease should not contain a jury-trial waiver. Vermont's ejectment statute gives either party to an eviction case the right to a trial by jury, and the Vermont Constitution declares the right to trial by jury in issues of fact properly tried to a jury "ought to be held sacred." Vermont also has a standard-form contract statute: when a contract is drafted by one side and only one party is an individual who had no meaningful opportunity to negotiate, such as a form lease from a business landlord to an individual tenant, a waiver of the individual's right to a jury trial or to bring a class action is presumed substantively unconscionable. A court that finds the term unconscionable may refuse to enforce it or the whole contract, and if you tried to enforce it, may find an unfair and deceptive practice and award up to $1,000 in statutory damages per term plus attorney's fees. The same statute presumes unconscionable a waiver of punitive damages, a shortened time to sue, an out-of-state venue and excessive claim fees. Leave these terms out of residential leases.

title: No Key Control Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring a written key-control policy, restricting staff access to master keys, or requiring background checks of employees who can enter tenants' units, whatever the size of the complex. The rules that do apply govern entry, not key handling. You may enter a unit with the tenant's consent (which may not be unreasonably withheld), or between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, supply agreed services or show the unit; without consent or notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property. These limits apply to your employees and contractors who hold keys, and entering in other circumstances, or using keys to lock a tenant out, can expose you to illegal-eviction damages and attorney's fees. A protected tenant (a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking) may require you to change the locks within 48 hours, and if you do not, may change them and must give you a key. Good practice: log key issuance, limit master keys to staff who need them, re-key between tenants, and screen employees who have unit access.

title: Keys and Lock Changes
bodyText: Vermont regulates locks only in limited situations, so key and lock rules are mostly lease terms. A protected tenant (a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or a parent or caretaker with custody of one) may ask you to change the locks within 48 hours, notwithstanding any contrary lease provision; if the perpetrator is a co-tenant, the request must include a court order requiring that person to leave, and you give new keys to every other tenant. If you do not change the locks as requested, the protected tenant may change them without your permission but must use locks and installation of equal or better quality, notify you within 24 hours and give you a key. Unless you agree otherwise, the protected tenant pays for the new locks, and you may not unreasonably refuse a request to install additional security measures such as a camera. Outside that rule, a lease may require tenants to get your consent before changing locks, to give you a duplicate key, and to return all keys at the end, and may charge the reasonable cost of re-keying for unreturned keys. You may never change locks or withhold keys to remove a tenant; possession can be recovered only through court.

title: Penalties for Using Banned Terms
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute makes prohibited lease terms unenforceable but sets no separate penalty for knowingly including one. Any provision that attempts to circumvent the statute's obligations and remedies is unenforceable and void, a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void, and since July 1, 2026 a rental agreement may not prohibit a tenant from possessing cannabis on the premises or using non-inhaled cannabis inside the unit (a ban on smoking or vaping it is allowed). The newer cannabis section states its own prohibition but no separate remedy. Penalties come from other laws. Vermont's consumer protection act covers rental housing: a tenant who relied on, or was damaged by, an unfair or deceptive practice may recover damages or the consideration paid, attorney's fees and exemplary damages up to three times the consideration. Under the standard-form contract statute, if a business landlord tries to enforce a presumptively unconscionable term against an individual tenant (such as a jury or class-action waiver, an out-of-state venue, a punitive-damages waiver, a shortened time to sue or excessive claim fees) and the court finds it unconscionable, the court may award up to $1,000 in statutory damages per term plus attorney's fees. Remove void terms rather than relying on a severability clause.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: When you breach the lease or your statutory duties, a Vermont tenant has several routes, and the lease cannot take them away. For habitability problems that materially affect health and safety, after actual notice from the tenant, a government agency or a qualified independent inspector and your failure to repair within a reasonable time, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, get an injunction, recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or terminate on reasonable notice. For a minor defect that breaches the statute or a material lease provision, the tenant may repair it after 30 days and deduct the reasonable cost, up to half a month's rent. Illegal eviction, including a willful utility shutoff or a lockout, lets the tenant recover injunctive relief, damages, costs and attorney's fees. Retaliation gives the tenant damages, attorney's fees and a defense to eviction. Wrongly keeping a deposit forfeits your right to withhold any of it, and willful withholding costs double plus fees. Fair housing violations bring Human Rights Commission complaints, punitive damages and fees. None of these remedies is available for conditions the tenant or the tenant's guests caused. Respond to written repair requests promptly and keep records.

title: Entry Rules
bodyText: Vermont sets three entry routes. You may enter with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold. Without consent, you may enter between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice only to inspect when necessary, make necessary or agreed repairs, alterations or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors; the same 48-hour rule covers showings and repair work alike. You may enter without consent or notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or to property. A tenant's repair request can serve as consent for that repair if the tenant agrees to a time, but confirm it in writing. Vermont's statute sets no special penalty for unlawful or harassing entry and no landlord remedy for refused access, but entry that denies the tenant possession is an illegal eviction carrying damages and attorney's fees, and a tenant who unreasonably refuses lawful access may be in breach. After a code inspection, tenants must allow access for ordered repairs on the normal notice. Vermont has no statute on landlord-initiated temporary relocation.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to show proof of insurance to tenants or a town, or to register rentals with the state. Some Vermont towns and cities run their own rental registration or inspection programs that may ask about insurance, so check the municipality. Insurance appears indirectly in the lead law. If lead hazards make liability insurance hard to obtain for owners of pre-1978 rental housing, the Commissioner of Financial Regulation may, after a hearing, order insurers to provide or continue coverage for owners who comply with the lead law; that protection depends on your compliance. Carrying landlord liability coverage is still prudent: Vermont voids lease provisions that circumvent your statutory obligations, a fire-code violation is prima facie evidence of negligence, and the lead law imposes a duty of reasonable care to prevent lead hazards. You may require tenants to carry renter's insurance by lease; a standard renter's policy typically does not cover flood damage, as the state flood disclosure form notes.

title: No Landlord Lien
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give residential landlords no lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent and no distress for rent. Vermont's Uniform Commercial Code article on secured transactions expressly does not apply to a landlord's lien, and no statute authorizes a lease clause letting you seize and sell a tenant's property. Self-help is barred: you may not directly or indirectly deny a tenant access to and possession of the tenant's property except through proper judicial process. To collect unpaid rent, sue for a money judgment (ejectment judgments include rents due) and then use ordinary collection, subject to the statutory exemptions protecting household goods, a vehicle, tools of the trade and other property. The only points where you may hold or dispose of a tenant's belongings are set by statute: after abandonment, you must mail notice and store unclaimed property safely for 60 days, and the tenant may reclaim it by describing it and paying reasonable storage costs; property left after the tenant gave actual notice of vacating, or left at the end of the rental agreement, may be disposed of without notice; and after an eviction, property remaining 15 days after the writ is served or you are restored to possession, whichever is later, may be disposed of.

title: Your Repair and Habitability Duties
bodyText: In every Vermont rental, written or oral, you warrant that you will deliver and maintain, for the whole tenancy, premises that are safe, clean, fit for human habitation and compliant with building, housing and health regulations; the warranty cannot be waived. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code spells out your duties as owner, including: arrange removal of trash, recyclables and food scraps at least weekly and provide receptacles; keep common areas clean and free of infestation, and exterminate inside a unit when the infestation results from your failure to maintain the building or affects two or more units; provide heat able to keep 65°F; keep electrical systems safe and provide required outlets and lighting; and keep the foundation, roof, walls, windows, stairs, chimneys and other structural elements weathertight, watertight, rodent-proof, in good repair and free of moisture that can cause mold. You may not shut off required utilities except temporarily for repairs or emergencies, or let a noncompliant unit. Tenants who give notice may use rent withholding, injunctions, damages and termination for serious problems, and repair-and-deduct for minor defects not fixed within 30 days. A town may recover its expenses of maintaining a building it finds uninhabitable as a lien on the property.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration
bodyText: Vermont has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing requirement for long-term rentals, no county or assessor registration, and no rule that an out-of-state owner must hire an in-state broker or keep an in-state contact for tenants. General business registration can still reach you: an individual renting under an assumed business name, and any partnership, must register with the Secretary of State within 10 days after starting, and a nonresident registrant must name a Vermont agent for service of process; an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here needs a certificate of authority, and an LLC's application names a Vermont agent; and until the registration is made the business may not sue (11 V.S.A. §§ 1621, 1626, 4112 and 4119; 11A V.S.A. §§ 15.01-15.02; see `edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-vt`). Some Vermont towns and cities run their own rental registration or inspection programs, so check local rules where the property is. Short-term rental operators register with the Department of Taxes for meals and rooms tax and must post the account number in ads. Vermont's real estate licensing law excludes leaseholds from its definition of real estate and defines brokerage in terms of sales and exchanges, and an owner managing its own property (and its regular employees) is excluded, so the statute does not on its face require a license to lease or manage residential rentals for others; the Real Estate Commission's rules were not reviewed. What state law does require: when your interest in the property ends, the security deposit transfers to the new landlord, who must give tenants actual notice of the new landlord's name and address and that the deposit was transferred. Give tenants a reliable address for notices and repair requests.

title: Possession and Money Claims
bodyText: In Vermont, possession and money can be pursued in the same case. In an ejectment action, if the court finds you are entitled to possession, you get judgment for possession and for rents due, damages and costs, plus reasonable attorney's fees when a written rental agreement provides for them. You may also ask the court early in the case to order the tenant to pay rent into court as it accrues; if the tenant fails to pay as ordered, you are entitled to judgment for immediate possession. A tenant who stays after the tenancy ends without your express consent is liable for possession, damages and costs. If a tenant abandons the unit, the tenant remains liable for rent until the lease expires, but if you re-rent before then, the agreement ends on the date the new tenancy begins. You may keep deposit money only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, required unpaid charges and removal of abandoned articles, with an itemized statement within 14 days. A tenant's breach of the statutory duties not to damage the premises or disturb others also entitles you to damages, costs and attorney's fees and is a ground to terminate.

title: No Self-Cure Billed as Rent
bodyText: Vermont has no statute letting you fix a tenant's breach yourself and bill the cost as rent, and no procedure like the uniform act's landlord self-help remedy. What the statutes provide instead: you may enter on at least 48 hours' notice, between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., to make necessary or agreed repairs, and without notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property. If the tenant deliberately or negligently damages the premises, fixtures, mechanical systems or furnishings, or causes code noncompliance, you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the breach is a ground for a 30-day termination notice. At move-out you may deduct the cost of damage beyond normal wear and tear from the deposit with an itemized statement. Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, so a lease term requiring the tenant to reimburse repair costs makes that charge part of what the tenant owes under the lease; whether an unpaid repair charge alone supports a 14-day nonpayment notice is not settled by statute, so bill it separately and pursue it as damages if unpaid.

title: Assigning Yard and Upkeep Chores
bodyText: Vermont has no rule that tenant chores such as mowing, raking, watering or shoveling must be in a separate signed document or supported by extra payment, so your lease may assign routine yard upkeep to the tenant, as the library's landscaping clause does. Two Vermont limits apply. First, you cannot shift your own legal duties. The warranty of habitability cannot be waived, any lease provision that attempts to circumvent the rental statute's obligations is void, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code says a rental agreement that transfers responsibilities between owner and occupant is not effective for code purposes. So do not use chore clauses to make the tenant responsible for code items such as trash and recycling arrangements, heat, plumbing, electrical, structural repairs or pest control in common areas; and remember that safe access and lighted entrances are code requirements in multi-unit buildings. Second, describe chores clearly and provide the tools or equipment needed, and do not charge for chores the tenant performs as lease consideration. A tenant who negligently damages landscaping or irrigation equipment is responsible for the damage.

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not limit late fees on residential rent: there is no cap, no required grace period, no rule that the fee be disclosed in a particular way, and no limit on charging once per payment. (The statutory late-fee cap you may see applies to self-storage units, not dwellings.) Late fees are still shaped by other rules. Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, so a late fee is part of what the tenant owes under the lease; put the amount and when it applies in the written lease from the start, because adding or raising a fee during the tenancy is a rent increase that takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after 60 days' actual notice. Accepting a partial payment does not waive your nonpayment remedies, and a tenant served with a nonpayment notice keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering the rent due through the end of that rental period. Keep the fee reasonable and tied to your costs of late payment: an excessive fee may be challenged as an unenforceable penalty or an unfair practice under Vermont's consumer protection act, and courts' treatment of penalties was not searched.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no provision on crime-free lease addenda, on requiring tenants to cooperate with police, or on limiting penalties for tenants who call police or emergency services. Related rules shape any such clause. You may terminate on 14 days' notice for criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence that threaten the health or safety of other residents, and on 30 days' notice for breach of a material lease term, but every termination must go through court. Fair housing law protects victims of abuse, sexual assault and stalking: you may not refuse to rent to, set different terms for, or harass a person because the person is a victim, and you may not disclose a tenant's victim status to harass, retaliate, pressure the tenant to leave or recover possession. A protected tenant may also end the lease early or require a lock change. Do not use a clause that treats a tenant's calls for police help, or police responses to abuse against the tenant, as a lease violation; enforcing it against a victim risks a fair housing claim. Clauses aimed at the tenant's own criminal conduct that threatens other residents are consistent with Vermont's termination statute. Two duties bind every person, you and your staff included. Whoever discovers the body of a person who died from violence, suddenly while in apparent good health, unattended by a physician, by casualty, suicide or injury, or in any unusual, unnatural or suspicious manner, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the nearest medical examiner (18 V.S.A. § 5205(a)). And a person who knows that another is exposed to grave physical harm must give reasonable assistance if it can be done without danger to themselves and no one else is already helping; a willful failure carries a fine of up to $100 (12 V.S.A. § 519). Vermont's child and vulnerable-adult abuse reporting duties bind listed professionals and care providers, not landlords as such, though anyone may report (33 V.S.A. §§ 4913(a), (c), (e) and 6903(a)-(b)).

title: Vermont Lead Law Duties
bodyText: Besides the federal lead disclosure, Vermont's lead law imposes ongoing duties on owners of rental target housing: most units built before 1978, except 0-bedroom units and elderly or disability-only buildings, and except a rented room in your own home, unless a child six or younger lives or is expected to live there; transient units rented for 30 days or less are also excluded. Unless a licensed inspector certifies the property lead-free, you must follow lead-safe renovation, repair, painting and maintenance (RRPM) practices: regularly inspect painted surfaces, promptly and safely repair deteriorated paint, and do specialized cleaning after work that disturbs paint and at tenant turnover; have that work done by trained people (licensed supervisors if paid); avoid prohibited practices such as open-flame burning or dry sanding; and file a compliance statement with the Department of Health. Before a lease, give approved tenants the Department's lead materials and your latest compliance statement. If a young child in your unit has an elevated blood lead level, the Department may inspect and set a plan, and you must address the lead hazards within your control, though interim controls may suffice. You owe tenants reasonable care to prevent lead hazards; compliance shields you from certain habitability claims, and violations can bring penalties of up to $5,000 each.

title: Lead Compliance Statement and Lead-Free Exemption
bodyText: Vermont has no lead-safe certificate that must be attached to a lease as an exhibit. Two documents serve similar purposes. First, unless your pre-1978 rental is exempt, you must file a lead-safe maintenance compliance statement with the Department of Health, and before entering into a lease you must give approved tenants a copy of your most recent compliance statement along with the Department's approved lead materials; you may attach them to the lease packet, but they must actually be given before the lease is signed. Second, a property is exempt from the maintenance-practice requirements if a licensed lead-based paint inspector-risk assessor's written inspection report states that all accessible surfaces are free of lead-based paint and the owner and anyone doing the work have a copy; you must send the report to the Department for review and determination of exempt status. The exemption is lost if later work creates lead hazards or exposes previously inaccessible components, and a remodeled property is not exempt unless the full requirements are met. When you sell rental target housing, the seller must verify that a current compliance statement has been filed.

title: No Lease Completeness Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no rule that an incomplete lease is a breach by you. (The blank-space rules in Vermont's statutes cover consumer credit contracts and rent-to-own agreements for goods, not dwelling leases.) Fill in or strike every blank anyway, because several Vermont rules work only if the written lease states them: the court may award you attorney's fees in an eviction only when a written rental agreement provides for them; you may condition or prohibit subleasing, and use the expedited hearing against unauthorized occupants, only under the terms of a written agreement; a tenant's one-rental-period notice to quit applies unless inconsistent with a written agreement; no-cause notice periods differ depending on whether there is a written agreement and its stated term; and an automatically renewing lease of a year or more needs bold, plain-language renewal terms. An eviction complaint must attach a copy of the rental agreement, so a complete, signed copy is your best evidence. Give the tenant a copy too.

title: What a Vermont Lease Must Say
bodyText: Vermont has no single list of terms a residential lease must contain, and an oral rental agreement is valid. Content rules arise from particular statutes. Some things must be given separately, not in the lease: the FEMA flood-hazard disclosure, in a separate document on the state form at or before signing, and for pre-1978 housing the Department of Health's lead materials and your latest compliance statement before the lease. Some terms work only if written into the lease: attorney's fees in an eviction, conditions or a ban on subleasing, and a different tenant notice to quit. An automatically renewing lease with an initial term of a year or more must state the renewal terms clearly and conspicuously in plain language in bold-face type, the tenant must opt in, and you must send a renewal notice 30 to 60 days ahead. An agreement to arbitrate needs a signed, prominent acknowledgment in statutory words. Some terms are forbidden: waivers of the warranty of habitability, provisions circumventing the rental statute's obligations or remedies, and, from July 1, 2026, bans on possessing cannabis or using non-inhaled cannabis in the unit. In a business landlord's form lease, out-of-state venue, jury or class waivers and similar terms are presumed unconscionable.

title: No Lease Copy Duty
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to give a residential tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no rule that failing to do so is a defense to enforcing it. (A copy rule exists for mobile home park leases, which are outside this library.) Copies still matter. If you file an eviction, a copy of the rental agreement, if any, and of any termination notice must be attached to the complaint, and a motion for expedited relief against an unauthorized occupant must include a copy of the lease. Several Vermont rules depend on what the written lease says, such as attorney's fees in an eviction, sublease conditions and the tenant's notice to quit, so a tenant who never received the lease is well placed to dispute those terms. Some documents must be given before signing regardless: the flood-zone disclosure form and, for pre-1978 housing, the lead materials and compliance statement. If you send notices or the lease electronically, the tenant must have agreed to electronic transactions and be able to keep and print what you send. Best practice: give every tenant a complete signed copy at signing and keep proof of delivery.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Vermont statute requires a tenant to initial a lease term for it to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough as far as the statutes go. Initials cannot save a term the law forbids: a waiver of the warranty of habitability or a provision that circumvents the rental statute's obligations or remedies is void however it is signed. A few Vermont documents have their own signing or assent rules instead. An automatically renewing lease with an initial term of one year or longer may renew automatically only if the renewal terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in bold-face type and the tenant, in addition to accepting the lease, takes an affirmative action to opt in, such as a separate checkbox or signature. An agreement to arbitrate is enforceable only with a written acknowledgment of arbitration in the statutory words, signed by each party and displayed prominently if it is in the lease. The flood-zone disclosure is a separate form with signature lines for you and the tenant. Use initials as evidence that the tenant saw an important term, but do not rely on them to make an unlawful term enforceable.

title: Lease Length and Recording
bodyText: Vermont sets no maximum or minimum length for a residential lease, and the rental statute's protections apply to long leases as well as short ones. Length matters in three ways. First, an agreement that cannot be performed within one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged, so put any lease longer than a year in a signed written lease. Second, a lease for more than one year from the making of it is not effective against anyone other than you and your heirs, such as a later buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded in the town land records; instead of recording the whole lease, you may record an acknowledged notice or memorandum of lease listing the parties, renewal and extension rights, addresses, execution date, term with start and end dates, property description, any purchase option or right of first refusal, assignment restrictions and where the original is kept. Third, an automatically renewing lease with an initial term of a year or more must meet the bold-type, opt-in and advance-notice rules for automatic renewal. Tenancies over two years also lengthen your no-cause termination notice.

title: No Rule on Lease-Type Parity
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to offer the same rent or terms to a tenant without a written lease (or on a month-to-month or week-to-week basis) as to a tenant on a fixed-term written lease, and no limit on how much the rent offered for the two may differ. Several Vermont rules turn on the type of tenancy, so weigh them when you choose. With no written agreement, a no-cause termination needs 60 days' notice for monthly rent (90 days after two years) or 21 days for weekly rent; with a written agreement, notice must come at least 30 days before the end of the stated term (60 days after two years), or 7 days under a written week-to-week agreement. Shared housing in your own residence has 15-day and 7-day periods. Subleasing may be conditioned or prohibited only under a written agreement, and attorney's fees in an eviction are available only if a written agreement provides for them. A tenant may end a tenancy on one rental period's notice unless that is inconsistent with a written agreement. Rent increases always need 60 days' actual notice. Offering different terms must never track a protected characteristic.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Vermont sets no minimum type size for a printed residential lease and no evidence rule penalizing small print in a lease. Type-size and format rules apply only to particular provisions or documents. An automatically renewing lease with an initial term of one year or longer must state the renewal terms clearly and conspicuously, in plain, unambiguous language, in bold-face type, and the tenant must separately opt in. An agreement to arbitrate needs a signed acknowledgment in the statutory words, displayed prominently if it appears in the lease. The flood-zone disclosure must be a separate written document substantially in the state form. If your mortgage lender forecloses, the lender's summons to tenants must carry a statutory notice in at least 14-point type; that duty is the lender's, not yours. Other Vermont type-size rules (consumer credit, rent-to-own goods, self-storage, motor vehicle rentals) do not apply to dwelling leases. Use a readable size anyway, generally 10 to 12 point, because a court weighing whether a form-lease term is unconscionable may consider whether the tenant had a meaningful opportunity to see and negotiate it.

title: No Liquidated Damages Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute permitting or forbidding a liquidated-damages clause in a residential lease, but several rules limit one. A tenant who has the statutory right to terminate, such as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking giving 30 days' notice with documentation, does so without penalty or liability despite any contrary lease term. A tenant who abandons a fixed-term lease stays liable for rent until the lease ends, but if you re-rent the unit before then the agreement ends on the date the new tenancy begins, so a fixed fee that keeps running after re-renting conflicts with that rule. Deposit money may be kept only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid required charges and removal of abandoned articles, never as a set forfeit; missing the 14-day itemized return forfeits it, and willful withholding costs double. Vermont's rental statute voids lease terms that circumvent its obligations and remedies. A reasonable early-termination option the tenant may choose is generally safer than a penalty for leaving, and whether a court would enforce a particular agreed-damages amount depends on general contract law, which was not searched.

title: No Lockouts
bodyText: Vermont forbids locking out a tenant for unpaid rent, even if the lease allows it. You may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service being supplied to the tenant, except temporary interruptions for emergency repairs, and you may not directly or indirectly deny a tenant access to and possession of the rented premises, or of the tenant's property, except through proper judicial process. A tenant hurt by an illegal eviction may sue for an injunction, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees; you can recover fees from the tenant only if the court finds the suit was frivolous or brought only to harass. A lease clause authorizing a lockout, lock change or utility shutoff for nonpayment is void as an attempt to circumvent the statute's obligations and remedies, and Vermont has no opt-in self-help procedure. For unpaid rent, serve a written termination notice giving at least 14 days, accept a full tender of the rent due through the end of the rental period if offered, and if the tenant stays, file an ejectment action within 60 days after the termination date; the sheriff executes the writ no sooner than 14 days after service.

title: Shifting Landlord Duties to a Tenant
bodyText: Vermont's Rental Housing Health and Safety Code allocates specific duties between owner and occupant, and a lease cannot reassign them. The Code says no rental agreement provision purporting to transfer responsibilities between owner and occupant, other than as the Code itself imposes, is effective for code purposes, and it contains no item, like common-area trash removal, that a lease may shift on a landlord precondition. The Code's own split: you arrange weekly removal of trash, recyclables and food scraps and provide receptacles, keep common areas clean and free of infestation, exterminate in a unit when the infestation results from your failure to maintain or affects two or more units (and in every rooming unit of a rooming house), and maintain heat, electrical systems and the structure; the occupant keeps the space the occupant exclusively occupies clean and free of infestation, pays to exterminate an infestation caused by the occupant's own failure, uses the unit without creating code violations, and exercises reasonable care with the structure. Separately, Vermont's rental statute voids any waiver of the warranty of habitability and any provision circumventing the statute's obligations. A lease may still decide who pays for services the law leaves to agreement, such as heating fuel or utilities, as long as code-required facilities remain your responsibility.

title: Energy Charges and Usage Data
bodyText: Vermont has no meter conservation charge or similar energy-efficiency surcharge on a utility account that a landlord must disclose to new tenants or offset against rent, and no statewide energy-efficiency disclosure for rentals. Property-assessed clean energy (PACE) financing is an assessment on the owner's property through a municipal district, with no tenant notice rule located. One related statute matters to owners of multiunit buildings: on your request, the electric distribution company and energy efficiency utility must aggregate and release anonymized monthly energy usage data for the building's units within 30 days, for benchmarking or preparing an energy label. In a building with four or more unit holders, you must first notify each unit holder at least 14 days ahead and let them opt out; in a building with fewer than four, you need each unit holder's signed release authorization, which may be a clause in a lease the tenant signs. If you include such a clause, make it clear and limited to building-level benchmarking or energy labeling. If the lease makes the tenant pay utilities, describe which services and accounts the tenant must carry.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to disclose to a tenant that a rental was used to make methamphetamine, set no cleanup or decontamination standard for former drug labs, impose no ban on re-occupancy and no civil penalty for renting a contaminated unit, and create no duty for a landlord to report a suspected lab to police within a set time. Other rules still matter. Every rental carries a warranty that the premises are safe, clean and fit for human habitation and comply with health regulations, so a unit contaminated by drug manufacturing can breach the warranty and support rent withholding, damages and termination once the tenant gives notice and you fail to repair. Town health officers must investigate conditions that may be a public health hazard and may order hazards removed. Renting a unit while concealing known contamination risks a deceptive-practice claim under Vermont's consumer protection act, which covers rental housing. Criminal drug activity that threatens other residents supports a 14-day termination notice, and a non-tenant caught selling drugs at a dwelling faces next-business-day arraignment and possible stay-away conditions. If you suspect a lab, contact police and have the unit professionally assessed before re-renting.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military installation, airport or air base, or within a noise, clear or accident potential zone, and no tenant termination right tied to such a location. No Vermont statute creates a military impact district with lease disclosures. Towns may adopt airport hazard area bylaws under the state aeronautics law governing land use and building location and size near airports, so check local zoning for any overlay affecting the property. If a property is near an active airfield or training area, telling prospective tenants about noise and flight activity before signing is good practice and helps avoid a later claim that you hid a material fact, since unfair or deceptive acts in rental housing violate Vermont's consumer protection act. The only location disclosure Vermont requires for rentals is the separate FEMA flood-hazard disclosure form, given at or before lease signing.

title: Minor Tenants and Eviction Defendants
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not say whom you must name as defendants in an eviction or bar filing against a minor, and set no special rules for minor tenants. The ejectment complaint names the person who holds possession unlawfully and must attach the rental agreement and termination notice. Name every adult who signed the lease or whose tenancy you accepted; minors living with a parent or guardian are occupants under the adult's tenancy, and Vermont's statutes have no 'all other occupants' rule, so court rules (not reviewed) govern any further naming. In Vermont a person under 18 is a minor. Renting directly to a minor is risky: Vermont's statutes do not address enforcing a minor's lease, so the common-law rule on minors' contracts (not searched) applies. A minor who has been emancipated by court order, or who is on active duty in the armed forces, is treated as an adult for binding contracts, buying or selling real property, and suing and being sued. Fair housing law lets you refuse to rent to a person because the person is under the age of majority, but you may not refuse because a household includes minor children. Practical step: have an adult co-sign or guarantee in writing.

title: Mold and Moisture
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring a written mold disclosure to tenants, but its rental housing code treats moisture and mold as maintenance duties. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, every dwelling unit must be kept free from the regular or periodic appearance of standing water or excessive moisture that may result in visible mold growth; you must keep the foundation, roof, walls, windows and other structural elements weathertight and watertight; and neither you nor the tenant may use vaporizers or humidifiers in a way that raises relative humidity above 60 percent and promotes microorganisms and visible mold. Tenants must exercise reasonable care in using the unit and the structure. Because the warranty of habitability requires compliance with health and housing regulations, persistent leaks or moisture-driven mold can support the tenant's rent withholding, damages and termination remedies once the tenant gives notice and you fail to repair within a reasonable time, and code complaints can lead to inspection, an order not to re-rent the unit until corrected, and penalties. Inspect for leaks and moisture before each tenancy, fix them promptly, and answer tenant questions about past water problems truthfully.

title: Tenant Utility Bills and Liens
bodyText: In Vermont, a tenant's unpaid municipal water or sewer bill can become your problem. Municipal water charges are a lien on the real estate served, in the same manner as property taxes, and the owner or occupant who takes the water is liable for it; municipal sewer charges are likewise a lien on the real estate served, enforceable through tax-collection procedures and, after two years unpaid, through tax-lien enforcement. Vermont's statutes provide no lease clause, affidavit or filing that shields an owner from these liens, whoever's name is on the account. Tenants have protections when an owner's account goes unpaid: the municipality must send a copy of any disconnection notice to the occupant if different from the ratepayer, and a tenant of a dwelling noticed for disconnection may request and pay for continued service or reconnection; if water and sewer are included in the rent, the tenant may deduct those payments from rent, and the utility may not require the tenant to pay more than one billing cycle of arrears. If tenants pay these bills directly, require proof of payment and check the account status with the municipality periodically; keep accounts in your name current.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: To end a Vermont tenancy for unpaid rent, give the tenant actual notice (written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the last known address) that states a specific termination date at least 14 days after the notice is received. Vermont prescribes no wording or state form, and no move-in acknowledgment is needed; the same 14 days applies to a written week-to-week lease. The tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made, and accepting a partial payment does not waive your remedies. Do not rely on e-mail alone: Vermont's electronic-transactions law does not cover notices of default or eviction for a primary residence. If the tenant stays, you must file ejectment within 60 days after the stated termination date and attach the lease and the notice to the complaint. Even after suit, the tenant can end the case by paying into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, with interest and costs, before the writ is executed, but only once in 12 months. A lease cannot shorten or waive these protections. Vermont's statutes say nothing about charging a fee for serving the notice.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposit Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not mention nonrefundable deposits, and they set no notice rule for them. What matters is how Vermont defines the money. A security deposit is any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, that is refundable at the end of the tenancy, and you may keep it only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant had to pay, and removal of abandoned items, returning the rest with an itemized statement within 14 days. Money that is not refundable is not a security deposit; Vermont's rental statute counts all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, other than security deposits, as rent. You may not charge any application fee at all. The cautious course: do not call any payment a "nonrefundable deposit". If you collect a one-time charge, describe it plainly in the lease as a fee for a stated purpose, and treat prepaid last month's rent and any pet or damage money you intend to apply against losses as a refundable security deposit governed by the 14-day return rule.

title: Out-of-State Owners: Agents, Business Names and Entities
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require an out-of-state individual landlord who rents under their own name to name a Vermont agent in the lease or to file an agent designation before suing a tenant, and they do not require tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. If you rent under an assumed business name, though, you must register it with the Secretary of State within 10 days after starting and, as a nonresident, name an agent for service of process in Vermont; until you register you may not maintain an action, or raise a counterclaim or affirmative defense, in a Vermont court, the Secretary of State is your agent for service on claims arising from the business, and the State may collect $50 a day, up to $10,000 a year (11 V.S.A. §§ 1621(a)-(b) and 1626). An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here must obtain a certificate of authority, faces the same bar on suing and the same penalty, and an LLC that transacts business without one appoints the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process (11 V.S.A. §§ 4112, 4113 and 4119; 11A V.S.A. §§ 15.01-15.02). Owning property is not by itself transacting business, but renting it out may be; that is a case-law question. And a court may enter a personal judgment against an owner served outside Vermont whose contacts with the State support one (12 V.S.A. § 913(b)). Related duties still apply. A business entity that owns rentals and is required by Vermont's business-organization laws to keep an agent for service of process must designate a Vermont resident or an authorized business with a place of business here, and keep that information current with the Secretary of State. Every owner of rental property must file a landlord certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes by January 31 each year, listing the renters and the owner's or landlord's name, phone number, e-mail and mailing address. If ownership changes, the new landlord must give tenants actual notice of its name and address with the deposit-transfer statement. Because Vermont notices run by hand delivery or mail to a last known address, state in the lease the name and mailing address where tenants should send notices and rent, and name any local manager who handles repairs and entry.

title: How Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute requires rent-increase and termination notices, among others, to be "actual notice": receipt of a written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the tenant's last known address. If you prove you sent it by first-class or certified mail, receipt is presumed three days after mailing, though the tenant may rebut that. Deposit statements and refunds must likewise be hand-delivered or mailed to the last known address, and a notice that you will dispose of an abandoned tenant's property must be mailed there. Vermont's statutes do not limit who may deliver a notice: you, a manager or anyone else may hand it over, and a sheriff is needed only for court papers. E-mail does not replace these methods. Vermont's electronic-transactions law applies only between parties who agreed to deal electronically, either may refuse further electronic dealings, a record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing is unenforceable against the recipient, a statute's own delivery method still controls, and the law does not reach notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence. Use e-mail for routine communications and as an extra copy, and keep proof of hand delivery or mailing.

title: No Notice Fee Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes neither allow, cap nor ban a fee charged to a tenant for preparing or serving a termination or other notice. Treat such a fee cautiously. Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to or for the benefit of the landlord under the rental agreement, other than a security deposit, so a lease fee is part of the rent and is collected like rent. Termination notices themselves can be delivered by hand or by mail at little cost, so a large fee could look like a penalty. What Vermont does provide: in an ejectment case the court awards the winning landlord possession, rent due, damages and costs, and may award reasonable attorney's fees when a written rental agreement so provides; a tenant who stops an ejectment for unpaid rent by paying into court must pay the rent due, interest and the costs of suit. A security deposit may be kept only for unpaid rent, damage, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant had to pay you, and removal of abandoned property. The cautious course is to charge no separate notice fee and to recover court costs and, if your written lease provides, attorney's fees through the court.

title: No Waiver of Termination Notice
bodyText: A Vermont lease cannot shorten or waive the notice you must give to end a tenancy. Vermont's rental statute makes void any lease provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies it establishes, and the termination notice periods are among them: at least 14 days for unpaid rent, 30 days for breach of a material term, 14 days for criminal or drug activity or violence threatening other residents, and the no-cause periods tied to whether there is a written lease and how long the tenancy has lasted. Each notice must be actual notice with a specific termination date. Two related points. First, the tenant's own notice to end a periodic tenancy (one rental payment period) applies unless inconsistent with a written rental agreement, so a written lease may set the tenant's notice. Second, a fixed-term written lease ends by its terms only if you give the no-cause notice the statute requires before the term expires. If a building is being converted to condominiums, tenants' conversion notice rights cannot be waived in any lease. Do not include "tenant waives notice to quit" or "lease ends without notice" language; it is unenforceable and can confuse your eviction case.

title: No Move-Out Form Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no rule on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep the form to what the tenant's notice needs. Unless your written lease says otherwise, a tenant ends a periodic tenancy by actual notice at least one rental payment period before the termination date stated in the notice. Do not use the form to obtain waivers: any rental agreement term that attempts to circumvent the tenant's statutory rights or remedies is void, and a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void. Two practical points make the form worth having. Asking for the move-out date matters because your 14-day deadline to return the deposit with an itemized statement runs from the date the tenant vacates if the tenant told you that date. And property left behind after a tenant gives actual notice of having vacated, or after the tenant vacates at the end of the rental agreement, may be disposed of without notice or liability. Ask for a forwarding address, since deposit refunds and statements go to the tenant's last known address.

title: Nuisance and Drug Premises
bodyText: Vermont has no nuisance-receivership, rent-escrow or building-closure statute aimed at rental owners, and no rule requiring the lease to summarize a criminal statute. Nuisance still matters in three ways. As a tenant duty, every tenant must not disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment and must make guests behave; a violation lets you recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees and is ground for termination on at least 30 days' actual notice. When the problem is criminal activity, illegal drug activity or violence that threatens other residents' health or safety, the notice may be 14 days. As owner exposure, a dwelling resorted to for using regulated drugs or used for illegally keeping or selling them is a common nuisance that no one may keep or maintain; knowingly permitting a dwelling you own or control to be used for illegal drug sales is a crime (up to two years and $15,000), but not if you take action to address it; and knowingly permitting a building you control to be used for prostitution is prohibited. As public abatement, towns may sue for an injunction to abate public nuisances and may adopt nuisance ordinances. Act promptly on reports, document your response, and never evict a tenant for being a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking.

title: Rules That Depend on the Lease
bodyText: Several Vermont rules turn on what your written lease says; an oral or silent agreement gets the statutory default. (1) Attorney's fees: in an eviction case the court may award you reasonable attorney's fees only when a written rental agreement so provides. (2) Subletting: you may condition or prohibit subleasing, and require written notice of a sublessee's name and contact information, under a written rental agreement; a written ban also allows an expedited hearing against an unauthorized occupant. (3) Tenant's notice: a tenant may end a periodic tenancy on one rental period's actual notice unless that is inconsistent with a written rental agreement. (4) Your no-cause notice periods differ for written and unwritten agreements. (5) Heat: if the lease has you provide heat, you must supply a reasonable amount at all times. (6) Promised repairs and services: the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy covers minor defects breaching a material lease provision. (7) Protected tenants pay for lock changes unless you agree otherwise. (8) From July 1, 2026, a lease may ban smoking or vaping cannabis on the premises but not possession, or other use inside the unit. (9) A lease of one year or more may renew automatically only with bold-face terms, the tenant's opt-in and a 30-60 day notice. The lease cannot change deposit-return rules, habitability or termination notices.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no lease disclosure for a former military ordnance or munitions site near the property, for a planned demolition of the building, or for a tenant's gas or electric meter that also serves common areas or other units. Related rules still apply. Vermont's required pre-lease disclosures are the flood-hazard disclosure in a separate document and, for pre-1978 rental target housing, the lead materials and compliance statement. Demolition plans do not change how you end a tenancy: you must give the ordinary statutory notice, which depends on whether there is a written lease and how long the tenant has lived there; a state or municipal order to close or demolish an unsafe building is served on recorded interest holders. On utilities, you may not willfully interrupt or terminate a utility service supplied to the tenant except temporarily for emergency repairs, and a deposit may be applied to utility charges only if the tenant was required to pay them to you or to a utility. The cautious course is to tell the tenant in writing if the tenant's meter serves any space outside the unit and to put any cost-sharing in the lease.

title: Facilities Vermont Requires
bodyText: Vermont's warranty of habitability requires premises that are safe, clean, fit for habitation and code-compliant, with heating facilities capable of safely providing a reasonable amount of heat and adequate hot and cold water (summer and hunting-camp rentals are exempt from the heat and water part). The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code lists specific facilities every rental unit needs: kitchen space with a sink; a private bathroom with toilet, sink and tub or shower (two small units may share under strict limits); potable water and sewage connection; hot water at showers and tubs of at least 100°F but below 120°F; heat able to hold 65°F in habitable rooms, kitchens and baths when it is below 55°F outside, with no unvented fuel-fired space heaters; trash, recycling and food-scrap receptacles and weekly removal; screens on operable windows; an openable window or door in each habitable room; vented bathrooms and dryers; minimum outlets and lights; lighted entrances and common areas; and a weathertight, watertight, rodent-proof structure. Rented residential buildings must have properly installed carbon monoxide detectors. You may not let a unit that fails the Code. Vermont's statutes do not require deadbolts, door viewers, a stove or a refrigerator; if you supply appliances, a lease promise to maintain them is enforceable.

title: No Owner Identity Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant, at or before the start of a tenancy, the name and address of the owner or of a property manager or agent, and no statute bars an eviction because such a disclosure was not made. Identity comes up in three other places. When your interest in the unit ends, for example on a sale, the security deposit must be transferred to the new landlord, and the new landlord must give the tenant actual notice of its name and address with a statement that the deposit was transferred. Every owner of rental property must file an annual landlord certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes by January 31 listing the owner's or landlord's name and contact information. If you have been served with a foreclosure complaint, you must tell each new tenant who signs a rental agreement that the premises are the subject of a pending foreclosure and that the tenant may have to vacate on 30 days' notice, or longer if federal law requires, if you cannot redeem. Because tenants send repair and termination notices to you by hand or mail, put the owner's or manager's name and mailing address in the lease.

title: No Owner Move-In Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give an owner no special right to end a tenancy early to move in, and they do not regulate an owner-move-in ground. What they do provide are no-cause terminations. With no written lease, you may end a monthly tenancy for no cause on at least 60 days' actual notice (90 days if the tenant has lived there more than two years), or a weekly tenancy on 21 days; if you have contracted to sell the building, 30 days. With a written lease, a no-cause notice must be given at least 30 days before the end of the stated term (60 days after two years), or 7 days for a written week-to-week agreement. The statute ties written-lease no-cause termination to the end of the term and voids lease terms that circumvent its obligations, so a clause letting you end a fixed term early to move in is untested; do not rely on one without legal advice. If you may need the unit, use a shorter term or a month-to-month agreement. Any termination must not be retaliatory or discriminatory, the notice must state the termination date, and possession still requires a court ejectment if the tenant stays. Shared housing in your own residence has its own 15-day or 7-day notice.

title: Parking Is a Lease Term
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to provide parking for a rental or say how spaces are assigned, so parking is a lease term. Two parts of the rental statute shape how it works. First, Vermont counts all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, other than a security deposit, as rent, so a parking charge is rent: it is payable when and where agreed, and an increase takes effect only on the first day of a rental period following at least 60 days' actual notice. Second, the premises you must keep up include grounds, areas and facilities whose use is promised to the tenant, so a parking space the lease promises becomes part of the premises; if you promise it, keep it usable, including through the winter. State the space or area, any charge, and any vehicle rules in the lease or a signed addendum. Building entrances and common areas must be adequately lighted under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code. Removing a vehicle is limited: see the separate vehicle-removal row. Local zoning or parking ordinances may also apply.

title: Removing Vehicles From Your Property
bodyText: Vermont's towing law for private property reaches only an "abandoned motor vehicle": one left on the property without the consent of the owner or person in control for more than 48 hours if it has a valid registration plate and intact public VIN, or for any time if it lacks a valid plate or VIN or a law enforcement officer has asked that it be towed. A landowner, which includes a person who leases or otherwise controls the property, may move such a vehicle elsewhere on its property or have a towing service remove it without civil liability to the vehicle's owner, but must immediately notify the local police with the plate number, VIN if available, make, model and color, and must apply to the Department of Motor Vehicles for an abandoned-vehicle certification within 90 days. The towing service may charge a reasonable fee to the vehicle owner or the landowner. A tenant's car parked with your permission is not abandoned, so a lease rule should say when permission ends (for example, an unregistered or inoperable vehicle, or one in an unassigned space). Your town may also have an ordinance on removing unauthorized vehicles from private lots. Never block, boot or tow a tenant's car outside these rules.

title: Rights a Vermont Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Vermont has a general non-waiver rule for its rental statute and several specific ones. Generally, no rental agreement may contain a provision that attempts to circumvent, or does circumvent, the obligations and remedies of Vermont's residential rental chapter; such a provision is unenforceable and void. That reaches the deposit rules, entry limits, notice periods, habitability remedies, repair-and-deduct, the ban on self-help eviction and the anti-retaliation rule. Specific sections add: a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void; a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking may end the lease on 30 days' notice, and may require a lock change, notwithstanding any contrary lease term; from July 1, 2026, a lease may not ban possessing cannabis or using it inside the unit other than smoking or vaping; lease terms shifting Rental Housing Health and Safety Code duties between owner and occupant are ineffective for Code purposes; condominium-conversion rights cannot be waived; and the right to stop dealing electronically cannot be waived. Under consumer law, a confession-of-judgment clause is void, and in a standard-form lease terms waiving a jury trial, class actions or punitive damages, shortening limitation periods, requiring out-of-state venue or imposing excessive claim fees are presumed unconscionable, with statutory damages if you try to enforce one found unconscionable.

title: No Scheduled-Service Entry Exception
bodyText: Vermont has no exception letting you enter a unit without notice for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes, smoke-alarm checks or pest treatment, even if the lease says so. Without the tenant's consent at the time, you may enter to supply agreed services, make necessary or agreed repairs, inspect, or show the unit only between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. and on no less than 48 hours' notice. Entry without consent or notice is allowed only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or to property. You may always enter with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold, so the practical approach for recurring services is to send a notice at least 48 hours ahead for each visit, or to agree with the tenant on a specific date and time. Vermont voids lease provisions that circumvent its rental statute, so do not rely on a lease clause giving blanket advance permission to enter without notice. If a state inspector orders repairs, the inspection report tells the tenant that you must have access to make them, consistent with these same entry rules.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Vermont's statutes set no statewide limit on how many people may live in a rental unit, no persons-per-bedroom or floor-area standard, and no neighbor standing to enforce one; the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code sets facility standards but no occupant count. Towns may adopt housing ordinances with minimum floor space per occupant, so check local rules. The lease may name the tenants and authorized occupants. Three Vermont rules shape how you use that list. First, fair housing law bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because a person intends to live with minor children; Vermont's exemption applies only where the unit is inadequate under occupancy laws and ordinances to house everyone who intends to live there, so tie any limit to a genuine code limit. Second, under a written lease you may condition or prohibit subleasing and require written notice of any sublessee's name and contact information; where the written lease prohibits subleasing, a person occupying without right can be removed through an expedited court hearing. Third, an unauthorized occupant is a breach of a material term only if the lease makes it one, and termination needs at least 30 days' actual notice. A short-term guest is not an occupant; define guest stays clearly.

title: Pest Control Duties and Notice
bodyText: Vermont's pesticide rule, adopted by the Agency of Agriculture, requires notice. Before a pesticide is applied inside a rental unit, whether by you or by a hired applicator, when the tenant did not ask for the treatment, the owner or landlord must give the tenant written notice at least 24 hours and no more than seven days ahead. The notice may be mailed, sent electronically or handed to the tenant, and must name the applicator or company, the expected date and time, the product and its EPA registration number, the pests treated, and your contact information. On request, you must give the tenant any other information about the application. The notice is not required for an urgent hand or non-powered treatment of stinging insects that threaten someone's health or safety, routine cleaning with antimicrobial products, paint, stain or wood preservative that is not a restricted-use product, a tenant treating their own unit or hiring their own applicator, or treatments injected into closed systems. For outdoor lawn or ornamental-plant treatments at an apartment building, you must post the applicator's notice form in a central area all occupants can reach, or send it to them electronically, at least 24 hours and no more than seven days before; the applicator must post its own notice and warning signs too. What Vermont law does set is who handles pests. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, you must keep all common spaces free of infestation and exterminate there, and you must exterminate inside a unit when the infestation is caused by your failure to maintain the building or exists in two or more units in the building; in a rooming house you are responsible throughout. A tenant must keep the tenant's own unit free of infestation and must pay for extermination when the tenant's failure to maintain the unit caused it. A lease cannot shift these Code duties. Extermination includes removing harborage and food sources as well as treatment. To enter for an inspection or treatment you need the tenant's consent, or 48 hours' notice and entry between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., unless there is imminent danger.

title: Pet Deposits and Fees
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing specific about pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent, so the general money rules decide. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit: Vermont defines a security deposit as any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, that is refundable at the end of the tenancy. It is therefore covered by the deposit rules: you may keep it only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear (pet damage beyond normal wear and tear qualifies), unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay you, and removal of abandoned articles, and you must return it, with an itemized statement, within 14 days after the tenant vacates. Vermont sets no cap on deposits. A nonrefundable pet fee or a monthly pet charge is not a deposit; Vermont counts all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement as rent, so pet rent is rent, and raising it takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice. Do not charge pet rent, fees or deposits for an assistance animal a person with a disability needs; Vermont's fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. State any pet charge clearly in the lease.

title: Pet Rules in Vermont
bodyText: Vermont lets you allow, limit or ban pets by lease; no statute gives tenants, including seniors, a right to keep a pet. The limits come from general rules. Assistance animals: fair housing law bars discriminating against a person who relies on specially trained animals and requires reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, so a no-pets rule must yield for an assistance animal a person with a disability needs. Money: a refundable pet deposit is a security deposit, governed by the 14-day itemized return rule, and pet rent is rent, so increases need 60 days' actual notice. Entry: you may enter only with the tenant's consent, for listed purposes (inspection, repairs, agreed services, showing the unit) on 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., or without notice when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property; removing a pet is not a listed purpose. Removal: you may not deny a tenant access to the tenant's property except through judicial process, so do not seize, board or remove a pet yourself; enforce a pet rule as a breach of a material lease term on 30 days' actual notice and, if needed, in court. If an animal is left behind or in distress, call animal control or the police; abandoning an animal is a crime.

title: No General Plain-Language Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no general plain-language or readability law for residential leases, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers, and no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms. Format rules apply only to particular documents. If a lease of one year or more is to renew automatically for a term longer than one month, the renewal terms must be stated clearly and conspicuously in plain, unambiguous language in bold-face type, and the tenant must separately opt in. The flood-hazard disclosure must be a separate written document substantially in the state's form. If you are an owner served with a foreclosure complaint, you must tell each new tenant about the pending foreclosure. Because Vermont consumer protection law covers real estate, misleading or confusing lease terms can also be challenged as unfair or deceptive, and in a standard-form lease with an individual tenant certain terms, such as jury or class-action waivers and out-of-state venue clauses, are presumed unconscionable. Clear, readable lease terms are the safer course: use plain words, define fees, and do not include provisions Vermont law makes void.

title: No Political Access Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to give political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration volunteers access to your building, and they do not give tenants a right to post political signs in or on a rental. The nearest rule covers common interest communities, such as condominiums: the association may not prohibit a unit owner from displaying the Vermont flag or signs about candidates for public or association office or ballot questions on the unit or an adjoining limited common element, though it may regulate time, place, size, number and manner, and any rule on displaying the United States flag must be consistent with federal law. That protection runs to unit owners, not to their tenants. For an ordinary rental, political signs and building access are lease and house-rule matters. Apply any sign or solicitation rule evenly: Vermont's fair housing law bars different terms or conditions because of protected characteristics such as religious creed or national origin, and you may not retaliate against tenants who organize or join a tenants' union. Towns may also regulate door-to-door selling and signs by ordinance.

title: No Pool Safety Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes impose no pool fence, barrier, lifeguard or pool-safety notice duty on residential landlords, and no statute classifies an apartment or rental-community pool for health-code purposes. Related duties still apply if your rental has a pool or hot tub. Vermont's fire-safety law bars maintaining premises under your control in a manner likely to harm others in case of fire, and the warranty of habitability requires premises that are safe and comply with applicable building, housing and health regulations. A pool you make available to tenants is part of the premises, since premises include facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or promised to the tenant. Public-swimming-pool rules of the Department of Health and local building or zoning codes may set barrier or water-quality standards; those rules were not searched. The cautious course: fence any pool with a self-latching gate, post rules and hours, keep water-quality and drain covers maintained, carry liability insurance, and check with the town and the Department of Health before opening a shared pool.

title: No Portable Cooling Right
bodyText: Vermont gives tenants no statutory right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device, and requires no lease statement about limits on such devices. You also have no statutory duty to provide air conditioning: Vermont's warranty of habitability addresses heat and hot water, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code sets a heating standard (65°F in habitable rooms, kitchens and baths when it is below 55°F outside) plus ventilation rules, including an openable window or door in every habitable room and screens on operable windows. Whether to allow window units is a lease or house-rule matter; if you allow them, address installation, window and screen safety, weight, and who pays the electricity. Two limits apply. A tenant with a disability may need a cooling device as a reasonable accommodation in your rules, which fair housing law requires you to consider. And plug-in solar devices are different: from July 1, 2026, Vermont lets tenants install small plug-in solar devices after notice to you, subject to your reasonable restrictions (see the plug-in solar row). If you supply air conditioning under the lease, a lease promise to maintain it becomes enforceable through the tenant's repair remedies.

title: Plug-In Solar Devices
