bodyText: From July 1, 2026, Vermont lets an electric customer, including a tenant, install plug-in solar devices with a combined inverter capacity of no more than 1,200 watts per meter, connected only to systems with smart meters and temporarily but securely attached to the ground or a structure; no utility approval, fee or interconnection agreement is needed. A tenant must give you at least 10 days' notice of the intent to install. You must respond within 10 days with any reasonable restrictions, which may include requiring the tenant to pay for any required electrical work and to hire a licensed electrician; if you do not respond in time, the tenant may proceed. The tenant may not perform, or hire someone to perform, electrical work on the premises for the installation without your permission, and you cannot be compelled to perform or pay for electrical work. Vermont's condominium patio-railing exception to the renewable-device law does not apply to plug-in solar devices. Answer every notice in writing within 10 days, state reasonable conditions (location, attachment, cords, removal at move-out, damage responsibility), and keep a copy. The statute applies to all landlords, regardless of how many units you own.

title: Building-Size Exemptions
bodyText: Vermont's size tests look at the building or living arrangement, not how many units you own; there is no portfolio-size rule and no general small-landlord exemption from the rental statute. (1) Fair housing: the rental rules do not apply to a unit in a building with three or fewer units where you or a member of your immediate family lives in one of them; both parts must be met, and your advertising must still comply. (2) Shared housing: renting rooms in your own residence with shared living room, kitchen or bathroom can be ended by either side on 15 days' notice (monthly rent) or 7 days (weekly). (3) Lead: a single rented room in a dwelling where the owner lives is not rental target housing unless a child six or younger lives or is expected to live there. (4) Condominium conversion: notice periods differ for buildings of more than five units and five or fewer. (5) Energy data: an owner seeking aggregated utility data needs each unit holder's release, which may be a lease clause, in a building with fewer than four unit holders, and notice with an opt-out in larger buildings. (6) Housing code: only two small units may share a bathroom.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Vermont has no possession bond for residential evictions, at the end of a term or otherwise, and no confessed-judgment mechanism; a consumer's agreement giving a power of attorney to confess judgment, or an agreement of similar effect, is void. Possession comes only through an ejectment action. After a judgment for possession the writ issues the same day unless the court stays it, and the sheriff may put you in possession no earlier than 14 days after serving it. Security for you during the case comes from the rent-into-court procedure: you may move for an order that the tenant pay rent into court while the case is pending, and if the tenant fails to pay as ordered you are entitled to judgment for immediate possession, with a writ served and possession no earlier than 7 days after service. On an appeal to the Supreme Court in an ejectment case, the appealing party must give security, by recognizance or bond approved by the court, within three business days after judgment to cover costs, and an appealing tenant must also secure rent then due and rent that comes due during the appeal. Do not put a bond or confession-of-judgment clause in the lease.

title: Late Move-In
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on what happens if you cannot deliver possession when a lease begins, for example because a prior tenant holds over or work is unfinished; the lease and contract law govern, so the lease should say whether rent abates, when the tenant may cancel and what is refunded. Vermont's warranty of habitability is a covenant to deliver over and maintain safe, clean, fit and code-compliant premises for the whole tenancy, so the unit must be habitable on the start date, and the housing code bars letting a noncompliant unit. If a prior occupant stays, only the courts can remove that person: you must give any required termination notice and bring ejectment, and you may not use self-help. During a tenancy, Vermont imposes no general duty to provide alternate housing when a unit becomes unfit, but a tenant facing a habitability failure that materially affects health and safety, after notice and a reasonable time to repair, may withhold rent for the period, seek an injunction and damages, or end the agreement on reasonable notice. Refund promptly any rent and deposit if the tenancy never starts; a refundable advance is a security deposit governed by the 14-day return rule.

title: Belongings After the Writ
bodyText: After a judgment for possession, the writ issues and the sheriff may put you in possession no earlier than 14 days after serving it. Vermont then lets you dispose of any personal property still in the unit without notice or liability to the tenant or the property's owner 15 days after the writ is served or after you are legally restored to possession, whichever is later. If the court stayed the writ, you may dispose of remaining property one day after you are legally restored to possession. Vermont sets no storage, inventory, care or sale procedure for this period and no separate warehouse option, but until the disposal date the property remains the tenant's, and you may not deny a tenant access to the tenant's property except through judicial process, so keep it intact and let the tenant arrange pickup. Vermont has no animal-specific post-eviction rule; do not abandon or harm an animal left behind (abandonment is cruelty under Vermont law) and call animal control. Vermont gives no special immunity for writ execution beyond the no-liability disposal rule. A person who returns or stays after notice against trespass from you or a law enforcement officer may be prosecuted for unlawful trespass, and entering a residence in violation of a court order carries a higher penalty.

title: Private Well Water
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a landlord to test a private well periodically or to give tenants well-test results. Related rules still matter if a well, spring or other private source supplies your tenants. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires that water to every kitchen sink, bathroom sink and tub or shower come from a regulated public water system or from a private supply free from impurities in amounts that could cause disease or harmful physiological effects under Department of Health testing guidelines for private supplies; any health-based contaminant found elevated in a private supply must be treated down to the maximum contaminant level, or the Vermont health advisory level where none exists. Owners must provide an alternate, adequate and accessible supply for drinking and sanitation during short-term water quality or quantity problems. Before a new groundwater source is first used as a potable supply, whoever owns or controls it must test it for arsenic, lead, uranium, gross alpha radiation, coliform bacteria, nitrate and nitrite, fluoride and manganese and send the results to the Department of Health. Testing a rental's well regularly and keeping the results is the practical way to show Code compliance.

title: What Tenants Must Not Do
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute lists what a tenant must not do, and those duties are implied in every rental agreement. A tenant must not create or contribute to the unit's noncompliance with building, housing and health regulations; must behave, and require anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent to behave, so as not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment; and must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the premises or its fixtures, mechanical systems or furnishings, or deliberately or negligently let anyone else do so. If a tenant violates these duties you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the violation is ground for termination on at least 30 days' actual notice (14 days for criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence, any of which threatens the health or safety of other residents). The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code adds occupant duties: keep the space the tenant exclusively occupies clean and free of trash and infestation, use structural elements with reasonable care, do not run humidifiers above 60% relative humidity, and do not use the unit so as to cause Code violations or health hazards for neighbors. Add other rules, such as pets or smoking, in the lease.

title: Terms a Vermont Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute has no closed list of banned lease terms; instead it voids any provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies of the residential rental chapter, which reaches deposit, entry, notice, habitability, repair, retaliation and illegal-eviction rights. Specific terms Vermont law makes void or ineffective: a waiver of the warranty of habitability; terms blocking a protected tenant's lease termination or lock change; from July 1, 2026, bans on possessing cannabis or using it inside the unit other than smoking or vaping; transfers of housing-code duties between owner and occupant; prospective waivers of condominium-conversion rights; and confessions of judgment. In a standard-form lease with an individual tenant, out-of-state venue, jury or class-action waivers, punitive-damage waivers, shortened limitation periods and excessive claim-fee terms are presumed unconscionable; a court that finds such a term unconscionable when you try to enforce it may award up to $1,000 per term plus costs and attorney's fees. Discriminatory terms violate fair housing law, and automatic renewal of a lease of a year or more is allowed only with bold-face terms and the tenant's opt-in. Vermont has no specific statute on exculpatory or indemnity clauses, home-warranty deductibles or repair fees, but those cannot shift your habitability or code duties, and anything payable to you is rent.

title: No Rule on Repair Promises
bodyText: Vermont has no rule requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date or to be made before the lease is signed. A promise still has consequences. If the promise is a material provision of the rental agreement and you fail to fix a minor defect within 30 days after notice, the tenant may make the repair and deduct the actual, reasonable cost from rent, up to half of one month's rent, giving you actual notice of the cost. You may enter on 48 hours' notice, between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., to make agreed repairs, alterations or improvements. You may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to you of a violation of the rental statute or to a code agency. Separately, every unit must meet the warranty of habitability and the housing code from the start of the tenancy whether or not you promised anything, and a lease cannot accept defects in their place. Because Vermont consumer protection law covers real estate, misrepresenting the condition of a unit or promised work can be an unfair or deceptive act. Put any promised work in the lease or an addendum with a description and target date.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning for rental housing has no Vermont counterpart. Vermont's statutes do not require a landlord to post or give tenants a general warning about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and they tie no chemical list to rentals. Vermont's chemical-safety laws, such as the chemicals-of-high-concern program for children's products and limits on phthalates, bisphenol A and flame retardants, regulate manufacturers and sellers of products, not landlords. The hazard disclosures Vermont does require of landlords are specific: for pre-1978 rental target housing, Department of Health-approved lead materials and a copy of your most recent lead-safe maintenance compliance statement before the lease is signed (with the federal lead disclosure separately); and the flood-hazard disclosure in a separate document at or before signing. Vermont's statutes impose no radon disclosure. Beyond these, keep the unit safe and code-compliant under the warranty of habitability, and if you know of a hazardous condition, telling the tenant in writing is the cautious course; misrepresenting a known hazard can be an unfair or deceptive act under Vermont consumer law.

title: No Property Tax Share Statement
bodyText: Vermont does not require you to give tenants an annual statement of the share of their rent that goes to property taxes, or to state it in the lease or at each rent change. Vermont's tax rule for landlords runs to the state instead: the owner of each rental property must furnish a landlord certificate of rent to the Department of Taxes on or before January 31 each year, on the Commissioner's form, listing each renter, the property's address and School Property Account Number, the owner's or landlord's name and contact information, the type and number of rental units and the number of ADA-accessible units. An owner who knowingly fails to file owes a $200 penalty for each failure. Renters claim Vermont's renter credit on their own income tax filing, and the Department may set the rent figure itself if the rental is not at arm's length. A separate certificate, which does go to the claimant as well as the Department, applies only to an owner who rents out land that forms part of someone's homestead (for example, land under the renter's own home). File the certificate on time each year and keep your renter list current; tenants may ask you to confirm the rent they paid.

title: Protected-Class Questions
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law has no separate rule that bars landlords from asking applicants about protected characteristics or keeping records of them; it bans the discrimination itself and discriminatory statements. That still reaches your application forms and screening. It is unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, marital status, religious creed, color, national origin, citizenship, immigration status or disability, or because a person intends to live with minor children, receives public assistance (including housing assistance) or is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking. A question on an application can be such a statement, and asking about a protected trait creates evidence if you later deny the application. Verifying immigration status is allowed only if federal law requires it. For background or credit checks you must accept an unexpired government ID, an ITIN or a Social Security number, and you may not require a Social Security number. An applicant whose criminal record was expunged may lawfully answer only about records that have not been expunged. Ask every applicant the same neutral questions about income, rental history and references, and keep protected-class information out of your files.

title: Unlawful Use of the Premises
bodyText: No Vermont statute voids or annuls a residential lease automatically because the premises are used for an unlawful purpose such as drug dealing, prostitution or gambling. Vermont handles unlawful use through termination and the courts. When termination is based on criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence that threaten the health or safety of other residents, you may end the tenancy on at least 14 days' actual notice stating the termination date; other unlawful use that breaches a material lease term or a tenant duty (such as disturbing other tenants or creating code violations) requires at least 30 days' actual notice. You must then bring an ejectment action within 60 days after the termination date; possession is recovered only through the court, never by lockout. Owners also have their own exposure: knowingly permitting a dwelling you own or control to be used for illegal drug sales is a crime unless you take action to address it, and knowingly permitting a building you control to be used for prostitution is prohibited. Do not treat a tenant's status as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking as a lease violation. A residential-use or lawful-use clause in the lease makes the breach easier to prove.

title: No Quiet Possession Statute
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that creates a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment running from landlord to tenant. Several statutes protect the same interest. You may not willfully interrupt or terminate a utility service supplied to the tenant, except temporarily for emergency repairs, and you may not deny a tenant access to the unit or to the tenant's property except through judicial process; a tenant harmed by an illegal eviction may sue for an injunction, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Entry is limited to the tenant's consent, listed purposes on 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M., or a reasonable belief of imminent danger. You may not retaliate against a tenant for complaints or tenant-union activity, and fair housing law bars harassing a tenant because of a protected characteristic. The warranty of habitability also runs for the whole tenancy. In the other direction, each tenant must not disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises and must make guests behave, and a breach is ground for termination. The common law may also imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment in leases, but no case law was searched here. Respond promptly to complaints about other tenants' conduct.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require landlords to test rental buildings for radon or to disclose radon information to tenants, do not limit any such duty by floor level, and do not mandate radon-resistant construction for new buildings. Related rules still matter. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires a safe, habitable unit and treatment of any elevated health-based contaminant in a private water supply, and installing a whole-house water treatment system to reduce or eliminate radon in a potable water supply is exempt from Vermont's potable-water permit requirement. The warranty of habitability requires premises that are safe and fit for human habitation and that comply with health regulations. The hazard disclosures Vermont does require of landlords are the lead materials and compliance statement for pre-1978 rental target housing and the flood-hazard disclosure. Radon guidance and any testing standards come from the Department of Health, whose rules were not searched. The cautious course: test lowest-level living spaces, mitigate high results, and if you know results, share them in writing rather than leaving a tenant unaware of a known hazard.

title: Trash, Recycling and Food Scraps
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to give tenants a written notice of where and how to recycle, but Vermont does require recycling service at rentals. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, the owner of any dwelling or rooming house must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for trash, recyclables and food scraps, and must make arrangements for their removal, in accordance with Vermont's solid-waste law, as often as needed to keep the building sanitary and at least once a week. Outdoor receptacles must be durable and cleanable, and those for trash and food scraps must be watertight with fitting covers. You keep common areas free of trash, recyclables and food scraps; each tenant keeps the space the tenant exclusively occupies clean. Statewide, no one may knowingly dispose of mandated recyclables in the trash or in landfills, and licensed haulers must offer to collect recyclables separately. A lease cannot shift the owner's Code duties to tenants. Practical step: post or include in your house rules where the recycling and food-scrap containers are and what goes in each, so tenants can comply.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Vermont gives tenants two chances to stop an eviction for unpaid rent by paying. After a nonpayment notice: the rental agreement does not terminate if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made or tendered; the statute sets no once-a-year limit on this. After you file ejectment: before the writ of possession is executed, a defendant who pays into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, with interest and the costs of suit, ends the case, but a tenant may defeat an ejectment this way only once in 12 months, counted from the day of payment. Vermont prescribes no reservation wording for accepting partial rent: by statute, accepting partial payment does not waive your remedies for nonpayment and is not an accord and satisfaction, and accepting rent after terminating for other reasons, or during an ejectment based on breach or no cause, does not waive the eviction or require dismissal. Still, a short written note that you accept the money without waiving the notice or case avoids disputes. During the case you may also ask the court to order rent paid into court; if the tenant fails to pay as ordered, you are entitled to judgment for immediate possession.

title: No Religious Display Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, and no statute giving tenants a right to fly the United States or Vermont flag. The nearest rule protects condominium and other common-interest-community unit owners: an association's rule on displaying the United States flag must be consistent with federal law, and it may not prohibit display of the Vermont flag or of signs about candidates or ballot questions, though it may regulate time, place, size, number and manner. That protection runs to unit owners, not to their tenants. For an ordinary rental, display rules are lease or house-rule matters, subject to fair housing law: you may not discriminate against or harass a tenant in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religious creed, national origin or another protected characteristic. So any rule about door-frame items, decorations or flags must be neutral and applied to everyone, and a rule singling out religious items invites a discrimination claim. A request to keep a disability-related item may call for a reasonable accommodation. Small door-frame items are best allowed with a restoration duty at move-out.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that specifically regulates rent concessions such as a free first month, a rent credit or a move-in discount. If you give one, state it in the lease, as the library's rent concession clause does, including the amount and the rental periods it covers. Three Vermont rules affect how a concession works. Rent is payable at the time and place agreed, so the lease's rent schedule controls. A rent increase takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice; if a concession is described as temporary in the lease, say exactly when it ends so the higher amount is part of the agreed schedule rather than a new increase. And if a tenant abandons the unit, the tenant remains liable for rent until the lease expires, but if you re-rent before then the agreement ends on the date of the new tenancy. Be careful with clauses that take back a concession if the tenant leaves early: Vermont's statutes do not address them, but a large recapture can look like a penalty, and you may keep a security deposit only for the purposes the statute lists.

title: Rent Control and Local Rules
bodyText: Vermont has no statewide rent control, rent cap or limit on how often or how much rent may rise; the only statewide rule is notice: an increase takes effect on the first day of a rental period following at least 60 days' actual notice. Owners of privately owned age-restricted housing (not licensed care facilities or publicly subsidized housing) must give 60 days' written notice on a state form to the residents and the Department of Housing and Community Development, or the increase is unenforceable. No Vermont statute expressly preempts local rent regulation, but Vermont towns act through powers the Legislature grants. Statutes let towns adopt housing-code ordinances (including rules on owners' and occupants' responsibilities and security deposits, which may not limit how a deposit is held) and supplemental deposit ordinances, which may require interest. Some city charters add tenant protections; Burlington's charter, for example, authorizes ordinances requiring longer no-cause notice where there is no written lease and 90 days' notice of rent increases. Mobile home lot rent increases have their own rules. The state's rental housing inspections are complaint-driven, and towns may also enforce local housing codes. Check the city or town's charter and ordinances before raising rent.

title: Collecting Rent for a Substandard Unit
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that flatly forbids you from asking for or collecting rent because a unit has a defect, but substandard conditions limit what you can collect. If you fail to meet your habitability obligations and, after actual notice of the problem from the tenant, a government agency or a qualified independent inspector, you do not repair within a reasonable time, and the problem materially affects health and safety, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of the noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice. These remedies are not available if the tenant, or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, caused the problem through negligence or a deliberate act. For minor defects, the tenant may repair and deduct up to half a month's rent after 30 days' notice. Separately, the housing code bars letting a unit that does not comply, and after a state inspection finds a violation you may not rent the affected unit to a new tenant until it is corrected. A termination notice served within 90 days after a government notice of noncompliance, other than for nonpayment, is presumed retaliatory. Fix reported conditions promptly and document the repairs before pressing for rent.

title: Rent Increases During a Lease Term
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not give you a right to raise rent in the middle of a fixed-term lease; under contract principles the rent stated for the term binds unless the lease reserves a change, so a mid-term increase is available only through a lease clause. Any increase, scheduled or not, takes effect only on the first day of a rental period that follows at least 60 days' actual notice to the tenant, and Vermont voids lease terms that circumvent the rental statute, so the lease cannot shorten that notice. Vermont has no rent cap and no retaliation safe harbor tied to an escalation clause. Instead, you may not retaliate by establishing or changing terms of a rental agreement, which includes raising rent, because a tenant complained to a code agency or to you about a violation of the rental statute, or joined a tenants' union; the tenant can recover damages and attorney's fees. Vermont's 90-day retaliation presumption applies only to termination notices after a government noncompliance notice, not to rent increases, but an increase soon after a complaint invites a retaliation claim. Special limits apply in buildings being converted to condominiums, in age-restricted housing, and in units with program rent restrictions. Some city charters, such as Burlington's, authorize longer increase notices.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: Before you raise the rent on a Vermont residential tenancy, you must give the tenant at least 60 days' actual notice: a written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the tenant's last known address (receipt is presumed three days after first-class or certified mailing). The increase takes effect on the first day of the rental period following those 60 days, not mid-period. The rule is in the general residential rental statute, not a mobile-home rule, and it covers every residential tenancy: month-to-month and week-to-week, written or oral, and any increase a fixed-term lease allows. Because Vermont counts all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement as rent, raising a recurring fee, such as parking or pet rent, needs the same notice. A lease cannot shorten the notice. Separate rules: owners of privately owned age-restricted housing must give 60 days' written notice on a state form to residents and to the Department of Housing and Community Development; mobile home lot rents have their own procedure. Ending a tenancy at the end of a lease term is a separate no-cause termination with its own notice period. Vermont's emergency price-gouging law covers heating fuel and petroleum products, not rent. Some city charters, such as Burlington's, authorize longer notice by ordinance.

title: Rent Into Court During Eviction
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a tenant to pay rent into court before raising defenses in an eviction, and they do not bar or require tenant counterclaims in a residential ejectment; how counterclaims are handled is a court-rules question. Rent goes into court when you ask for it. In any action against a tenant for possession, you may file a motion, with an affidavit stating particular facts, for an order that the tenant pay rent into court. The hearing may be held any time after 14 days' notice. If the court finds the tenant owes rent and has not paid, it orders full or partial payment of rent as it accrues while the case is pending, plus rent accrued from the filing or service of the complaint, whichever is first. You may ask for early release of funds on hardship; the tenant may ask to reduce the amount. If the tenant fails to pay into court as ordered, you are entitled to judgment for immediate possession, and possession may occur no earlier than 7 days after the writ is served. Either party may demand a jury, and an appealing tenant must post security for rent then due and rent that comes due during the appeal.

title: When a Vermont Tenant May Deduct from Rent
bodyText: In Vermont, rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed in the rental agreement, so the lease sets the due date, place and method; Vermont's statutes set no grace period and no weekend or holiday rule. A lease may say rent is paid without deduction or setoff, but Vermont law lets a tenant subtract certain amounts from rent that a lease cannot remove. Repair and deduct: if you fail within 30 days of notice to repair a minor defect required by the rental statute or a material lease provision, the tenant may repair it and deduct the actual, reasonable cost, up to half of one month's rent, giving you actual notice of the cost. Withholding: if a habitability problem materially affecting health and safety is not repaired within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance. Municipal water and sewer: if your unpaid municipal water or sewer bill leads to a disconnection notice, the tenant may pay to keep or restore service and, if those charges are included in rent, deduct the payment from rent. None of these apply if the tenant or the tenant's guests caused the problem.

title: No Rent-Receipt Anti-Waiver Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that specifically bars a lease, assignment, deed, mortgage or other instrument from letting someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit habitable. Related Vermont rules point the same way. The rental statute's obligations are implied in every rental agreement, and the warranty of habitability is deemed part of any residential rental agreement for the whole tenancy; any lease provision waiving it, or circumventing the statute's obligations and remedies, is void. A "landlord" includes the owner, the lessor and, where applicable, a sublessor, and under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code an "owner" includes anyone with title, anyone with charge, care, management or control of the property, the landlord or lessor, and the owner's authorized agent, so a manager or rent collector can be responsible for Code compliance. Rental agreements containing provisions that purport to shift Code duties between owner and occupant are ineffective for Code purposes. When your interest in the property ends, the security deposit must be transferred to the new landlord, who must notify the tenant. If you assign rents to a lender or hire a manager, keep repair responsibility clearly assigned and make sure someone acts on repair notices.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a landlord to give a receipt for rent or a security deposit, whether paid in cash or otherwise, and a missing receipt is not an eviction defense under any Vermont statute. The written-receipt rule found in Vermont law covers retail installment buyers, not tenants. Receipts still protect you. In a nonpayment case you must prove what was paid; the tenant can stop the termination by paying or tendering rent due through the end of the rental period, and accepting partial payment does not waive your remedies, so a dated record of each payment and the period it covers matters. You must give the Department of Taxes an annual landlord certificate listing your renters, and itemize any security deposit deductions in writing when you return the deposit, so consistent payment records help with both. Good practice: give a written or electronic receipt for every cash payment showing the date, amount, payer, rental period and whether it is rent or deposit, and keep copies. Some towns' ordinances may add requirements.

title: No Rule on Rent Reporting
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, no state rent-reporting program, and no rule on whether you may require a tenant to enroll in a rent-reporting service. If you report rent payments, or negative information such as unpaid rent, to a consumer reporting agency, you are furnishing information and federal credit-reporting law applies. Vermont adds its own rule on the screening side: no one may obtain a consumer's credit report without either a court order or the consumer's consent, and the report may be used only for the purpose the consumer agreed to, so get each applicant's written consent before pulling a credit report and state the purpose. For a background or credit check you must accept an unexpired government ID, an ITIN or a Social Security number, and may not require a Social Security number or refuse an application for lack of one. If a rent-reporting service costs the tenant money and is paid to you, it is part of the rent under Vermont's definition, so state it in the lease and give 60 days' actual notice before increasing it. Report only accurate, complete information.

title: Rooms Tax on Rent
bodyText: Ordinary residential rent in Vermont is not subject to a state tax collected from the tenant. Vermont's rooms tax applies to occupancy of a room in a "hotel", which Vermont defines broadly to include inns, rooming houses, furnished-room houses, boarding houses, short-term rentals and any building held out to the public by offering sleeping accommodations for pay. The operator must collect a tax of nine percent of the rent of each occupancy. But occupancy by a "permanent resident", meaning an occupant who has occupied the room or rooms for at least 30 consecutive days, is excluded, so a tenant living in the unit for 30 days or more is outside the tax. A furnished dwelling rented to the transient, traveling or vacationing public for fewer than 30 consecutive days, and for more than 14 days a year, also carries a three percent short-term rental impact surcharge on top of the rooms tax. Towns may adopt a one percent local option rooms tax. If you rent rooms or furnished units for short stays, collect and remit these taxes; once a tenant's stay reaches 30 consecutive days, it is a permanent residency for the rooms tax. Short stays taxed as hotel occupancy are also excluded from Vermont's residential rental statute.

title: False Applications and Sealed Records
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that lets you end a tenancy specifically because an applicant gave false information on a rental application. A false application is handled through the lease: if the lease makes accurate application information a material term, a materially false answer is a breach of a material term, and you may end the tenancy on at least 30 days' actual notice stating the termination date, followed by ejectment if needed. Vermont limits what counts as false. A person whose criminal record has been expunged or sealed is treated as never having been arrested or convicted for that offense, and in any application for a civil right or privilege may be required to answer only about records that have not been expunged or sealed; so an applicant who omits an expunged or sealed record has not lied. Other screening rules: you may not charge any application fee; for a background or credit check you must accept an unexpired government ID, an ITIN or a Social Security number and may not require a Social Security number; you need the applicant's consent before obtaining a credit report; and fair housing law bars statements indicating a preference based on protected characteristics. Do not treat an applicant's silence on information you were not allowed to request as a misrepresentation.

title: Code Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: Vermont has no statewide rental registration, licensing or periodic inspection program. State rental housing inspections are complaint-driven: the Department of Public Safety, Division of Fire Safety, inspects under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, and a local health officer may assist and must issue the same kind of report. The report sets correction deadlines, tells you that you may not rent the affected unit to a new tenant until the violation is corrected, and tells the tenant that you or your agents must have access to make the ordered repairs consistent with Vermont's entry statute; failing to meet the deadlines can bring an administrative penalty of up to $1,000 per violation. Towns may adopt housing-code ordinances that let the enforcing officer enter and survey dwellings between 8:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., and a judge may issue a daytime warrant to an official inspector to search for code violations if entry is refused. No Vermont statute lets a lease authorize a housing inspector to enter without the tenant's consent; inspectors rely on consent or a warrant. Your own entry to inspect needs the tenant's consent or 48 hours' notice between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M.

title: No Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not regulate renter's insurance in residential leases: nothing requires or forbids a renter's insurance clause, lets the tenant choose the carrier, limits force-placed coverage or administrative fees, or requires a separate statutory notice that you do not insure the tenant's belongings. One related notice does reach every tenant: the flood-hazard disclosure you must give at or before lease signing, in a separate document substantially in the state form, carries a notice to tenants that flood insurance may be available through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program or privately, that a standard renter's policy does not typically cover flood damage, and that the landlord's insurance policy does not cover the tenant's personal property. Other limits: any amount the tenant pays to you under the lease, including a charge for landlord-placed coverage, is rent under Vermont's definition, and an increase needs 60 days' actual notice; an insurance clause cannot shift your habitability or code duties or waive tenant remedies; and an assistance-animal policy cannot be conditioned on extra insurance without considering reasonable accommodation. If you require renter's insurance, state the minimum coverage, the proof deadline and what happens if the tenant fails to provide it.

title: No Termination for Costly Repairs
bodyText: Vermont gives you no right to end a tenancy because a repair would cost too much compared with the rent, and its statutes have no rule ending or abating a lease when fire or other casualty damages the unit. The warranty of habitability runs for the whole tenancy and cannot be waived, so under a fixed-term lease you must keep the unit safe, clean, fit and code-compliant for the rest of the term unless the lease itself provides for early termination after a casualty. If a habitability problem that materially affects health and safety is not repaired within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may withhold rent for the period, seek damages or end the agreement on reasonable notice. With no written lease, you may end a periodic tenancy without cause on the statutory notice (60 or 90 days for monthly tenancies, 21 days for weekly), and with a written lease, by no-cause notice before the term ends. But a termination served within 90 days after a government notice that the unit violates health or safety rules, other than for nonpayment, is presumed retaliatory. A local officer may order an unfit dwelling vacated, and a state order may require repair, closure or demolition of an unsafe structure.

title: Repair Request Notice Rules
bodyText: Vermont's repair remedies turn on notice, and the wording differs by remedy. Rent withholding, an injunction, damages and termination for a habitability problem materially affecting health and safety require that you received "actual notice" of the noncompliance, meaning written notice hand-delivered or mailed to your last known address, from the tenant, a government entity or a qualified independent inspector, and then failed to repair within a reasonable time. Repair-and-deduct for a minor defect runs from "notice" to you (the statute does not say written) and a 30-day repair period; when the tenant deducts the cost, the tenant must give you actual notice of the cost. Retaliation protection covers a tenant who complained to you of a violation of the rental statute, or to a code agency, with no writing requirement. A government inspection report is also sent to you. Vermont has no rule that lease language accepting verbal requests waives your right to written notice, but because a lease cannot circumvent the statute's remedies, do not rely on a lease term requiring written repair requests to defeat a remedy the statute grants on other notice. Practical course: accept requests in any form, confirm them in writing, keep a repair log, and act within 30 days at the latest.

title: Disclosures Due Before Signing
bodyText: Vermont has no single state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a just-cause or rent-increase law covers the unit. Its required disclosures are separate items. Flood: before entering a rental agreement, at or before signing, disclose whether any part of the premises is in a FEMA-mapped special flood hazard area, in a separate written document substantially in the Department of Housing and Community Development form; a lease clause is not enough. Lead: for pre-1978 rental target housing, before entering into a lease give approved tenants the Department of Health-approved lead materials and a copy of your most recent lead-safe maintenance compliance statement (unless the property is certified lead-free), along with the federal lead disclosure. Foreclosure: if you have been served with a foreclosure complaint, tell each new tenant that the premises are subject to a pending foreclosure and that the tenant may have to vacate on 30 days' notice, or longer if federal law requires. Automatic renewal of a lease of one year or more requires bold-face terms and the tenant's opt-in. Age-restricted housing owners give a state-form notice of rent increases. Keep a signed copy of each disclosure; an acknowledgment clause in the lease can record receipt but does not replace the documents.

title: Listing and Adding Fees
bodyText: Vermont's residential rental statute has no rule that every fee, fine, interest charge or other charge must be listed in the written lease with its purpose, and no notice period specific to adding a fee. Vermont's definition of rent does most of the work instead. Rent means all consideration paid to you or for your benefit under the rental agreement, other than a security deposit, so any fee you charge under the lease is part of the rent: it is payable at the time and place agreed, and an increase, including adding a new recurring charge, takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice. You may not charge any fee to apply for a residential unit. Vermont has no statute on fees for partial payments; accepting a partial payment does not waive your nonpayment remedies. A security deposit may be kept only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay you or a utility, and removal of abandoned property, so a fee must be stated in the lease to count as a charge the tenant was required to pay. List every charge, its amount and purpose in the lease; undisclosed charges invite consumer-protection claims.

title: Enforcing a Residential-Use Clause
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that sets a special consequence when a tenant uses a rental for something other than a home, so a residential-use clause like the library's is enforced like any other material lease term. If the tenant breaches it, you may end the tenancy by actual notice at least 30 days before a termination date stated in the notice; the faster 14-day notice is available only when the use involves criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence that threaten the health or safety of other residents. The tenant's statutory duties also apply: not to create code violations, not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and not to damage the premises; a violation entitles you to damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees. You must bring any ejectment within 60 days after the termination date, and possession is recovered only through the court. Accepting rent after terminating for a breach does not waive the eviction. Before enforcing against a home office or similar low-impact use, consider whether it actually breaches the clause or local zoning, and apply the rule evenly; fair housing law bars different terms because of protected characteristics. A shared-occupancy rental of rooms in your own home has its own short notice periods.

title: Retaliation Rules
bodyText: Vermont bars a residential landlord from retaliating, by establishing or changing the terms of a rental agreement or by bringing or threatening to bring an action, against a tenant who has complained to a government agency responsible for building, housing or health regulations about a violation materially affecting health and safety; has complained to you of a violation of Vermont's residential rental statute (not just the deposit section); or has organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization. A tenant subjected to retaliation may recover damages and reasonable attorney's fees and has a defense to a retaliatory action for possession. Vermont's presumption is narrow: if you serve a termination notice on any ground other than nonpayment of rent within 90 days after a municipal or state agency notifies you that the premises do not comply with health or safety regulations, the termination is presumed retaliatory, and you must rebut it. The presumption is triggered by the government's notice, not by the timing of the tenant's complaint. Separately, fair housing law bars coercing, threatening or interfering with anyone who opposed discrimination or took part in a Human Rights Commission complaint. Document legitimate reasons for any increase, rule change or termination, and avoid acting soon after a complaint or inspection.

title: Returned Checks and Payments
bodyText: Vermont does not cap the fee a lease may charge for a returned rent check or failed electronic payment, and its bad-check law neither fixes nor forbids a contract fee. Because Vermont counts all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement as rent, a returned-payment fee in the lease is part of the rent; keep it reasonable and state it in the lease. Without relying on the lease, Vermont's bad-check law gives the holder of a check dishonored for lack of funds, a closed account or a stop payment issued without cause a civil claim for court costs, costs of service, the check amount, bank fees, interest, attorney's fees and $50 in damages. Attorney's fees and the $50 are available only if you first send written notice stating the check date, payee, bank fees, mailing costs, check amount and a payment deadline, and the tenant does not pay the check amount plus bank fees and mailing costs within 30 days. Send it by certified and first-class mail to the address on the check or the last known address. In a criminal bad-check case, restitution includes a service charge of no more than $5. Vermont statutes say nothing about postdated checks or electronic-payment network rules.

title: House Rules
bodyText: Vermont has no statute setting when house rules bind a residential tenant or limiting mid-tenancy rule changes; the detailed park-rule statute applies only to mobile home parks. Rules work through the rental agreement, which Vermont defines as all agreements, written or oral, embodying terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of the unit, so written house rules the tenant agreed to are part of it. Several rules reach them. A rule cannot circumvent the obligations and remedies of the rental statute, waive the warranty of habitability, or shift Rental Housing Health and Safety Code duties between owner and occupant. You may not retaliate by establishing or changing terms of a rental agreement, which includes adopting or changing rules, because a tenant complained to a code agency or to you or joined a tenants' union. Fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations in rules for people with disabilities and bars applying rules differently because of protected characteristics. From July 1, 2026, a rule may ban smoking or vaping cannabis on the premises but not possession or other use in the unit. If you want to add or change rules during a term, reserve that right in the lease, give written notice, keep rules reasonable and apply them evenly; a breach of a material rule supports a 30-day termination notice.

title: Selling or Changing Management
bodyText: Selling a Vermont rental, or changing who manages it, triggers a few rules. Deposits: when your interest in the unit ends, the security deposit must be transferred to the new landlord, and the new landlord must give each tenant actual notice of its name and address with a statement that the deposit has been transferred; the statute does not say when the selling landlord is released, so document the transfer and the tenant notice. Tenancies: a sale does not end a tenancy. With no written lease, a landlord who has contracted to sell the building may end the tenancy on at least 30 days' actual notice; otherwise the ordinary no-cause notices apply, and a written lease runs to its term. Showings: you may enter to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers or mortgagees between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice, or with the tenant's consent. Foreclosure: tenants must be joined in a foreclosure with a 14-point notice, and an owner served with a foreclosure complaint must tell each new tenant about it. Sale of a single-family dwelling requires the seller's smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certification at closing. Retaliatory or discriminatory terminations remain barred, and the buyer must follow the same court process to remove a tenant.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Vermont has no rule that a housing or health code variance must be given to tenants or attached to the rental agreement, and the state Rental Housing Health and Safety Code contains no variance procedure. Variances exist in two other places. A town that adopts a minimum housing ordinance must create a housing board of review, which may vary the strict application of the ordinance, to the least extent necessary, where an extraordinary condition unique to the property would cause exceptional hardship and relief can be granted without substantially impairing the ordinance's purpose; its records are public. The Commissioner of Public Safety may grant variances or exemptions from the state fire and building safety rules where strict compliance would entail practical difficulty or unnecessary hardship, if public safety and health are secured. What Vermont does not allow is a private variance by lease: any rental agreement provision waiving the warranty of habitability is void, and Vermont has no exception for a tenant who accepts known defects in exchange for lower rent. If you hold a variance for a rental, giving tenants a copy and noting it in the lease is sensible, because tenants may otherwise report the condition as a violation.

title: What Vermont's Rental Law Covers
bodyText: Vermont's residential rental statute applies statewide to every rental agreement, written or oral, for a dwelling unit used as a home, with no county, population or local-adoption limit and no exclusion for long leases. It does not apply, unless an arrangement is created to avoid it, to: occupancy in medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar institutions; a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; members in a fraternal, social or religious organization's building; transient hotel, motel or lodging occupancy subject to the rooms tax; an owner of a condominium unit or cooperative proprietary lease; mobile home park lots (a separate statute); campgrounds; emergency-assistance or hospital-funded transient motel placements; and a person occupying without right who is not a tenant. Special rules apply within the statute: certified recovery residences may immediately exit a resident under strict conditions; renting rooms in your own home with shared living spaces ends on 15 or 7 days' notice; seasonal, non-primary-residence rentals get a 60-day deposit deadline; summer rentals and hunting camps are exempt from the heat and water standard; and farm housing provided as a benefit of employment has its own court process. The housing code covers all rented dwellings used as a regular residence. Some cities' charters, such as Burlington's, add local ordinances.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Vermont has a few rules for seasonal rentals. A seasonal rental of a dwelling not intended as the tenant's primary residence is still a rental agreement under the residential rental statute, with its notice, habitability and eviction rules, but the deposit deadline is longer: return the deposit with an itemized statement within 60 days instead of 14. The statute's heat and hot-and-cold-water standard does not apply to a unit intended and rented for summer occupancy or as a hunting camp, though the rest of the warranty of habitability does. Transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or lodging that is subject to the rooms tax is outside the residential rental statute, and campgrounds are excluded. A short-term rental, meaning a furnished dwelling rented to the transient, traveling or vacationing public for fewer than 30 consecutive days and for more than 14 days a year, owes the nine percent rooms tax plus a three percent surcharge, must not be run under unclean, unsanitary or unhealthful conditions, and must physically post the Division of Fire Safety's health and safety guidance and include it in every listing. State in the lease whether the rental is seasonal and not a primary residence, its fixed dates, and that it ends at the end of the season; a no-cause notice is still required under a written lease.

title: No Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: Vermont sets no limit on the amount of a residential security deposit, for any type of tenancy, and has no rule stepping a deposit down over time or barring increases after years of possession. Several rules still shape the amount. Everything refundable counts as one security deposit: Vermont defines a security deposit as any advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named, refundable at the end of the tenancy, so a refundable pet, key, furniture or last-month's-rent payment is part of the deposit and follows the same retention and 14-day return rules. When a tenant with a disability makes a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense, you may, if reasonable, require restoration at move-out, but you may not require an additional security deposit for that purpose. Do not charge deposits or higher deposits because of a protected characteristic, such as having children or receiving public assistance including housing assistance, and consider accommodation requests for assistance animals. Raising a deposit mid-tenancy is a change in the terms of the rental agreement; do it only as the lease allows and never in retaliation. Towns may adopt supplemental deposit ordinances, so check local rules.

title: Holding Security Deposits
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not tell you how to hold a residential security deposit: there is no requirement to use a separate, escrow, trust or interest-bearing account, no rule against commingling, no duty to tell the tenant where the deposit is held, and no bond alternative. In fact, Vermont law protects your choice: a town's security-deposit ordinance, and a town housing ordinance that addresses deposits, may not limit how a security deposit is held. What Vermont does regulate is the deposit's use and return: you may keep it only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant had to pay, and removal of abandoned articles; you must return it with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates (60 days for a seasonal, non-primary-residence rental); and when your interest ends, the deposit must be transferred to the new landlord. Missing the deadline forfeits your right to keep any part, and a willful failure costs double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. Because you must be able to refund promptly, keeping deposits in a separate account and tracking each tenant's balance is the prudent course. A town ordinance may require interest, so check local rules.

title: No Statewide Deposit Interest
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require landlords to pay interest on residential security deposits. Interest is left to local option: a town or municipality may adopt an ordinance governing security deposits that supplements, and is not inconsistent with, the state's minimum protections, and the ordinance may authorize the payment of interest on a security deposit. The same ordinance may not limit how a deposit is held, and it may let the town's housing board of review hear and decide deposit disputes at the request of a landlord or tenant. So whether you owe interest, at what rate and when, depends on the town where the unit is located; check for a local deposit ordinance before collecting a deposit. State law otherwise governs the deposit: retain it only for the listed purposes, return the balance with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates (60 days for seasonal non-primary-residence rentals), hand-deliver or mail it to the last known address, and transfer it to a buyer if you sell. If a lease promises interest, the promise is enforceable as a lease term.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Vermont's deposit section has no waiver clause of its own, but a Vermont tenant still cannot give up its protections. The obligations of Vermont's residential rental chapter, which includes the security deposit section, are implied in every rental agreement, and any rental agreement provision that attempts to circumvent, or circumvents, the chapter's obligations and remedies is unenforceable and void. That reaches the deposit definition (any refundable advance, deposit or prepaid rent, however named), the closed list of reasons you may keep deposit money, the bar on keeping it for normal wear and tear, the 14-day return with an itemized statement (60 days for a seasonal non-primary-residence rental), delivery by hand or mail to the last known address, transfer to a new landlord on sale, and the forfeiture and double-damages remedies. So a lease clause making a deposit "nonrefundable", allowing a longer return period, letting you keep the deposit for any default, or waiving the double-damages remedy will not hold. In a standard-form lease with an individual tenant, a shortened time to sue is also presumed unconscionable. Write deposit clauses that track the statute.

title: Deposits When Property Is Sold
bodyText: When your interest in a Vermont rental ends, for example by sale, the security deposit must be transferred to the new landlord. The new landlord must then give each tenant actual notice, meaning written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the tenant's last known address, of the new landlord's name and address with a statement that the security deposit has been transferred. Vermont's statute sets no deadline such as the closing date, requires no accounting to the buyer, and does not say when the selling landlord is released from liability for the deposit, so handle the transfer carefully: credit the deposits to the buyer at closing, give the buyer a list of each tenant's deposit, and keep written proof of the transfer. After the transfer, the new landlord is the one who must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates and who faces forfeiture and double damages for a willful failure. If you are buying, ask for each tenant's deposit amount and payment record, and send the statutory notice promptly. Tenancies continue after a sale, and the buyer must use the court process to remove anyone.

title: Deposit Penalties
bodyText: Vermont's deposit penalties are strict. If you fail to return the security deposit with a written statement itemizing any deductions within 14 days (60 days for a seasonal rental not intended as a primary residence), you forfeit the right to withhold any portion of the deposit. The statute speaks of returning the deposit "with a statement", so treat a late statement, or a return without the statement, as triggering forfeiture. If the failure is willful, you are liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld, not double the whole deposit, plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs. The statute requires no advance notice from the tenant before suing. Vermont has no deposit bank-account or bank-notice rule, so there is no separate penalty for how a deposit is held. Forfeiting the deposit does not by itself bar a separate claim for unpaid rent or damage, since the tenant remains liable for damages for violating the tenant's statutory duties, but you lose the right to keep the deposit money for them. In a town that has adopted a deposit ordinance, a housing board of review may hear deposit disputes. Calendar the 14-day deadline from the move-out date the tenant gave you or the date you discover the unit was vacated or abandoned.

title: Deposit Return Deadlines
bodyText: Vermont requires you to return the security deposit, with a written statement itemizing any deductions, within 14 days. The clock starts on the date you discover the tenant vacated or abandoned the unit, or on the date the tenant vacated if the tenant told you that date; the tenant does not have to demand the deposit, and the lease cannot set a longer period. For a seasonal rental not intended as a primary residence, the deadline is 60 days. Deliver the statement and any payment by hand or by mail to the tenant's last known address; the statute names those methods, and Vermont's electronic-transactions law does not displace a statutory delivery method, so use electronic payment only in addition, with the tenant's agreement. Deductions are limited to unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant had to pay, and removal of abandoned articles. Missing the deadline forfeits your right to keep any part; a willful failure costs double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. Vermont has no exception for a pending damage claim. If a mailed refund comes back or is never cashed, do not keep it: a security deposit owed in the course of a business is property under Vermont's unclaimed property law, generally presumed abandoned after three years.

title: No Rule on Deposit Standards
bodyText: Vermont has no rule requiring you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set the size of a security deposit, even if you charge different tenants different amounts, and no building-size trigger for such a rule. Vermont also sets no cap on deposits. Two limits apply. First, fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, marital status, religious creed, color, national origin, citizenship, immigration status or disability, because a person intends to live with minor children, receives public assistance (including housing assistance) or is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking; a higher deposit is a different term. You may use legitimate business practices such as references and credit history, but not as a pretext for discrimination. Second, you may not require an additional security deposit for a disabled tenant's reasonable modification, and an assistance animal is an accommodation question, not a pet. The cautious course is written, uniform deposit criteria (for example, tied to credit or rental history) applied the same way to every applicant, with records of how each deposit was set.

title: What a Deposit May Cover
bodyText: Vermont gives a closed list of what you may keep from a security deposit. The statute says the landlord may retain all or part of the deposit for: unpaid rent; damage to the landlord's property, unless it results from normal wear and tear or from actions or events beyond the tenant's control; unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you or to a utility; and expenses to remove articles the tenant abandoned. It is not a general fund for "any default": a lease clause letting you apply the deposit to any breach is void to the extent it goes beyond that list. Normal wear and tear means deterioration from reasonable use without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household or guests. Cleaning is not listed separately, so deduct for cleaning only where the condition amounts to damage beyond normal wear and tear, or the cost is a charge the lease required the tenant to pay you. Vermont has no rule authorizing pre-set cleaning or repair charges; deduct actual, documented costs and itemize each one in the written statement. Unpaid rent includes any lease fee, since all consideration paid to you under the agreement is rent. Return the rest within 14 days.

title: No Security Device Mandate
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers or peepholes, window locks, or rekeying between tenants, whatever the building's age, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code sets no lock standard; it requires doors and windows in good repair, operable windows with screens, and lighted entrances and common areas. Vermont's lock statute protects victims: a tenant who fears imminent harm from abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or who was sexually assaulted on the premises within six months, may ask you to change the locks within 48 hours (with a court order if the perpetrator is a co-tenant). If you do not, the tenant may change them with locks of equal or better quality, must notify you within 24 hours and give you a key, and pays the cost unless you agree otherwise. The tenant may also ask to install a security system or camera on seven days' notice at the tenant's cost, and you may not unreasonably refuse. These rights apply notwithstanding any contrary lease term. Rekeying at turnover is still sensible practice, and a lease promise to provide or maintain particular locks is enforceable through the tenant's repair remedies.

title: Self-Help Eviction Banned
bodyText: Vermont bans self-help eviction. You may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service being supplied to the tenant, except temporary interruptions for emergency repairs; the housing code likewise bars shutting off required water, sewer, equipment or utilities except temporarily during actual repairs or emergencies. You may not directly or indirectly deny a tenant access to and possession of the unit, or to the tenant's belongings, except through proper judicial process: no lockouts, changed locks, removed doors or seized property. A tenant who suffers damage or injury from an illegal eviction may sue for an injunction, damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and you can recover attorney's fees only if the court finds the tenant's suit was brought in bad faith and was frivolous or meant only to harass. Vermont also bars entering lands with force or in other than a peaceable manner, and a person who recovers in a forcible entry and detainer action may recover treble damages in a trespass action. To regain possession, give the proper termination notice, bring an ejectment action within 60 days after the termination date, and let the sheriff execute the writ. Utility shutoffs for a tenant's nonpayment of rent are never allowed.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Card Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes set no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for staff who work in 55+ or other age-restricted rental housing. Vermont's senior-housing rules are different: the fair housing ban on age and familial-status discrimination does not apply to a housing complex intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, to one intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit (only if it has facilities and services for older persons or is otherwise necessary, at least 80% of units are so occupied, and written, enforced policies show that intent), or to housing under a government elder program. Every other protected class, including disability accommodation, still applies. If you own privately owned age-restricted housing that is not a licensed care facility, any rent increase needs 60 days' written notice on the state housing department's form to the department and to every affected resident, or the increase is unenforceable (publicly subsidized housing monitored for rent limits is excluded). Keep your age-verification records and written policies current.

title: Penalties for Refusing Assistance Animals
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law makes it unlawful to discriminate in renting a dwelling because a person relies on aids such as attendants or specially trained animals, and to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services, including in common areas, when needed to give a person with a disability equal use and enjoyment of the unit. A no-pets clause, pet fee or breed or size rule must therefore yield where an accommodation is needed. The penalties are serious: a tenant or applicant can go to the Human Rights Commission or sue for injunctive relief, compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees, and any violation of the fair housing chapter is also a crime punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 per violation. Retaliating against someone who asks for an accommodation is separately prohibited. Vermont's separate guide-dog crime punishes injuring or interfering with a guide dog, not refusing housing, and its public-accommodation service-animal rule covers facilities offered to the general public; for housing, the fair housing rules govern. Handle every animal request as an accommodation request and decide it promptly and individually.

title: No Assistance Animal Misrepresentation Law
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not make it an offense to misrepresent a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else, and they set no rules for vests, registries or certificates. What still applies is Vermont's fair housing law: you may not discriminate because a person relies on specially trained animals, and you must make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, including no-pet rules, when needed for a person with a disability to use and enjoy the home. Violations carry damages, attorney's fees and a fine of up to $10,000 per violation. The cautious course: do not demand a registration, vest or certificate, and do not accuse a tenant of fraud. Treat every animal request as an accommodation request and decide it promptly and individually. If you believe a document is false, get legal advice before denying the request or acting on a lease violation.

title: Military Tenants
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give military tenants no state right to end a lease early, no shortened notice for periodic tenancies and no application-decision deadline; those rights, where they exist, come from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which applies in Vermont on its own terms. Vermont adds one court protection. If a member of the Vermont National Guard is ordered to State active duty by the Governor and is a party to a civil proceeding in a Vermont court, which includes an eviction (ejectment) case, the court may stay the case on its own motion, and must stay it on the member's application unless it finds the member's absence would not materially affect the case or the member can take part by phone or video. The application must explain how duty prevents the member from appearing and when the member will be available, with any needed information from the commanding officer. A stay can last no more than 30 days after State active duty ends. If a tenant tells you they are on military orders, check federal SCRA requirements before giving notice or filing, and expect delays.

title: Services and Utilities You Provide
bodyText: In Vermont, a service or utility you promise in the lease becomes an enforceable duty. If you provide heat as part of the rental agreement, you must supply a reasonable amount of heat at all times; whoever pays for fuel, you must always furnish heating facilities able to safely provide a reasonable amount of heat, and adequate hot and cold water (summer and hunting-camp rentals are exempt from the heat and water rule). If you fail to fix a minor defect needed to meet a material provision of the rental agreement within 30 days of notice, the tenant may repair it and deduct the reasonable cost, up to half a month's rent; failures that materially affect health and safety open the withholding, damages and termination remedies. You may not willfully cause any utility service to the tenant to be interrupted except temporarily for emergency repairs, and the housing code bars shutting off required water, sewer or utilities except during repairs or emergencies. If municipal water and sewer are included in rent and your account goes delinquent, the tenant may pay to keep service on and deduct it from rent. Anything the tenant pays you for a service is rent. List clearly what you provide and what the tenant pays.

title: Severability and Void Terms
bodyText: Vermont's rental statutes void offending lease terms one at a time rather than the whole lease: a provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies of the residential rental chapter is unenforceable and void, a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void, a confession-of-judgment clause is void, and a lease term shifting housing-code duties is not effective for code purposes. No Vermont statute was found that voids an entire residential lease because one term is unlawful, so a severability clause is consistent with Vermont law. It is not a guarantee, though. Under Vermont's standard-form contract statute, when a court finds an illegal or unconscionable term in a form contract with an individual, the court must either refuse to enforce the entire contract or the part containing the term, or limit the term to avoid an unlawful result, and it may consider whether severing the term would encourage drafters to keep including such terms. Terms such as out-of-state venue, jury or class waivers and shortened limitation periods are presumed unconscionable. Keep the severability clause, but remove terms Vermont law voids instead of relying on it.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to tell tenants or applicants that a registered sex offender lives in the building or nearby, and they do not give you immunity for staying silent. Vermont's Sex Offender Registry is run by the Department of Public Safety. Certain offenders are posted on the state's internet registry, searchable by name and town, and the Department, the Department of Corrections and authorized local police release registry information to members of the public who ask about a specific person under written protocols; an offender's current address is released only in limited cases. The registry's own required notice warns that anyone who uses registry information to injure, harass or commit a crime against a listed person is subject to prosecution. If a tenant or applicant asks, point them to the state registry or local police rather than describing a particular person yourself, and do not share what you learn in ways that could be harassment or defamation. Treat any screening policy based on registry status as a criminal-history policy and apply it consistently.

title: No Sex Offender Residency Duty
bodyText: Vermont's statutes put no duty on a landlord about where registered sex offenders may live. There is no state proximity rule (such as a distance from schools or parks) that you must enforce, no crime of renting to two registered offenders who live together, and no lease statement that shields you from a fine. The only statutory placement rule is aimed at the state: before the Department of Corrections approves a residence for a sex offender being released from confinement or under community supervision, it must give careful consideration to the residence's proximity to any risk group associated with the offender. Supervision conditions are the Department's business, not yours, though a parole or probation officer may contact you about a proposed residence. Municipal ordinances were not reviewed. If you screen applicants for criminal history, apply a consistent written policy, and remember that a person with a sealed or expunged record is treated as never having been convicted.

title: No First-Page or Relative Font Rule
