bodyText: Vermont's statutes set no rule that a residential lease disclosure appear on the first page or in type larger than the rest of the lease, and no special occupancy disclosure for renting a single-family home. Format rules attach only to particular documents. An automatically renewing lease with an initial term of a year or more must state the renewal terms clearly and conspicuously in plain language in bold-face type, with the tenant's separate opt-in. The flood-hazard disclosure must be a separate written document substantially in the state form, given at or before signing. A lender foreclosing on your property must put a tenant notice in at least 14-point type in its summons; that duty is the lender's. If you rent a self-storage space under Vermont's self-service storage law, certain disclosures must be bold and at least as large as the agreement's general text. Otherwise, use a readable, consistent type size and keep important terms easy to find, since a buried term in a standard-form lease is more open to an unconscionability challenge.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a landlord to tell tenants about public access to lakes or rivers, shoreland zoning, public trust rights or easements across the property. Vermont's shoreland law regulates the owner's land use near lakes and ponds, such as clearing vegetation or adding impervious surface in a protected shoreland area, which may need a state permit; those duties stay with you as owner and are not tenant notices. The one lake- or water-related notice you must give every tenant is the flood-hazard disclosure: before signing, tell the tenant in a separate written document, substantially in the state form, whether any part of the premises is in a FEMA mapped special flood hazard area. For waterfront rentals, describe in the lease exactly what dock, beach, boat launch or shoreline access the tenant may use, and any limits from easements, association rules or shoreland permits, so the tenant is not misled about what is included. Tell tenants not to cut vegetation or build near the shore without your written approval.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give federal or state employees no special rent protection during a government shutdown: no grace period, no late-fee bar and no eviction pause. Vermont's ordinary rules already protect every tenant who falls behind. To end a tenancy for unpaid rent you must give actual notice stating a termination date at least 14 days away, and the tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made. Accepting a partial payment does not waive your remedies. After you file an eviction, the tenant can still end the case once in any 12 months by paying into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, with interest and costs, before the writ of possession is executed. Vermont has no statute setting or capping late fees. If a tenant tells you a shutdown has stopped their pay, consider a written payment plan; it costs little and avoids an eviction the tenant can defeat by paying.

title: No Single-Family Zone Rental Limit
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not limit renting a home in a single-family zone to owners who live on the lot. State zoning law runs the other way. Every town must allow one accessory dwelling unit as a permitted use within or attached to a single-family home (except under flood hazard and fluvial erosion bylaws), reviewed under the same controls as a home without one, and from July 1, 2026 that rule no longer applies only to an owner-occupied lot. Until January 1, 2028, Vermont's statute also says no bylaw may require a duplex to be built on an owner-occupied lot. Bylaws must allow duplexes wherever year-round housing is allowed, and must permit up to four units on a single-unit-size lot in districts served by municipal water and sewer. Towns may still regulate short-term rentals and adopt their own bylaws within these limits, so check local zoning before converting or renting a unit. A 2026 law asked the state housing department to report on large investors buying single- and two-family homes, but it imposes no restriction.

title: Smoke Drift and Common Areas
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not address smoke drifting between rental units: there is no statute making drift a nuisance, none letting a lease waive a tenant's drift claim, and no smoking-policy disclosure. Two state smoking laws can reach parts of an apartment building. The workplace law bans lighted tobacco and e-cigarette use in any enclosed structure where employees perform services for an employer; it excludes areas commonly open to the public and any part of a building that is also the employer's or employee's own residence. Whether an apartment building's enclosed hallways, laundry or maintenance areas where your staff work count as a workplace has not been settled by statute, but the definition is broad. The public-places law bans smoking in the common areas of enclosed places of public access, such as a leasing office open to the public. Towns may adopt stricter smoking ordinances. Remember also that a habitability waiver is void and a tenant's quiet-enjoyment duties run to other tenants. The cautious course: ban smoking and vaping in all enclosed common areas, say so in your written rules, and respond to drift complaints promptly.

title: Smoking and Vaping Rules
bodyText: Vermont lets you ban tobacco smoking and vaping in units and anywhere on your property; no statute requires a smoking-policy disclosure, a prescribed form or a tenant acknowledgment. Cannabis is different. From July 1, 2026, a rental agreement may not prohibit a tenant from possessing cannabis or cannabis products on the rental premises or using them inside the dwelling unit; you may prohibit only the use of lighted cannabis or cannabis products intended for inhalation, meaning smoking and vaping. A clause banning all cannabis use, or any possession on the property, is unenforceable unless federal law requires the ban, as in some federally assisted housing. State law separately bans smoking and e-cigarette use in enclosed workplaces where employees perform services and in common areas of places open to the public, and towns may be stricter. Vermont's statutes do not say how a smoking ban may be added during a tenancy; for a fixed-term lease, add a new ban at renewal or with the tenant's written agreement, and for a tenancy without a fixed term, give clear written notice well in advance. Apply the policy evenly and consider disability accommodation requests.

title: No Smart Lock Law
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not specifically regulate smart locks, keyless or app-based entry, or entry logs in residential rentals. Vermont's general rules apply to them. A remote or electronic lock does not change the entry rules: you may enter with the tenant's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, or for inspection, repairs, agreed services or showings between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice, and without notice only when you reasonably believe there is imminent danger to a person or property. Using a code or app to get in outside those rules is an unlawful entry, and locking a tenant out by disabling a code is an illegal eviction. A tenant who is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking may ask you to change the locks within 48 hours, which for a smart lock means new codes or credentials. From January 1, 2028, Vermont's new data privacy act may reach larger operators that process biometric or other sensitive data of at least 3,000 Vermont residents a year. Keep entry codes confidential and explain in the lease how credentials are issued and revoked.

title: No Snow Removal Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not say whether the landlord or the tenant must clear snow and ice at a rental, so the lease decides, within limits. The library's snow clause, which has the tenant clear only the walks, parking and access areas the tenant uses and not areas shared with other residents, fits Vermont. Keep shared areas and exits your responsibility: you must keep the premises safe and fit for habitation, a lease cannot waive that warranty or circumvent the rental statute, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code says a lease shifting code responsibilities between owner and occupant is not effective for code purposes; the Code requires entrances and common areas in buildings of two or more units to be lighted for safe access and egress. Towns may require the owner, occupant or person in charge of property next to a public sidewalk to clear it of snow and ice, and many city and village charters do, so check the local rule and say in the lease who clears the public sidewalk. If the tenant must clear snow, provide the shovels or other tools needed and say what happens when the tenant is away.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give a tenant no special continuance or defense in a nonpayment eviction because a Social Security check, other government benefit or housing-voucher payment arrived late. Vermont's general rules do much of the same work. A nonpayment termination notice must give at least 14 days, and the tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made, so a late benefit that arrives before the deadline cures the default. After you file, the tenant can end the case once in any 12 months by paying into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, plus interest and costs, before the writ is executed. Vermont's rental arrearage program can pay up to three months of arrears for eligible families with children, but only if you agree to end the eviction and not restart it over the arrears paid. You may not treat a tenant differently because they receive public assistance, including housing assistance. If a voucher payment is late, contact the housing authority before serving notice.

title: Public Assistance and Vouchers
bodyText: Vermont's fair housing law makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, or to set different terms, conditions or privileges, because a person is a recipient of public assistance, which includes any federal, state or local assistance, including medical and housing assistance. A housing voucher is housing assistance, so you may not advertise no vouchers, reject an applicant for having one, or charge a voucher holder a higher deposit or different rent. Neutral business practices such as references remain allowed if not a pretext. There is no statement you must put in the lease. The exemptions differ from the duty: the rental rules do not apply to a building with three or fewer units where you or your immediate family live in one, but your advertising must still comply. Separately, if you received a Vermont Rental Housing Improvement Program grant or forgivable loan, you must accept any available housing voucher for the unit and keep rent at or below fair market rent while the agreement is in effect. Violations can bring damages, punitive damages, attorney's fees and a fine of up to $10,000 per violation.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to tell a tenant whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, when it was last inspected, or that it lacks one, and they prescribe no lease notice or sign for unsprinklered buildings. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a separate question: any building in which people rent accommodations is a public building under the state fire-safety law, and the Division of Fire Safety's rules on construction, maintenance and operation of premises (the Fire and Building Safety Code, not reviewed here) and any local code decide what systems are required. The Rental Housing Health and Safety Code's introduction encourages home sprinklers but imposes no disclosure. If your building has a sprinkler system, keep it inspected and the records on file, and use the lease or house rules to tell tenants not to hang items from, paint, block or tamper with sprinkler heads and other fire protection equipment. If you are asked about sprinklers, answer accurately; a misleading answer could be an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute covers oral and written rental agreements alike, and it has no exclusion for long leases (such as five years or more). Three writing rules matter. First, an estate or interest in land created without a written instrument has the effect of an estate at will only, and a tenancy can be assigned, granted or surrendered only by a writing signed by the grantor or by operation of law, so put any fixed term in a signed written lease. Second, no lawsuit may be brought on an agreement that cannot be performed within one year, or on a contract concerning an interest in land, unless it or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party being charged. Third, Vermont's long-lease threshold is a recording rule, not a validity rule: a lease for more than one year from its making is not effective against anyone except you and your heirs, such as a buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded in the town land records; an acknowledged notice or memorandum of lease with the statutory contents may be recorded instead of the full lease. Several rental rules also turn on whether the lease is written.

title: Vermont Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Vermont sets few dollar limits for residential rentals; most money rules are bans or deadlines rather than caps. Application fees: none of any amount, and you may not require a Social Security number for a background or credit check if the applicant offers unexpired government ID or an ITIN. Security deposit: no statewide cap (towns may adopt supplemental ordinances); return it with an itemized statement within 14 days (60 days for a seasonal non-primary residence), or forfeit any right to withhold, and pay double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees if the failure is willful. Late fees: no statute sets or caps them, but anything payable to you under the lease is rent. Rent increases: no cap, but at least 60 days' actual notice, effective on the first day of a rental period. Returned checks: by statute you can recover the check amount, bank fees, interest, costs and, after written notice and 30 days without payment, attorney's fees and $50 damages. Tenant repair-and-deduct is capped at half of one month's rent. Fair housing violations carry a fine of up to $10,000 each, and enforcing a presumptively unconscionable form-lease term can cost up to $1,000 per term.

title: Statutory Termination Rights
bodyText: Vermont gives tenants several termination rights by statute that a lease cannot remove. If you fail to fix a habitability problem that materially affects health and safety within a reasonable time after actual notice, the tenant may end the rental agreement on reasonable notice (unless the tenant or a guest caused the problem). A tenant who reasonably fears imminent harm from abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or who was sexually assaulted on the premises within the past six months, may end the lease without penalty on 30 days' written notice with supporting documentation, which can be a signed self-certification on an approved form. After you give notice that the building will be converted to a condominium or other common interest community, a tenant may end the rental agreement on 30 days' written notice. Without a written agreement saying otherwise, a tenant may end a tenancy by actual notice one rental period ahead. Vermont has no statute letting a tenant end a lease for your misrepresentation, but the consumer protection act lets a tenant who contracted in reliance on false or fraudulent representations sue for equitable relief, damages or the consideration paid, attorney's fees and up to three times the consideration in exemplary damages.

title: Required Statutory Texts and Forms
bodyText: Vermont prescribes no lease form and no verbatim lease text; its required forms and wording are for side documents. Flood: before the lease is signed, give the tenant the separate state FEMA special flood hazard area disclosure form (substantially in the housing department's form), signed by you and the tenant. Lead: for pre-1978 rental housing, before the lease give the Department of Health-approved lead materials and a copy of your latest RRPM (lead-safe renovation, repair, painting and maintenance) compliance statement. Arbitration: if the lease or a side agreement requires arbitration, it is unenforceable without a signed acknowledgment substantially in the statutory words, displayed prominently if it is in the same document. Age-restricted housing: rent increases need 60 days' notice on the housing department's form to residents and the department. Victims: a protected tenant ending a lease may use a signed self-certification on a standard form adopted by HUD, the state children and families department or a support nonprofit, and you must accept it. Taxes: every rental owner files a certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes by January 31 on its form. Foreclosure: the foreclosing lender's summons to tenants must carry a statutory notice in at least 14-point type, and once you receive a foreclosure complaint you must tell each tenant who signs a new rental agreement that the property is in foreclosure and that, if you cannot redeem, the tenant may have to leave on 30 days' notice or any longer notice federal law requires.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no rule requiring you to install steam radiator covers or guards on request, and no required lease rider about radiators. The general rules still apply. You must keep the premises safe and fit for habitation, with heating facilities capable of safely providing a reasonable amount of heat, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code requires heating systems to be properly functioning and in good repair. In pre-1978 rental housing, radiators and other heating units are among the interior surfaces covered by Vermont's lead law, so painting, sanding or scraping old radiators or their covers is lead-safe maintenance work that must follow the lead rules. A lease clause cannot waive your habitability duties. The cautious course: if a tenant with young children, or a tenant with a disability, asks for a radiator cover or guard because of burn risk, treat it seriously, and consider a disability accommodation request under fair housing law; document what you install and maintain it.

title: No Stigmatized Property Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no stigmatized-property rule. Nothing says whether you must, or need not, tell a prospective tenant that a death, homicide, suicide or other crime happened in the unit, that it is said to be haunted, or that a past occupant had an illness such as HIV, and nothing gives you immunity either way. General rules govern instead. Vermont's consumer protection act covers real estate transactions, so misrepresenting a material fact, or answering a direct question falsely, can be an unfair or deceptive practice, and a tenant who contracts in reliance on a false representation can recover damages, attorney's fees and exemplary damages. Fair housing law bars discrimination because of disability, which counsels against volunteering a past occupant's medical condition. The cautious course: do not volunteer a former tenant's health information; if asked a direct question about the property's history, answer truthfully or say you will not discuss prior occupants, but never deny a fact you know.

title: Tenant Storage Space
bodyText: Vermont's self-service storage law, with its lien and sale procedure, applies to a self-storage facility, meaning real property designed and used for renting individual storage spaces; it does not fit a storage locker, basement cage or shed that comes with an apartment. Storage provided with a tenancy is part of the premises under Vermont's rental statute, which covers areas and facilities held out for tenants' use or promised to the tenant, so the ordinary landlord-tenant rules govern it. You have no lien on a tenant's stored belongings for unpaid rent. Entering a storage area inside the unit follows the 48-hour notice rules. If a tenant abandons the unit, you must mail notice and hold unclaimed property, including stored items, in a safe, dry, secure place for 60 days before it becomes yours; property left after the tenant gave actual notice of vacating, or left at the end of the lease, may be disposed of without notice. If you charge for storage, the charge is rent, and the lease should describe the space, any limits on what may be stored (no flammables or hazardous items), and that you are not insuring the contents.

title: No Appliance Supply Duty
bodyText: Vermont's statutes and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code do not require you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator. The Code requires every dwelling unit to contain space to store, prepare and serve food in a sanitary manner, including a kitchen sink, along with heat, hot water and other facilities, but it does not list cooking or refrigeration appliances. Whether appliances come with the unit is a lease term. If you do supply them, list them in the lease, because a lease promise to supply or maintain an appliance becomes a material provision the tenant can enforce: if you fail to repair a minor defect within 30 days of notice, the tenant may repair it and deduct the reasonable cost, up to half a month's rent, and a defect that makes the unit unsafe, such as a leaking gas range, can trigger the full habitability remedies. Towns may adopt housing codes with minimum standards for cooking facilities and refrigerated storage space, so check any local code before renting a unit without appliances.

title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText: Under a written lease, Vermont lets you condition or prohibit subleasing and require the tenant to give you written notice of the name and contact information of any sublessee. The statute ties that power to a written lease; without one, the tenant must still give you that written notice. Wording matters: the fast-track court remedy for removing someone occupying the unit without right or permission (a motion for immediate possession heard after 10 days' notice, with possession no sooner than five days after the writ is served) is available only when the written rental agreement prohibits subleasing. A lease that merely allows subletting with consent, without stating a prohibition, may forfeit that remedy, so say plainly that subleasing is prohibited except with your written consent. Vermont has no rule that your silence on a sublet request counts as approval, and no requirement that consent not be unreasonably withheld. An assignment of a lease longer than one year must be by recorded deed to bind anyone but the assignor and heirs. A sublessee who has your permission is not an unlawful occupant, and a sublease does not release the original tenant unless you agree.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not address a subsidized tenant's refusal of a housing program inspection, and none lets you refuse a voucher tenancy, or end one, because of the program's inspection requirements. Refusing to rent to, or setting different terms for, someone because the person receives public assistance, including housing assistance such as a voucher, is unlawful housing discrimination (buildings of three or fewer units where you or your family live are exempt, except for advertising). For entry, ordinary Vermont rules apply to every tenant: you may enter with the tenant's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, and you may enter to inspect between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on at least 48 hours' notice, so a program inspection can be scheduled on that basis. A tenant who keeps blocking lawful entry may be in breach of the lease, which can support a 30-day termination notice for breach of a material term, but treat that as a last resort and coordinate with the housing authority first. Federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may add their own requirements.

title: No Subsidy Rule for Habitability Rent Reductions
bodyText: Vermont has no special rule for reducing rent on a subsidized unit when part of it becomes uninhabitable, or for splitting a reduction between the tenant's share and the part a housing subsidy pays. The general remedies apply to every tenant. If you fail to make repairs within a reasonable time after actual notice of a habitability problem that materially affects health and safety, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of the noncompliance, seek an injunction, recover damages, costs and attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice, unless the tenant or a guest caused the problem. For minor defects you do not fix within 30 days of notice, the tenant may repair and deduct up to half a month's rent. The statutes do not say whether withholding or deductions reach only the tenant's share or the subsidy-paid portion; that is governed by your housing assistance contract and federal program rules, which may let the housing authority abate or stop its payments. Fix reported problems quickly and keep the housing authority informed.

title: No Subsidy Late Fee Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, such as barring a late fee when the housing authority's share arrives late, and no general statute that sets or caps residential late fees at all. Anything the lease requires the tenant to pay you counts as rent under Vermont's rental statute. Two rules still shape the practice. You may not set different terms for a tenant because the tenant receives public assistance, including housing assistance, so do not impose fees on voucher holders that other tenants do not pay. And federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may limit what you may charge the tenant for the subsidy's late payment. The cautious course: charge a late fee, if at all, only on the tenant's own share and only when the tenant's share is late, state the amount in the lease, keep it reasonable, and never treat a housing authority's delay as the tenant's default.

title: No Housing Receivership; Code Enforcement
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not let a court appoint a receiver to collect rents and repair substandard rental housing. Enforcement runs through orders instead. On a complaint, the state Division of Fire Safety inspects under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code and issues a written report with correction deadlines; you may not rent an affected unit to a new tenant until the violation is corrected, tenants must give you access to make the ordered repairs, and missing the deadlines can bring an administrative penalty of up to $1,000 per violation. The fire-safety Commissioner may order premises repaired or rehabilitated, closed if not fixed, closed immediately for imminent hazards, or demolished if dangerous, with orders served on recorded interest holders. Towns may adopt their own minimum housing standards, with an enforcement officer, a housing board of review that hears appeals, recorded orders that bind later buyers and lenders, fines of up to $200 per day of violation, and court suits for injunctions and, where the defense lacks substantial merit, attorney's fees. Tenants keep their own habitability remedies. Fix cited violations within the stated time.

title: Ending at the End of the Term
bodyText: Vermont has no good-cause renewal rule, but the end of a written lease term does not by itself let you take back the unit. To end a written lease for no cause, you must give the tenant actual notice at least 30 days before the end of the stated term if the tenancy has lasted two years or less, or at least 60 days before if longer (7 days for a written week-to-week agreement), stating the termination date. If the tenant stays after the tenancy ends without your express consent, you must bring an ejectment action, within 60 days after the termination date in your notice, and you may never remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself. Whether the tenant must give notice to leave at the end of the term depends on the lease; without a written term saying otherwise, a tenant ends a tenancy by actual notice one rental period ahead. Put any early surrender in writing. Property left behind after the tenant gave actual notice of vacating, or left at the end of the rental agreement, may be disposed of without notice. Return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days. Check for any local ordinance on notice periods.

title: Property Tax Increases and Rent
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on passing real estate tax increases through to residential tenants: nothing authorizes or forbids a tax-escalation clause, requires the lease to state the tenant's exact share, or requires you to refund a share of any abatement. So the right exists only if your written lease provides it. Three Vermont rules apply to any such clause. Anything the tenant must pay you under the lease is rent, so a tax pass-through is a rent increase and takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice; in a fixed-term lease you may raise rent mid-term only if the lease reserves that right. Your security deposit may cover unpaid charges only when the lease required the tenant to pay them to you. And you may not raise rent to retaliate against a tenant's code complaint or tenants' union activity. Vermont's tax rules for landlords run to the state: you file an annual certificate of rent with the Department of Taxes by January 31. If you use a pass-through, state the formula, the tenant's percentage, the base year and how abatements are credited.

title: Cable and Antenna Access
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give tenants no state right to cable television, broadband or satellite access in a rental building, set no consent or installation rules for providers wiring multifamily buildings, and do not bar charging cable subscribers a different rent. Vermont's cable chapter regulates providers' certificates, service and line extensions through the Public Utility Commission, not landlord-tenant access. Federal rules on satellite dishes, antennas and cable contracts in apartment buildings may also apply; they were not reviewed here, so check them before limiting a tenant's dish or antenna. Your lease and house rules can address how and where equipment may be installed and who pays to repair any damage. If a tenant installs equipment, entry, alteration and damage rules in Vermont's rental statute apply as usual: the tenant may not deliberately or negligently damage the premises and is liable for damage caused.

title: Tenancies Without a Written Lease
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute does not use the term tenancy at will; it distinguishes tenancies with and without a written rental agreement. An interest in land created without a written instrument has the effect of an estate at will only, but an oral rental agreement is still a rental agreement fully covered by Vermont's landlord-tenant law. Without a written agreement, you may end the tenancy for no cause by actual notice stating a termination date: for monthly rent, at least 60 days if the tenant has lived there two years or less and at least 90 days if longer; for weekly rent, at least 21 days. If you have contracted to sell the building, 30 days. Nonpayment notices (14 days) and breach notices (30 days, or 14 for criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence, any of which threatens the health or safety of other residents) are the same as under a written lease. The tenant may end the tenancy by actual notice at least one rental period ahead. Without a written agreement you cannot rely on lease-only rights such as attorney's fees in an eviction or a sublet prohibition with the fast-track occupant hearing. Rooms rented in your own home with shared living space follow a 15-day (monthly) or 7-day (weekly) rule.

title: No Tenant Bankruptcy Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no rule on what happens to a residential tenancy, a security deposit or an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law, including the automatic stay, governs that situation and was outside the searched material, so get advice before you serve a notice, start or continue an eviction, or try to collect pre-filing rent from a tenant who has filed. Vermont's ordinary rules otherwise continue to apply: termination notices, the 60-day deadline to file ejectment after the termination date, the tenant's right to end a nonpayment case by paying into court once in 12 months, the 14-day deposit return, and the abandoned-property procedures. The only general Vermont statute on bankruptcy in litigation lets a court allow or disallow costs when a defendant wins solely by pleading bankruptcy. Don't rely on a lease clause that makes a bankruptcy filing itself a default; how federal law treats one was not reviewed here.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: Vermont treats damage the tenant causes differently in several places. A tenant may not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the premises, fixtures, systems or furnishings, or deliberately or negligently let anyone else do so; if that happens you may recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and the violation is a ground for a 30-day termination notice. Tenant-caused conditions are excluded from the tenant's own remedies: rent withholding, damages, termination and repair-and-deduct are not available if the problem was caused by the negligent or deliberate act or omission of the tenant or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent. When the tenant leaves, you may keep deposit money for damage beyond normal wear and tear, which excludes deterioration from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, but not damage from events beyond the tenant's control. Vermont has no casualty statute, so a tenant-caused fire is handled under these rules and your lease. Write lease damage clauses around the tenant, household members and people present with the tenant's consent, matching the statutes' wording.

title: Tenant Information Privacy
bodyText: Vermont has no general statute barring a landlord from disclosing tenant or applicant information, but several specific rules apply. If you hold documents or information about a tenant's status as a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking, you must keep it confidential and may not let anyone else see it unless the tenant authorizes it, a court order, government regulation or audit requires it, or it is needed as sealed evidence in a court case about the victim's lease termination or lock-change rights. It is a fair housing violation to disclose a tenant's or occupant's victim status to harass, intimidate, retaliate, pressure the tenant to leave or recover possession. A business may not intentionally make an individual's Social Security number available to the public, or disclose it to a third party without written consent when it knows or should know the recipient lacks a legitimate purpose. When you discard applications or files, take reasonable steps to shred or erase personal information. From 2028, Vermont's new data privacy act may cover larger operators. Share tenant information only for a legitimate business purpose, and get written consent before sharing anything sensitive.

title: Tenant Records and Data
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to keep a rent ledger, give tenants a payment history on request, or include a ledger in a nonpayment notice. Several rules govern tenant data. Vermont's security breach law applies to anyone who handles personally identifiable information, which includes a landlord holding names with Social Security, driver's license or other ID numbers, ITINs, or financial account numbers: if a breach occurs you must notify affected Vermont residents in the most expedient time possible and within 45 days of discovery, and notify the Attorney General with a preliminary description within 14 business days. When records with personal information are no longer kept, you must take reasonable steps to shred, erase or otherwise make them unreadable. You may not post or publicly expose Social Security numbers, print them on mailed materials, or require their transmission over an unsecured internet connection, and you may not require an SSN to complete a rental application or refuse an application because it lacks one; for a background or credit check you must accept unexpired government ID or an ITIN instead. Vermont has no written information security program requirement for ordinary businesses (it applies to data brokers), but from January 1, 2028 larger operators meeting the new data privacy act's thresholds have added duties. Keep payment records anyway; they are your proof in court.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not end a lease when a tenant dies, set a special procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings or deposit, or let a lease or a separate form name someone with authority to remove property, collect the deposit or receive unearned rent. A death does not by itself end the tenancy. Deal with the estate's personal representative, or the heirs if no estate is opened, and give whatever termination notice the tenancy requires: for a written lease, notice before the end of the term; without one, 60 or 90 days for monthly rent. Remaining co-tenants keep their tenancy. Vermont's abandoned-property procedure assumes a living tenant (it turns on whether the unit is still a full-time residence, rent is unpaid and you tried to learn the tenant's intentions), and the no-notice disposal rule applies only after the tenant gave notice of vacating or the lease ended, so do not dispose of a deceased tenant's belongings without the estate's agreement or legal advice. An emergency contact named in the lease is useful for notification only. Return the deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days of when you learn the unit has been vacated, to the estate.

title: No Tenant Display Rights Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes give tenants no right to display a flag, political sign or banner at a rental, and none stops you from restricting such displays or requires your consent before a tenant posts a sign. The nearest rule protects condominium and other common-interest-community unit owners, not their tenants: the association may not prohibit display of the Vermont flag or signs about candidates for public or association office or ballot questions on a unit or adjoining limited common element, though it may regulate time, place, size, number and manner, and any rule on the United States flag must be consistent with federal law. If you rent a condominium unit, your tenant is also bound by the association's reasonable rules. For an ordinary rental, your lease or house rules may set reasonable, neutral display rules, such as where flags and signs may go and how they are attached to avoid damage, applied the same way to everyone. Apply them evenly: fair housing law bars different terms because of protected characteristics such as religious creed or national origin, and you may not retaliate against tenants for organizing.

title: Forwarding Notices of Proceedings
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a tenant to tell you about, or send you, a notice of a lawsuit or other proceeding affecting the property, and they do not make a tenant's attornment (acknowledging someone else as landlord) void. The lease may require the tenant to notify you promptly and deliver any written notice, as the library's clause does; a tenant who fails to do so may be in breach of the lease, but Vermont sets no statutory penalty. Two Vermont rules point the other way. In a foreclosure, the lender must join and serve each tenant occupying under a residential rental agreement, with a statutory notice telling the tenant to give the court a name and address, and once you are served with a foreclosure complaint you must tell each new tenant that a foreclosure is pending and that the tenant may have to leave on 30 days' notice, or longer if federal law requires. And when a court officer sells the right to collect rents from real estate on execution, the tenant must attorn and pay rent to the purchaser. Keep your mailing address current with tenants.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing about whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance, or about claims against a tenant's policy. Related rules set the boundaries. You cannot use the lease to push your own duties onto the tenant or the tenant's insurer: a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void, any provision that circumvents the rental statute's obligations or remedies is void, and the housing code says a lease shifting code duties between owner and occupant is not effective for code purposes. You may require renter's insurance for the tenant's own belongings and liability if the lease says so, and you may hold the tenant responsible, directly or through the deposit, for damage the tenant or people present with the tenant's consent cause beyond normal wear and tear, with damages, costs and attorney's fees for deliberate or negligent damage. The state flood-disclosure form you give every tenant warns that your insurance does not cover the tenant's personal property. Pursuing a tenant's insurer generally needs the tenant's cooperation or a judgment against the tenant.

title: Tenant Upkeep and Well and Septic Systems
bodyText: Vermont sets the tenant's upkeep duties by statute and code, and a lease may add reasonable housekeeping rules but cannot shift your own code duties. The tenant must not create or contribute to code violations, must not disturb other tenants, and must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, fixtures, systems or furnishings or let anyone else do so; you may recover damages, costs and attorney's fees and terminate on 30 days' notice for a violation. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, the occupant keeps the space the occupant exclusively occupies clean and free of trash, recyclables and food scraps, exterminates an infestation caused by the occupant's own failure to maintain the unit, and uses reasonable care so the unit does not create a hazard for neighbors. Wells and septic systems stay your responsibility: the Code requires a supply of potable water (a private supply free of harmful impurities under Health Department guidelines, with elevated contaminants treated), an alternate supply during short-term deficiencies, a properly operating wastewater system that does not back up or surface, and plumbing in good repair. A lease clause making the tenant maintain the well or septic system is not effective for code purposes; you may ask tenants not to flush harmful items.

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on tenant portals, so whether you may require tenants to sign, pay or receive notices online turns on general rules. Vermont's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the circumstances, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically; that right cannot be waived, so a lease term requiring every future signature or notice to go through a portal cannot take it away. An electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if the tenant can print or store it, and a record the sender blocks from printing or saving is unenforceable against the tenant. Notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence are excluded from the electronic transactions law entirely, and Vermont's rental statute defines actual notice as written notice hand-delivered or mailed, so serve termination and rent-increase notices on paper. Vermont's statutes do not regulate rent payment methods or portal convenience fees, but any fee you collect under the lease is rent. Offer a non-electronic way to pay and sign.

title: Agreements for Tenants to Make Repairs
bodyText: Vermont has no statute that lets you hand your repair and maintenance duties to a tenant by agreement, and no separate-writing or good-faith formality for such arrangements, whether the rental is a single-family house or an apartment. The limits run the other way. Any lease provision by which the tenant waives the warranty of habitability is void, any provision that attempts to circumvent the rental statute's obligations and remedies is void, and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code says a rental agreement purporting to transfer responsibilities between owner and occupant, other than as the Code itself assigns them, is not effective for code purposes. Unlike some states, Vermont has no exception for a tenant who accepts specified defects in exchange for reduced rent. A tenant may still agree to do specific work for pay or a rent credit, as long as you stay responsible for the result: if the work is not done properly, the habitability duty and the tenant's remedies remain. Put any work-for-rent arrangement in writing, describe the tasks, the credit and who supplies materials, and never make it a condition of the tenancy.

title: Tenant Repair Remedies
bodyText: A Vermont tenant facing a repair problem has statutory remedies a lease cannot waive, none available if the tenant or a person present with the tenant's consent caused the problem negligently or deliberately. Habitability: if you fail to comply with the warranty of habitability and, after actual notice from the tenant, a government agency or a qualified independent inspector, do not make repairs within a reasonable time, and the problem materially affects health and safety, the tenant may withhold rent for the period of noncompliance, get an injunction, recover damages, costs and attorney's fees, or end the rental agreement on reasonable notice. Minor defects: if you do not fix a minor defect needed to comply with the rental statute or a material lease provision within 30 days of notice, the tenant may repair it and deduct the actual, reasonable cost, up to half a month's rent, with actual notice of the cost. Municipal water and sewer included in rent may be kept on and deducted. A tenant may also ask the Division of Fire Safety to inspect; you then may not re-rent an affected unit until violations are fixed. Vermont has no repair-escrow program, and retaliation is barred.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Vermont protects tenants who organize through its anti-retaliation rule. You may not retaliate by establishing or changing the terms of a rental agreement, or by bringing or threatening to bring an action against a tenant, because the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organization. The same protection covers tenants who complain to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or who complain to you about a violation of the rental statute. A tenant who proves retaliation can recover damages and reasonable attorney's fees and has a defense to a retaliatory eviction. Separately, a termination notice for any reason other than unpaid rent served within 90 days after a municipal or state agency notifies you that the premises are out of compliance with health or safety rules is presumed retaliatory. Vermont's statutes do not give organizers a right to enter your building or require you to provide meeting space. Apply house rules on solicitation, flyers and common-room use evenly, and document legitimate reasons for any rent increase, nonrenewal or termination that follows organizing activity.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Vermont has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that you must give tenants, attach to a lease or have tenants sign, and no rule that you cannot sue until one is provided. The state's Rental Housing Advisory Board, staffed by the Department of Housing and Community Development, provides information and educational materials on rental housing statutes, rules and ordinances to landlords and tenants, but using them is voluntary. The documents Vermont does require are specific: the separate FEMA flood-hazard disclosure form before signing, the Department of Health-approved lead materials and your compliance statement for pre-1978 housing, and, in age-restricted housing, the state form for rent increases. If a Division of Fire Safety inspection finds violations, the report and any building-wide notice go to affected tenants. Giving tenants a short plain-language summary of key rules, such as entry notice, repair requests and deposit return, is good practice but not required; if you do, keep it accurate and current, because a misleading statement about tenants' rights can be an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: Tenant Screening Rules
bodyText: Vermont regulates screening through several separate rules rather than one screening statute. You may not charge any application fee. For a background or credit check you must accept unexpired government ID, an ITIN or a Social Security number, and may not require an SSN or reject an application for lacking one. You need the applicant's consent to obtain a credit report and may use it only for the purpose consented to. Screening criteria may not discriminate on any protected basis, including receipt of public assistance such as housing vouchers, immigration status, age, disability or having children; legitimate business practices such as references are allowed if not a pretext. A person whose criminal record has been sealed or expunged is treated as never arrested or convicted and may be asked only about unsealed records. Vermont has no conditional-offer or look-back rule for criminal history and no rule limiting income tests to the tenant's share, but income tests that screen out voucher holders invite a discrimination claim. If an applicant has a court order of limited relief or certificate of restoration of rights and you knew of it, it can be evidence of your due care if you are later sued for leasing to them.

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: Vermont has no general statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, so for most tenants your lease's alteration and installation rules govern, along with the tenant's duty not to damage the premises. One group of tenants has a statutory right: a tenant who is a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking may ask your permission to install additional security measures, such as a security system or security camera, at least seven days before installation, and you may not unreasonably refuse. That tenant pays to install and operate the equipment, must ensure its quality and safety, and is liable for damage from installation. Two privacy laws limit cameras for everyone, including you. No one may place a hidden or obscured camera or surveillance device on private property to watch a person or the property without the property owner's prior written consent (the law counts a person who leases or controls use of the land as an owner), with civil penalties. And recording another person's intimate areas, or secretly surveilling them, where they reasonably expect privacy is a crime. Set clear rules on placement, keep cameras out of other units' private spaces, and never install hidden cameras in a tenant's unit.

title: Tenants' Duties Under Vermont Law
bodyText: Vermont law puts these duties on every residential tenant, whether or not the lease repeats them. Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed. The tenant must not create or contribute to a violation of building, housing or health regulations; must behave, and require guests and others present with the tenant's consent to behave, so as not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment; and must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the premises, fixtures, systems or furnishings, or let anyone else do so. A violation of these duties entitles you to damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees and is a ground for termination on 30 days' notice. Under the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code, the occupant keeps the space the occupant exclusively occupies clean and free of trash and food scraps, exterminates infestations the occupant caused, and uses reasonable care so the unit does not become a hazard to neighbors. Without a written lease, a tenant who sublets must give you the sublessee's name and contact information in writing, and a tenant ends the tenancy by actual notice one rental period ahead unless the lease says otherwise.

title: Notice of Changes to Terms and Fees
bodyText: Vermont sets one notice rule for changes: a rent increase takes effect only on the first day of a rental period that follows at least 60 days' actual notice (written notice hand-delivered or mailed). Because anything the tenant must pay you under the rental agreement counts as rent, raising a fee the lease already provides, or adding a new recurring charge, is a rent increase and needs the same 60 days; there is no longer period for fees, and a lease cannot shorten the notice. Owners of private age-restricted housing must also give the state form notice. A fixed-term lease can be changed during the term only as the lease allows or by agreement. Vermont's statutes do not address changing other terms of a tenancy without a written lease, such as house rules, and do not treat such a change as a termination; to impose a new term over a tenant's objection, you would end the tenancy with the full no-cause notice (60 or 90 days for monthly rent) and offer a new one. You may not establish or change terms to retaliate against a tenant's code complaint, complaint about a rental-law violation, or tenants' union activity.

title: Termination Notice Periods
bodyText: Vermont sets every landlord notice period by statute, and a lease cannot shorten them. All notices must be actual notice (written, hand-delivered or mailed) and must state the specific termination date. Nonpayment: at least 14 days; the tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders rent due through the end of the rental period in which payment is made. Breach of a material lease term or statutory duty: at least 30 days, or 14 days for criminal activity, illegal drug activity or acts of violence, any of which threatens other residents' health or safety. No cause, no written lease: 60 days (monthly rent, tenancy two years or less), 90 days (longer), 21 days (weekly rent); 30 days if you have contracted to sell the building. No cause, written lease: at least 30 days before the end of the stated term (60 days if the tenancy has lasted more than two years); written week-to-week, 7 days. Rooms in your own home with shared living space: 15 days (monthly) or 7 days (weekly). A fixed term does not end your duty to give notice. You must file ejectment within 60 days after the stated date. Vermont has no elderly or disabled extension and no required payment-plan offer.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: Vermont's private-property towing statute covers only abandoned motor vehicles: a vehicle left without the consent of the owner or person in control of the property for more than 48 hours if it has a valid registration plate and intact public VIN, or for any time if it lacks a valid plate or VIN or a police officer has asked that it be towed. A landowner, which includes a person who owns, leases or otherwise controls the property (so a tenant may qualify for spaces the tenant controls), may move the vehicle elsewhere on its property or have a towing service remove it without civil liability, but must immediately notify the local police with the plate number, VIN if available, make, model and color, and apply to the Department of Motor Vehicles for an abandoned-vehicle certification within 90 days. The tow company may charge a reasonable fee to the vehicle owner or landowner. Vermont's statute sets no signage, written-authorization, rate-cap or kickback rule, and expressly does not preempt municipal abandoned-vehicle ordinances; towns may also authorize removal of vehicles parked without authorization on private lots. The person in charge of disability parking spaces must have violators removed. A tenant's car parked with your permission is not abandoned until that permission ends.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because Vermont has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law, there is nothing for a property to be exempt from at the state level, and no notice or lease statement telling tenants that a property is exempt. Several Vermont rules have their own exclusions that you apply without any notice: the residential rental statute does not apply to listed situations such as transient hotel occupancy, occupancy in institutions, campgrounds, mobile home lots (which have their own law) and certified recovery residences' exits; the fair housing rental rules do not apply to a building of three or fewer units where you or your family live (advertising rules still apply); the heat and hot-water warranty does not apply to summer or hunting-camp rentals; the age-restricted rent-increase form does not apply to monitored subsidized housing; and the lead-safe maintenance rules exclude certain units such as 0-bedroom units and housing for the elderly or disabled without young children. Some programs, such as the weatherization program, may ask a landlord to sign a rent stabilization agreement as a condition of aid; those are contract terms, not statewide rent limits. Check local ordinances.

title: No Rent Cap or Just Cause Notice
bodyText: Vermont has no statewide tenant protection act capping rent increases or requiring just cause for ending a tenancy, so there is no statutory lease notice telling tenants that such limits apply. What Vermont has instead: any rent increase takes effect only on the first day of a rental period after at least 60 days' actual notice; you may not raise rent or change terms to retaliate against a tenant who complained to a code agency or to you or joined a tenants' union; a termination notice other than for unpaid rent within 90 days after a government noncompliance notice is presumed retaliatory; ending a tenancy without cause requires the statutory notice (for example 60 or 90 days for a monthly tenancy without a written lease, or 30 or 60 days before the end of a written lease's term); and rent increases in private age-restricted housing need the state form notice. Rent limits can also come from program agreements, such as housing grants or weatherization aid, and from local charters or ordinances, which you should check.

title: No Sunset on Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Vermont's core landlord-tenant statutes, the residential rental agreements chapter and the ejectment chapter, carries a repeal or expiration date as of October 2026. The one dated repeal in the rental chapter, a special rule letting certified recovery residences immediately exit or transfer residents who violate their substance-use policy, was scheduled to end July 1, 2026; a 2026 law removed that sunset and revised the rule, which now also requires written notice to the resident and a grievance process. Recent changes run forward instead: from July 1, 2026, a lease may not ban tenants from possessing cannabis or using non-inhaled cannabis inside the unit, and since July 1, 2025 landlords may not charge application fees of any amount or require a Social Security number. Plan for current rules to stay in force, and check each year for new legislation, since Vermont amends its rental laws regularly.

title: No Translation Duty
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring you to translate a lease, notice or disclosure into another language, even if you advertise or negotiate in that language, and no verbatim lease text with type-size and translation rules. The translation provisions found in Vermont's statutes apply elsewhere, such as tax notices, driver testing and public outreach programs. Two rules still matter. Vermont's fair housing law bars discrimination because of national origin, citizenship or immigration status, so do not refuse to rent, or set different terms, because an applicant does not speak English well, and keep advertising neutral. And Vermont's standard-form contract statute and general unconscionability principles consider whether the individual had a meaningful opportunity to understand and negotiate the terms; a tenant who cannot read the language of the lease may later argue that a harsh term should not be enforced. The cautious course: if you negotiate in another language, offer a translated copy or summary, state which version controls, and make sure required notices such as the flood disclosure are explained.

title: No Truth in Renting Law
bodyText: Vermont has no Truth in Renting Act, no state booklet of tenant rights you must give or post, and no rule that the lease must state it complies with landlord-tenant law or that bars offering a lease containing terms that violate clearly established rights. Vermont reaches similar goals through other rules. Any lease provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies of the residential rental statute is unenforceable and void, and a waiver of the warranty of habitability is void. In a standard-form lease with an individual tenant, out-of-state venue, jury or class-action waivers, punitive-damage waivers, shortened limitation periods and excessive claim fees are presumed unconscionable, and a court that finds such a term unconscionable when you try to enforce it may award the tenant up to $1,000 per term plus costs and attorney's fees as an unfair and deceptive practice. Vermont's consumer protection act covers real estate transactions, so misleading lease terms or statements can bring damages and attorney's fees. Review your lease form against Vermont law and remove void terms rather than relying on a severability clause.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no rule requiring you to price parking separately from rent, to offer units without parking, or to let tenants opt out of a parking charge. Whether parking comes with the unit, and at what price, is a lease term. Any parking charge you collect under the lease is rent under Vermont's rental statute, so increasing it needs the same 60 days' actual notice as any rent increase, and a parking space you promise in the lease becomes part of the premises you must provide. Vermont's zoning law limits what towns may demand of developers: in districts served by municipal water and sewer that allow housing, a town may not require more than one parking space per dwelling unit (1.5 for duplexes and multiunit buildings in some areas without sewer and water or far from public parking), must cap the standard residential space size at 9 by 18 feet, and may count nonconforming spaces and spaces in nearby lots under agreement. Those rules shape how many spaces a building has, not how you charge for them. If you charge separately, describe the space and price in the lease.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Vermont has no police or sheriff removal of squatters on an owner's affidavit outside the courts, but it has three court routes and a trespass law. First, the rental statute does not apply to someone occupying a unit without right or permission who is not a tenant. If your written lease prohibits subleasing, you or the tenant may sue to eject such an occupant and move for immediate possession on an affidavit with a copy of the lease; the hearing can be held after 10 days' notice, and the sheriff may put you in possession no sooner than five days after serving the writ. Second, for someone who wrongfully holds possession without force and does not leave after a written demand, a wrongful-detainer complaint is available, with treble damages from the time of the notice to quit; it does not apply to a tenant holding over after a written lease. Third, ordinary ejectment. Unlawful trespass is a crime when a person enters or stays after notice against trespass is communicated by the person in lawful possession or police; entering a dwelling knowing one is not licensed to do so carries up to three years. A guest your tenant lawfully invited is not your trespasser to remove. Never change locks or remove belongings yourself.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Vermont has a statute aimed at unfair terms in standard-form contracts that reaches a form residential lease between a business landlord and an individual tenant who did not draft or meaningfully negotiate it. These terms are presumed substantively unconscionable: requiring claims to be resolved outside Vermont (a Vermont state or federal court is allowed), waiving the tenant's right to a jury trial or to join a class action, waiving punitive damages, shortening the time to sue or waiving the statute of limitations, and requiring the tenant to pay fees to bring a claim well above court filing costs. If a court finds a term illegal or unconscionable, it must refuse to enforce the whole lease or the offending part, or limit the term, and may weigh whether severing it would encourage drafters to keep using such terms. If you try to enforce one of the listed terms and the court finds it actually unconscionable, it may treat that as an unfair and deceptive practice and award up to $1,000 per term plus costs and attorney's fees. Other unfair terms are judged under general common-law principles. Vermont has no statute declaring any particular lease clause, such as an assistance-animal misrepresentation default, fully enforceable.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Vermont's rental statutes do not address interest on money a tenant owes, but general law sets the outer limit. Except as a specific statute provides otherwise, Vermont's legal rate of interest for the use or forbearance of money is 12% a year, and anyone who knowingly or willfully contracts for or collects more than legal interest risks civil liability for the excess plus attorney's fees and criminal penalties; the business-loan exceptions do not fit an ordinary residential lease. Vermont has no statute requiring an interest term to be stated in the lease before interest can be charged, and no statute making the legal rate depend on a written agreement; whether a court awards prejudgment interest on a tenant's debt is governed by court practice and case law, which were not searched. Interest on a judgment lien accrues at 12%. Remember that anything payable to you under the lease is rent under Vermont's definition, and in a nonpayment case the tenant can stop the eviction once a year by paying rent due plus interest and costs into court. If you want interest on unpaid damages, state a simple rate of no more than 12% in the lease and start it only after a written itemized demand.

title: Utilities You Pay
bodyText: If the lease makes you responsible for a utility, Vermont law holds you to it. A lease promise to provide a service is enforceable through the tenant's repair-and-deduct and habitability remedies, and if heat is included you must supply a reasonable amount at all times. You may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service supplied to the tenant, except temporarily for emergency repairs, and the housing code bars shutting off required water, sewer or utilities except during repairs or emergencies; letting an account in your name go unpaid until service is cut can violate both. For municipal water and sewer, the municipality must send the occupant a copy of any disconnection notice; the tenant may then pay to keep service on or reconnect, and if water and sewer are included in rent, deduct those payments from rent, owing no more than one billing cycle of your arrears. Unpaid municipal water and sewer charges are also a lien on your property. Rules for electric and gas accounts in a landlord's name are set by the Public Utility Commission and were not reviewed here. List in the lease each utility you pay.

title: Tenant Utility Accounts
bodyText: Vermont lets the lease make the tenant responsible for arranging and paying utilities to the unit, with limits. You cannot use the lease to shift code-required owner duties: the housing code says no rental agreement transferring responsibilities between owner and occupant is effective for code purposes, so a tenant-paid account should not leave the unit without required heat, water or sewer. For municipal water, the owner or occupant who takes the water is liable for the charges; sewer charges are the property owner's liability; and unpaid water and sewer charges are a lien on the real estate like property taxes, enforceable through tax collection, whoever's name is on the account; no lease clause or affidavit defeats the lien. Unpaid sewer assessments can go to the tax collector after 30 days. If a tenant fails to pay a utility the lease requires, that can be a breach of a material term supporting a 30-day termination notice, and the deposit may cover utility charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you or to a utility. Whether a utility may refuse service to a new tenant over a former occupant's bill is governed by Public Utility Commission rules, not reviewed here. Require proof of payment and check municipal accounts.

title: Utility Allowances
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing about utility allowances, where you pay a utility up to a set amount and the tenant reimburses the overage, and nothing in them bars or regulates passing a master-metered utility through to tenants. The Public Utility Commission's rules have no rule on landlords reselling or re-billing electricity or gas from a master meter; the only submetering rule covers campgrounds. A company that sells electricity or gas directly to the public falls under the Commission's jurisdiction, and whether a landlord who re-bills metered usage counts is not settled by the statutes or rules (no court decisions were searched), so get regulatory advice before billing tenants for metered usage. If you use an allowance, Vermont's general rules apply. Anything the tenant must pay you under the lease is rent, so an overage charge is rent; raising the allowance terms or adding a new overage charge is a rent increase needing 60 days' actual notice. Your deposit may cover utility charges the tenant was required to pay to you. You may not interrupt a utility to collect an overage. Keep the allowance limited to the tenant's own unit, give the tenant copies of the bills used to compute any overage, and state the method, the allowance amount and the payment deadline in the lease.

title: Shared and Common-Area Utilities
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not make unenforceable a lease term requiring a tenant to pay for utilities that are not separately metered to the unit, and they set no rule for splitting a shared meter's cost among tenants. Related rules limit how far a lease can go. The housing code makes the owner responsible for keeping common areas clean and lighted and for required facilities, and says a rental agreement transferring responsibilities between owner and occupant is not effective for code purposes, so do not make one tenant pay for hallway lighting, a shared boiler or other common-area service as if it were the tenant's own. Anything a tenant pays you under the lease is rent. You may not willfully interrupt a tenant's utility service. Whether the Public Utility Commission's rules restrict billing tenants for a shared or master-metered utility was not reviewed here. The cautious course: put each unit on its own meter where you can; if a tenant's meter also serves space outside the unit, tell the tenant in writing before signing, describe exactly what it serves, and give a stated rent reduction or other fair credit that approximates the extra cost.

title: Utility Deposits Held by a Landlord
bodyText: Vermont has no separate rule for a utility deposit that a landlord holds. If you collect an advance or deposit that is refundable at the end of the tenancy to secure a tenant's payment of utility charges, it is a security deposit under Vermont's definition, which covers any advance, deposit or prepaid rent however named. You may keep it only for the permitted purposes, which include unpaid utility or other charges the tenant was required to pay directly to you or to a utility, and you must return it with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates (60 days for a seasonal non-primary residence), or forfeit the right to keep any of it; willful failure costs double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. There is no statewide cap or interest requirement, though some towns' deposit ordinances may require interest. Deposits that utility companies themselves hold are governed by Public Utility Commission rules, which must set a reasonable interest rate on them. Fold any landlord-held utility deposit into your security deposit accounting.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Vermont has no required utility disclosure that must be attached to a lease when you apportion shared-meter costs, no water submeter certificate, and no notice of energy-improvement charges on a tenant's utility bill. Vermont's required pre-lease disclosures are the separate FEMA flood-hazard form and, for pre-1978 housing, the lead materials and compliance statement. One utility-related lease clause is permitted rather than required: if you own a multiunit building and want aggregated, anonymized energy usage data for benchmarking or an energy label, a building with fewer than four unit holders needs each unit holder's release authorization, which may be a clause in a lease the tenant signs; for four or more, you instead notify each unit holder at least 14 days ahead with a chance to opt out. If a tenant pays you for any utility, anything payable under the lease is rent, so list each charge and how it is calculated in the lease. Telling tenants in writing which utilities they pay, and roughly what they cost, avoids disputes.

title: No Right to Cut Off Utilities You Bill
bodyText: Vermont has no regime letting a landlord who submeters, allocates or resells electricity, gas or water to a tenant cut off service when the tenant does not pay. The opposite rule applies: no landlord may willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service being supplied to the tenant, except for temporary interruptions for emergency repairs, and the housing code bars shutting off required water, sewer, equipment or utilities except during repairs or emergencies. A tenant who suffers an illegal utility cutoff can sue for an injunction, damages, costs and attorney's fees. Vermont's statutes do not authorize landlord submetering of electricity at all (the only express submetering permission is for recreational campgrounds), and Public Utility Commission rules on resale were not reviewed. If a tenant does not pay utility charges owed to you under the lease, your remedies are the ordinary ones: the charge is rent, so you may give a 14-day nonpayment notice or sue, and the deposit may cover unpaid utility charges at move-out. Never shut off, disconnect or reduce service yourself.

title: Unpaid Utilities in Your Name
bodyText: When a utility account for a tenant's home is in your name and goes unpaid, Vermont law protects the tenant. Letting service be cut off can be an illegal eviction: no landlord may willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service supplied to the tenant, except temporarily for emergency repairs, and the tenant may sue for an injunction, damages, costs and attorney's fees. For municipal water and sewer, the municipality must send a copy of any disconnection notice to the occupant if different from the ratepayer; the tenant may request and pay for continued service or reconnection, which the utility must provide, and if water and sewer are included in rent, may deduct those payments from rent, with the utility unable to demand more than one billing cycle of your arrears. Unpaid charges are a lien on your property. Vermont has no rent-receivership remedy for unpaid utilities. Rules on electric and gas shutoffs for landlord-held accounts, including any notice to each unit before a building-wide shutoff, are set by the Public Utility Commission and were not reviewed here. Keep accounts in your name current.

title: Keeping Utilities On
bodyText: Vermont law bars you, not the tenant, from cutting off utilities: no landlord may willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service supplied to the tenant, except for temporary interruptions for emergency repairs, and the housing code bars shutting off required water, sewer, equipment or utilities except during repairs or emergencies. A tenant harmed by an illegal cutoff may sue for an injunction, damages, costs and attorney's fees. No statute imposes a general duty on the tenant to keep the tenant's own utility accounts paid, but the lease may require it, as the library's clause does, and the tenant must not cause a code violation; a tenant's failure to keep required service on can be a breach of a material term supporting a 30-day termination notice. If municipal water or sewer is about to be disconnected for the owner's unpaid bill, the tenant may pay to keep it on and, where those charges are in the rent, deduct the cost. During a declared state of emergency for an event causing financial hardship, water and sewer providers may not disconnect anyone, and customers get at least 90 days after it ends to pay.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Vermont's utility shutoff protections come from several sources. For electric, gas and other regulated utilities, the statute requires the Public Utility Commission to adopt rules on the grounds and procedures for disconnecting and reconnecting customers, aimed at protecting customers' health and safety so service can continue on reasonable terms; those rules, including any winter protections, were not reviewed here. For municipal water and sewer, the statute itself sets the protections: a bill is delinquent only after 30 days; the pink statutory notice must be sent 14 to 20 days before disconnection, with a copy to a tenant-occupant; disconnection is barred for small balances of $15 or less, disputed amounts on appeal, nonrecurring charges, a physician-certified serious health hazard, or while the customer keeps a reasonable payment agreement; shutoffs occur only between 8:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m. on business days; and service must be restored within 24 hours once the cause is removed. During a declared emergency causing financial hardship, water and sewer providers may not disconnect anyone. Propane sellers follow Attorney General rules on notice before disconnection. You may never cut off a tenant's utilities yourself.

title: Submetering and Utility Billing
