bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no submetering, ratio (RUBS) billing or other landlord utility-billing regime for residential tenants: no prescribed lease disclosure, type-size rule, billing cap, late-fee cap, building-size threshold or mid-term opt-in procedure. The only express statutory permission to submeter electricity is for recreational campgrounds, on a nonprofit basis under Public Utility Commission rules, and electric service is organized by Commission-set service territories. The Commission's rules don't address landlord resale or re-billing of electricity, gas or water either: its only submetering rule covers campgrounds, and its disconnection rule calls for individual meters for the units of a master-metered building, where possible, when the landlord's service is being shut off. A company that sells electricity or gas directly to the public, and a water company other than a municipality or an exempt system, falls under the Commission's jurisdiction; whether a landlord billing tenants for utilities counts is not settled by the statutes or rules, and no court decisions were searched. Get regulatory advice before billing tenants from submeters or by formula. If you do bill utilities, Vermont's landlord-tenant rules apply: anything payable to you under the lease is rent, so new or increased charges need 60 days' actual notice; your deposit may cover utility charges the tenant was required to pay to you; and you may never interrupt a tenant's service to collect. Describe any billing method, meter and charge in the lease, and give tenants the bills behind each charge.

title: No Utility Cutoff to Force Transfer
bodyText: Vermont does not allow a landlord to cut off a utility in the landlord's name because the tenant has not transferred the account into the tenant's name, and no statute provides an opt-in lease procedure for doing so. No landlord may willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service being supplied to the tenant, except temporarily for emergency repairs, and the housing code bars shutting off required water, sewer or utilities except during repairs or emergencies; a tenant can sue for an injunction, damages, costs and attorney's fees. If the lease requires the tenant to put a utility in the tenant's name and the tenant does not, your remedies are contractual: the cost of service you keep paying can be billed to the tenant as a charge under the lease (which counts as rent), a persistent failure may be a breach of a material term supporting a 30-day termination notice, and the deposit can cover utility charges the tenant was required to pay to you. Utility rules on closing a landlord account while a tenant is in possession are set by the Public Utility Commission and were not reviewed. Put the transfer deadline and the reimbursement method in the lease.

title: Utility Disconnection Notices to Owners
bodyText: Vermont's statutes don't address this, but the Public Utility Commission's disconnection rule does for the gas, electric and water utilities the Commission regulates. A utility must notify the owner of a residential rental when service there has been disconnected, even if the tenant is the customer, as long as you have given the utility your contact information; keeping it current is your job. The utility must tell you once by phone, text or email before 3:00 p.m. on the day of disconnection. If you ask for it, the utility must also send a follow-up written notice within two business days naming whom to contact, explaining how the Department of Public Service can help, and listing the fees and any deposit needed to restore service; it may charge a reasonable fee for that follow-up. You may name a property manager or other representative to receive the notices, and the utility may ask for proof of ownership, such as a deed or tax bill. This is notice of a disconnection that has happened, not a warning of a pending one. It may not include the tenant's name, phone number, account number, usage or payment history, beyond what is needed to restore service, and the utility may not give you the tenant's account information without the tenant's consent. When you are the customer and your account is to be disconnected, the utility must give your tenants notice first and offer them service in their own names. For municipal water and sewer, a separate statute applies: when the ratepayer is not the occupant, the municipality must send the occupant a copy of the disconnection notice, and the occupant may pay to keep service on. Because unpaid municipal water and sewer charges become a lien on the property whoever's name is on the account, ask your town's water and sewer office how it handles owner inquiries and notices, require tenants in the lease to give you proof of payment on request, and consider keeping water and sewer in your own name and including them in rent. Never interrupt a tenant's service yourself.

title: Veterans Housing Incentives
bodyText: Vermont has no tax credit or other statutory incentive for landlords who rent to veterans, and veteran status is not a listed protected class in Vermont's fair housing law (though Vermont protects many related traits, such as disability). Vermont does fund programs that can help veteran tenants pay rent. The Vermont Veterans' Fund, administered by the Military Department, makes grants to individuals and organizations, including to aid homeless veterans; the Office of Veterans' Affairs disburses aid to veterans in need and their dependents under criteria set by the Adjutant General, for applicants not better served by other programs; and the Vermont Veterans' Home board may provide or coordinate housing for veterans who do not live at the Home, including through contracts with private entities. Low-income veterans also receive a small refundable state income tax credit, which goes to the veteran, not the landlord. If a veteran applicant or tenant is struggling with rent, point them to the Office of Veterans' Affairs; government assistance counts as public assistance, and you may not treat a recipient differently.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: Vermont has specific rules on taking money after a termination notice. For a nonpayment notice, accepting a partial payment does not waive your remedies or create an accord and satisfaction, but the tenancy does not end if the tenant pays or tenders all rent due through the end of the rental period in which the payment is made, so a full payment before the termination date cures the default. For a termination based on breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, or a no-cause termination, accepting full or partial rent from or on behalf of the tenant after the tenancy has ended, or at any time during the eviction case, does not dismiss the case or waive your right to proceed. After you file for nonpayment, the tenant can still end the case once in any 12 months by paying into court all rent due through the end of the current rental period, with interest and costs, before the writ is executed. You may serve multiple notices on different grounds without one invalidating another. Give receipts that describe payments after termination as use and occupancy, and file within 60 days after the termination date.

title: Hot Water Temperature
bodyText: Vermont has no rule requiring you to reset a unit's water heater to a set temperature before each new tenant moves in, but the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code sets a temperature range at the tap. Every kitchen sink, lavatory sink, shower and tub-shower combination must be connected to working water-heating facilities capable of safely heating an adequate amount of water, and showers and tub-showers must be plumbed so the hot water reaches at least 100°F and stays below 120°F at the fixture. The rental statute separately requires hot water lines connected to water-heating facilities capable of heating enough water for an adequate amount to be drawn (summer and hunting-camp rentals are exempt from that statutory part). Vermont's plumbing rules may not require a water heater to be kept at a minimum temperature. In practice, set tank temperatures, or install anti-scald or mixing valves, so showers and tubs deliver water in the 100°F to under 120°F range, check it at each turnover, and tell tenants not to raise the setting. A violation can bring a state inspection report and penalties.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Vermont's statutes say nothing about waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: no right to have one, no ban you may impose or must follow, and no insurance or deposit rule tied to one. A lease may therefore prohibit waterbeds or allow them on conditions, such as proof of renter's liability insurance covering water damage, a liner, installation to the manufacturer's specifications and your approval of the location where floor loading is a concern. General Vermont rules still apply. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises and is liable for damages, costs and reasonable attorney's fees if that happens, and you may deduct from the security deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear. Any extra deposit you require for a waterbed is part of the security deposit and follows the 14-day return rule, and any extra monthly charge counts as rent. Apply the rule the same way to all tenants, and consider a disability accommodation request, such as for a therapeutic flotation mattress, on its merits.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes and the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code have no window-guard or window-stop requirement for units where young children live, no bold lease notice about window guards and no model text. The Code's window rules run the other way: every habitable room must have at least one window or door on an outside wall, in good repair, that can be opened for fresh air, and screens must be provided for operable windows. Any guard or stop you install should therefore not prevent the window from opening for ventilation, and should not block a window needed for emergency escape under the fire code (not reviewed here). In pre-1978 rental housing, windows and their trim are covered by Vermont's lead law, so work that disturbs old window paint must follow lead-safe practices. If a tenant with young children asks for window stops or guards, consider installing removable or openable devices, document what you install, and keep them in repair. The cautious course is to ask at move-in whether children under 10 will live in the unit and offer window safety devices.

title: Notices That Must Be Written
bodyText: Many Vermont notices must be written, and a lease cannot downgrade them because provisions that circumvent the rental statute are void. Actual notice, which the statute requires for most landlord-tenant notices, means written notice hand-delivered or mailed to the last known address (presumed received three days after first-class or certified mailing). Actual notice is required for: every termination notice from you, stating the termination date; a rent increase (60 days); a tenant's notice ending a tenancy without a written lease term to the contrary; the tenant's notice of a habitability problem before withholding or other remedies; and the tenant's notice of a repair-and-deduct cost. Other required writings: the itemized deposit statement; notice before disposing of an abandoned tenant's property; a sublessee's name and contact information when required; a protected tenant's termination notice and documentation; the separate flood disclosure; lead materials before the lease; and age-restricted rent-increase forms. Entry notice must be at least 48 hours but the statute does not require writing. Do not rely on email for eviction-related notices: Vermont's electronic transactions law excludes notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence.

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Charges
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require a separate written notice when part of what a tenant pays upfront is nonrefundable. The definition does the work instead: any advance, deposit or prepaid rent that is refundable at the end of the tenancy, whatever you call it, is a security deposit and follows Vermont's 14-day return rules. A charge that is truly not refundable is not a security deposit, and because Vermont defines rent as all consideration paid to you under the rental agreement, it counts as rent. You may not charge any application fee at all. Put any nonrefundable charge, its amount and what it pays for in the written lease before signing, and do not label part of a refundable deposit as nonrefundable.

title: No Parking Rules Notice Requirement
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, prescribe a heading for them, limit changes to them during the term, limit the vehicle information you may ask for, or tie a parking permit to the lease term. Two rules still shape parking. A parking charge you collect under the lease is rent, so adding or raising one during a tenancy is a rent increase that needs 60 days' actual notice. And you may remove a vehicle from private property only when it has been left there without the consent of the person in control of the property, after 48 hours if it has a valid plate, and you must notify the police immediately. Put your parking rules in or with the lease from the start.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any pet-specific notice, when you know the tenant has a dog or cat. Related rules still apply. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit, and pet rent is rent, so both follow the ordinary deposit and rent-increase rules. You may not take a tenant's pet or other property without going through court, and you may enter only for the purposes and on the notice Vermont's entry statute allows. An assistance animal a tenant needs because of a disability is a reasonable-accommodation question, not a pet question.

title: No Plain-Language Consumer Statement Rule
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers or restrictions, and no Attorney General preapproval. Two consumer rules still reach leases. An automatic-renewal term for a lease of a year or longer must be stated clearly and conspicuously, in plain, unambiguous language in bold-face type, with a separate opt-in. And when a business landlord uses a standard-form lease with an individual tenant, certain terms are presumed unconscionable, including a jury or class-action waiver, a punitive-damages waiver, an out-of-state venue and a shortened time to sue. Keep the lease clear and leave those terms out.

title: No Small-Building Exemption Notice
bodyText: Vermont has no small-building or owner-occupied exemption from a tenant's habitability remedies (withholding rent, repair and deduct) or from the security deposit rules, so there is no notice to give a tenant about one. Vermont's rental statute leaves out certain kinds of occupancy instead, such as institutions, transient hotel stays, campgrounds and mobile home lots in parks, not buildings by size. The one size-based exemption is in fair housing: a building of three or fewer units where you or an immediate family member live is exempt from the rental discrimination rules, but your advertising must still not show a discriminatory preference. Vermont also has no tenant-initiated rent escrow; rent into court is a motion you may file in an eviction case.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules
bodyText: Vermont's statutes have no casualty rule and no stated duty to mitigate damages for a lease to waive or keep. What a lease may not take away: the warranty of habitability and the tenant's remedies when the unit is unfit, which cannot be waived, and the rule that a tenant who abandons stops owing rent once you re-rent the unit, because a lease may not circumvent the rental statute's obligations and remedies. So a lease may set what happens after a fire (the library's optional Fire or Casualty clause does), but it may not take away the tenant's statutory right to withhold rent, recover damages or end the lease when a condition the tenant did not cause materially affects health and safety and you fail to repair within a reasonable time after actual notice, and it may not make a departed tenant pay rent for a period when someone else is renting the unit.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month After a Lease
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not say which no-cause notice applies when a written lease term ends and the tenant stays on month to month, or when the written lease is itself month to month. The statute has two tracks. With a written rental agreement, notice must be given at least 30 days before the end or expiration of the stated term (60 days if the tenancy has lasted more than two years). With no written rental agreement and monthly rent, the termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice (90 days if the tenant has lived there more than two years). A lease that continues month to month on the same terms keeps a written agreement in place, but what counts as the stated term of a month-to-month continuation is not settled by the statute. The cautious course is a notice that satisfies both tracks: actual notice (hand-delivered or mailed) giving at least 60 days (90 days after two years' residence), with a stated termination date on the last day of a rental period. File any ejectment within 60 days after that date. Burlington's charter authorizes longer local notice periods; check local ordinances.

title: Deposits When One Roommate Leaves
bodyText: Vermont's statutes do not say what happens to a security deposit when one of several co-tenants moves out and the others stay. The deposit statute defines a security deposit as money refundable to the tenant at the termination or expiration of the tenancy, and starts the 14-day return clock when the tenant vacates or abandons the unit; it does not address a partial departure, divide a joint deposit among co-tenants, or require a refund to a departing roommate while the tenancy continues. Because missing the 14-day deadline forfeits your right to keep any part of the deposit and willful withholding costs double, do not leave the question open. When a roommate leaves, get a short written agreement signed by all tenants saying whether the deposit stays with the continuing tenancy (with the departing tenant settling up privately with the others) or what part you will refund now, and update the lease or add the replacement roommate in writing. Absent such an agreement, the cautious course is to return the deposit with an itemized statement at the end of the tenancy, payable to all tenants on the lease, by hand delivery or mail to their last known addresses.

title: Farm Employee Housing
bodyText: Vermont has a special court process for housing a farm provides to an employee as a benefit of the job. It applies when a farm employer, one earning at least half of its annual gross income from farming, provides housing it owns or controls to a farm employee and the employee's household for no payment other than the employee's labor; the employee paying utility and fuel charges does not change that. Unless a written employment contract says otherwise, the employer may end the housing benefit when the employment ends, but only through court: a law enforcement officer must serve the former employee with a written notice in the statute's bold-face wording together with a summons and complaint for a writ of possession. The court holds an expedited show-cause hearing at least 10 days after service; if the employer proves actual hardship because the housing is needed for a replacement employee, the writ is executed no sooner than five business days and no later than 30 days after service. Otherwise the employer uses ordinary termination and ejectment. The rent-increase, security-deposit and termination-notice sections do not apply to this housing. If the employee pays rent, the ordinary rental rules apply. Fire-safety and housing-code rules still cover it.

title: Certified Recovery Residences
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute covers a certified recovery residence, a shared home supporting people recovering from substance use disorder that is certified by an organization approved by the Department of Health, but gives it one exception. Notwithstanding the 30-day breach notice, the action-for-possession requirement and the ban on denying a resident access, the residence may immediately exit or transfer a resident only if every condition is met: a written residential agreement with an approved exit and transfer policy (bed-hold time, return criteria, and possessions held at least 60 days after a permanent removal), program rules, alternative housing arrangements, a substance use policy exempting prescribed medication, and the resident's acknowledgment; the resident's written consent, reaffirmed after seven days; conduct that affected the health or safety of others at the residence, such as violating the substance use policy, repeatedly refusing services, a criminal charge, theft, interfering with others' recovery or violence; a re-engagement bed or other temporary housing; written or electronic notice of the date, reason and options to return; and an approved grievance process. Staff may enter at reasonable times for operations. A 2026 law made the rule permanent and broadened it from July 1, 2026. Ordinary landlords cannot use it.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Vermont Leases: Why the Library Does Not Offer One
bodyText: Vermont's arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, but only if the parties also sign a prominently displayed "Acknowledgment of Arbitration" in the form the statute sets out (12 V.S.A. § 5652). A right to a lawyer cannot be waived in advance, and no arbitration agreement can stop anyone from going to court over constitutional or civil rights (§§ 5653(b), 5655). Two other laws matter for leases. Your lease may not contain any provision that attempts to circumvent the rental chapter's obligations and remedies (9 V.S.A. § 4454). In a standard-form lease that an individual tenant couldn't negotiate, a waiver of the tenant's right to a jury trial or to bring a class action is presumed unconscionable. If you try to enforce one and a court finds it unconscionable, it may treat that as an unfair and deceptive practice and award up to $1,000 per term plus attorney's fees (§ 6055). An arbitration clause gives up a jury. Federal arbitration law may override some of these rules, but because Vermont attaches money damages to enforcing such a term, the library does not offer an arbitration clause for Vermont. Vermont case law was not reviewed.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Vermont follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (9A V.S.A. § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (9A V.S.A. § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. Vermont adds two rules of its own. For rent, accepting a partial payment is neither a waiver of your remedies for nonpayment nor an accord and satisfaction for nonpayment of rent (9 V.S.A. § 4467(a)); that rule does not mention checks marked paid in full, so the cautious course below still applies. And the uniform rule does not apply to residential security deposits (9A V.S.A. § 3-311(e)), so a tenant who cashes your deposit-return check marked as full settlement has not given up a claim to the rest of the deposit. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Vermont's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (9 V.S.A. ch. 137 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Vermont's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Showing Notice Cannot Be Shortened by the Lease in Vermont
bodyText: Vermont lets you enter to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees or tenants between 9:00 A.M. and 9:00 P.M. on no less than 48 hours' notice (9 V.S.A. § 4460(b)(4)). No rental agreement may contain a provision that attempts to circumvent the obligations and remedies of the rental statute, and any such provision is unenforceable and void (9 V.S.A. § 4454). So a lease term or addendum shortening or waiving the 48-hour notice for showings is void, and Vermont has no separate-document or buyers-only exception. You may still enter with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold (9 V.S.A. § 4460(a)). Cautious course: give 48 hours' notice for every showing; if a tenant agrees to a particular showing on shorter notice, get that agreement in writing for that showing rather than relying on a lease term.

title: No Carpet Cleaning Rule
bodyText: Vermont has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing lets you require professional carpet cleaning as a matter of law, nothing conditions such a requirement on the carpets having been professionally cleaned before the tenancy, and there is no age or depreciation test for carpet or paint. The deposit rule is general: you may keep all or part of the deposit for damage to your property, unless the damage is the result of normal wear and tear or of actions or events beyond the tenant's control (9 V.S.A. § 4461(b)(2)). You may also keep it for unpaid rent, unpaid utility or other charges the tenant had to pay, and the expense of removing articles the tenant abandoned (9 V.S.A. § 4461(b)). You must return the deposit with a written statement itemizing any deductions within 14 days (60 days for a seasonal unit that is not a primary residence) (9 V.S.A. § 4461(c)). Any lease term that tries to get around these rules is void (9 V.S.A. § 4454). Cautious course: charge for carpet cleaning only where the carpet is dirtier or more damaged than normal wear would leave it, document its condition at move-in and move-out with photos, and itemize the cost.

title: Renting to Students in Vermont
bodyText: Vermont has no student-housing licence, certification or special rent, deposit or termination rule; a student renting a private apartment or house is an ordinary tenant under the rental statute. The student-housing rules are exclusions, not duties. Unless the arrangement is created to avoid the statute, it does not apply to occupancy at a public or private institution operated for the purpose of providing educational or similar services (9 V.S.A. § 4452(a)(1)). It also does not apply to occupancy by a member of a fraternal, social or religious organization in the portion of a building operated for the benefit of the organization (9 V.S.A. § 4452(a)(3)). So a college's own residence hall and a fraternity or sorority house fall outside the statute, but a privately owned building rented to students, including by the bed, is covered in full. Because of the 'created to avoid' qualifier, you cannot take an ordinary student rental outside the statute by calling it a dormitory.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: Vermont has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give a housed employee a signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating conditions or to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. An employee who pays rent is an ordinary tenant under the rental statute. The one special rule is for farms: a farm employer, one earning at least half its annual gross income from farming, that provides housing to a farm employee and household for no payment other than the employee's labor may end that housing benefit when the employment ends, unless a written employment contract says otherwise (9 V.S.A. § 4469a(a)-(b)). It must do so through court, by written notice served by a law enforcement officer with a summons and complaint for a writ of possession, using the statute's boldface wording (9 V.S.A. § 4469a(c)). If the employer proves at an expedited hearing that it suffers actual hardship because the housing is needed for a replacement employee, the writ is executed no earlier than five business days and no later than 30 days after service; otherwise it must use the ordinary termination and eviction process (9 V.S.A. § 4469a(d)-(f)). See `edu-farm-employee-housing-vt` for the details. For any other resident manager or caretaker, put the housing terms in a written lease and use the ordinary notice and eviction rules when the job ends.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Six Years
bodyText: Vermont's rental statute sets no special deadline for a landlord's suit against a former tenant, so the general limitation statute applies. A civil action, including a suit for unpaid rent, lease charges or damage to the unit, must be commenced within six years after the cause of action accrues (12 V.S.A. § 511). Actions on specialties, such as sealed instruments, may be brought within eight years (12 V.S.A. § 507), but whether a residential lease counts as one is case law this library has not reviewed, so treat six years as your deadline. A claim for damage to personal property, such as furniture you supplied, has a three-year limit (12 V.S.A. § 512(5)). An acknowledgment or promise to pay affects the deadline only if it is in writing signed by the tenant (12 V.S.A. § 591). A part payment keeps whatever effect it has under the case law, but your own note of the payment is not enough proof of it unless it is in the tenant's handwriting (12 V.S.A. § 592). If the former tenant moves out of Vermont before the deadline runs and has no known property in Vermont that could be attached, the time of absence is not counted (12 V.S.A. § 552). For a periodic tenancy, count the six years separately for each unpaid installment from the date it fell due.

title: Recording a Vermont Lease Is Optional
bodyText: Vermont has no lease registry and does not require you to record an ordinary residential lease. Recording matters for long leases: a lease for more than one year from the making of it is not effective against anyone but you and your heirs, such as a later buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded (27 V.S.A. § 342). Between you and the tenant an unrecorded lease still binds. Instead of recording the whole lease, you may record in the town land records a notice or memorandum of lease, signed and acknowledged before a notary, giving the parties' names and addresses, any renewal or extension rights, the date the lease was signed, the term with its start and end dates, the property description and any purchase option or right of first refusal (27 V.S.A. § 341(a), (c)). Nothing in Vermont's rental statute turns on whether a lease was recorded. Record a notice of lease if the term runs past a year and the tenant needs protection against a later buyer or lender, or holds a purchase option.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Vermont)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Vermont property law does not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise here. The closest Vermont interest is a life estate, for example a parent who deeded the home to the children but kept a life estate. Vermont law says that a conveyance by a tenant for life that purports to grant a greater estate than the life tenant could lawfully convey does not forfeit the life estate but passes only the estate the life tenant could lawfully convey (27 V.S.A. § 3). So a lease signed by a life tenant generally cannot bind the remainder owners after the life estate ends; what happens to the tenant then is case law this library has not reviewed. One exception: under an enhanced life estate deed the grantor keeps the right to convey, which includes the right to lease, during the grantor's lifetime (27 V.S.A. § 653). The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign or agree in writing that the lease continues if your life estate ends first.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property in Vermont
bodyText: Vermont's unlawful trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. It is a crime, punishable by up to three months in jail or a $500 fine, to enter or remain on land or in a place without legal authority or the consent of the person in lawful possession after notice against trespass is given by actual communication from the person in lawful possession, that person's agent or a police officer acting for them, or by signs designed and placed to give reasonable notice (13 V.S.A. § 3705(a)(1)). A prosecution must be started within 60 days after the offense (13 V.S.A. § 3705(b)), so report a violation promptly. Because the test is the consent of the person in lawful possession, you control the common areas you keep, while your tenant is in lawful possession of the unit itself and decides who may visit there. So give the person a written no-trespass notice covering the common areas, deliver it in person or through the police, keep a dated copy, and tell the police; deal with a problem guest of a tenant through the lease and the rental statute's termination rules, not a trespass notice alone.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Vermont has no statute deciding whether you or your tenant holds the hunting and fishing rights on rented land or farmland, so the lease decides. Several Vermont rules treat the occupant like the owner. A person may post a safety zone within 500 feet of an occupied dwelling or farm building on land owned or occupied by him or her, and no one may shoot within it without advance permission of the owner or occupant (10 V.S.A. § 4710(a)). The youth hunting weekends require permission of the owner or occupant to hunt on private land (10 V.S.A. chapter 113). Land may be posted against hunting, fishing or trapping, or as by permission only, by an owner or a person having the exclusive right to take game on it, and the posting must be recorded with the town clerk every year to stay enforceable (10 V.S.A. § 5201(a), (c)). So if you rent a home with land and want to keep the hunting and fishing rights, or let others hunt, say so in the lease, describe where and when, and state that you, not the tenant, will post and record the land; if the tenant is to have the rights, grant them in writing with any limits.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Vermont does not require you to give a residential tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. No Vermont statute directs a state agency to prepare such a guide for tenants or requires a lease to carry a summary of the rental statute, and Vermont's fair housing chapter sets no brochure or poster duty for rentals. Vermont instead requires specific notices, such as at least 60 days' actual notice before a rent increase takes effect (9 V.S.A. § 4455(b)) and the termination notices the rental statute prescribes. Because a lease term cannot circumvent the rental statute (9 V.S.A. § 4454), a plain-language guide you hand out is useful but changes nothing the statute requires.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Vermont Lease
bodyText: No Vermont statute requires a residential lease to state that the property is inside a special district, such as a fire district or other municipal district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, rules or plans. We found no statute that passes district taxes or charges to a tenant; they reach the tenant only if the lease shifts them. If you want the tenant to pay a district charge, say so plainly in the lease at the start; a later increase in what the tenant pays you is a rent increase that needs at least 60 days' actual notice (9 V.S.A. § 4455(b)), and a lease term that tries to get around the rental statute is void (9 V.S.A. § 4454).

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Vermont Lease
bodyText: Vermont has nothing like the territorial communal-land schemes. No Vermont statute requires a lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land to be approved by a government officer before it is valid. Vermont recognizes Abenaki tribes, but its findings state that recognition does not create any basis for tribes to claim any interest in land or real estate in Vermont, and that state-recognized tribes and their members remain subject to all state laws (1 V.S.A. § 851(8)). More broadly, no Vermont statute conditions a residential lease's validity on government approval; the only filing rule is recording, which makes a lease of more than one year effective against later buyers and lenders (27 V.S.A. § 342), and between you and the tenant an unrecorded lease still binds. Land held in trust by the United States for a tribe would be governed by federal and tribal law, outside this library.
